subtopic_detail: Severe HTN antihypertensive choice
stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks presents to birth suite with a headache and epigastric pain. She has been reviewed weekly for suspected pre-eclampsia and is on labetalol 200 mg orally three times daily. On arrival her observations are recorded as shown.

On examination her reflexes are brisk with no clonus, urinalysis shows 3+ protein, and CTG shows a normal fetal heart rate trace with reactive baseline. Airway is patent, breath sounds are clear, and no peripheral oedema is noted apart from mild ankle swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 172/112 (repeated 168/110 after 15 min), RR 20, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C; fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 62 U/L (<30); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.35); urine PCR 320 mg/mmol (<30)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg TDS oral; iron; low-dose aspirin 150 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive?

options.text: Increase oral labetalol dose to 300 mg every 8 hours with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Oral labetalol is inadequate at this BP and pace of end-organ signs (headache, epigastric pain, transaminitis, thrombocytopenia). Waiting 60 minutes on an inadequate oral dose delays control and risks stroke. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine immediate release 10 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy for severe hypertension because of unpredictable BP drop and risk of fetal compromise. Oral nifedipine immediate release is the alternative when IV labetalol is contraindicated, but sublingual is not the route. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to a MAP of 100 mmHg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside is reserved for refractory severe hypertension and carries risk of fetal cyanide toxicity with prolonged use; it is not a first-line agent in obstetric hypertensive emergency. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeat with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: SOMANZ guideline first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeated at 15 min intervals with dose doubling to a max of 300 mg. Oral labetalol has failed to control her BP so IV is appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: The SOMANZ hydralazine dose is 5 mg IV slowly, repeatable to 20 mg total; a 20 mg single bolus risks precipitous maternal hypotension and fetal bradycardia. IV labetalol is the SOMANZ first choice unless contraindicated. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 160 or more, diastolic 110 or more) is a hypertensive emergency because of stroke and abruption risk. SOMANZ first-line is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes with dose doubling at 15 minute intervals up to 300 mg total. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated; hydralazine is second-line at 5 mg IV, not 20 mg bolus.
key_points: Severe HTN in pregnancy: IV labetalol 20 mg then double every 15 min to 300 mg max
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated - only oral immediate release is acceptable
Hydralazine second-line: 5 mg IV slow, not 20 mg
Pre-eclampsia with severe HTN plus end-organ signs requires simultaneous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Sublingual nifedipine is the wrong answer in obstetric hypertensive emergency every time - the trap is dose route, not drug class.

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic management
stem:
A 27-year-old G2P0 with one prior first-trimester miscarriage presents at 6+2 weeks by LMP with light PV spotting and mild left iliac fossa discomfort. Serum bhCG 48 hours ago was 2400 IU/L and is now 2900 IU/L. She has no medical comorbidities and is not on any regular medication. Her reliable partner will bring her back for follow up as required.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable with mild left adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous adnexal mass with no fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 2900 IU/L today (was 2400 IU/L 48 h ago); Hb 128 g/L (115-165); ALT 22 U/L (<30); creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90); Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous mass; no fetal cardiac activity; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG and outpatient review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling bhCG on trend; her bhCG is rising (2400 to 2900) so expectant is not indicated. Persistent or rising ectopic without treatment risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate eligibility: bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, normal LFTs and renal function. Single-dose IM methotrexate is the correct medical management with day 4 and day 7 bhCG check and weekly to negative. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Surgical management is indicated for haemodynamic instability, rupture, contraindication to methotrexate, or when methotrexate criteria are not met (bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L, mass at or over 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac activity). She meets none of these; medical management is preferred and preserves the tube. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is a tube-preserving surgical option but is not indicated when medical management with methotrexate is safe and appropriate. Both surgical routes commit to operative recovery when medical management would work. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound and bhCG in 1 week without other intervention with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: One week of no intervention with a confirmed rising ectopic risks rupture within that window. The diagnosis is already established and she is a methotrexate candidate now. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic are: haemodynamic stability, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, no MTX contraindications (normal LFT, renal, no immunodeficiency), and reliable follow up. Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 bhCG and weekly to negative is the standard.
key_points: MTX threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG under 5000 IU/L in the RANZCOG GPS
Other MTX criteria: mass under 3.5 cm, no FCA, no significant pain, reliable follow up, normal LFT/renal
Dose is 50 mg per m2 IM as a single dose; day 4 and day 7 bhCG expected to drop 15 percent between
Surgical if unstable, ruptured, MTX contraindicated, or criteria not met
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG MTX cut-off is 5000 IU/L, not the older 3000 IU/L number - AU exam trap answered with the newer threshold.

subtopic_detail: PPH pharmacological escalation
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 delivers a 3800 g baby vaginally after a 12 hour labour with syntocinon augmentation for slow progress. Placenta is delivered spontaneously and appears complete. Estimated blood loss at 10 minutes is 1200 mL and continues at 200 mL per 5 minutes.

On abdominal examination her uterus is soft and boggy at the level of the umbilicus. She has an in-situ intravenous line, no known allergies, and her blood pressure has just dropped from 118/72 to 96/58. She has a history of chronic hypertension in her booking notes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and boggy at umbilicus; perineum inspected with no obvious tear; placenta complete
data_table.Medications given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery of anterior shoulder (active third stage); no other drugs given

lead_in: After bimanual uterine massage what pharmacological agent would you give next?

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as first-line with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is given in parallel with uterotonics in PPH within 3 hours (WOMAN trial), but it does not replace the tonic. The primary problem is uterine atony and it needs a uterotonic first. TXA is an adjunct, not a substitute. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 500 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes marked vasoconstriction and BP rise. Her chronic hypertension makes this an unsafe choice; carboprost is the alternative uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a third-line uterotonic in AU practice reserved for when parenteral agents are unavailable or exhausted; it has slower onset (30-60 min) than carboprost (10-15 min). RANZCOG puts parenteral agents ahead of misoprostol. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: She has active postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony. The RANZCOG ladder after uterine massage and oxytocin bolus is ergometrine or carboprost. Carboprost is preferred here because ergometrine is contraindicated in her chronic hypertension. Carboprost 250 mcg IM can be repeated every 15 min to a max of 2 mg. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is not a uterotonic - it is a smooth muscle relaxant used in pre-eclampsia and tocolysis. It would worsen atony and precipitate BP drop in the shocked patient. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

explanation.summary: PPH from atony is treated with mechanical measures (bimanual compression, uterine massage) plus uterotonic escalation. RANZCOG sequences oxytocin then ergometrine or carboprost then misoprostol. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because of vasoconstriction; carboprost is the alternative. TXA and volume resuscitation run in parallel.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Carboprost is contraindicated in severe asthma but is the go-to when ergometrine cannot be used
TXA 1 g IV should be given in parallel within 3 hours - it does not replace uterotonics
explanation.pearls: The tone ladder splits on comorbidity - hypertension blocks ergometrine, asthma blocks carboprost, and the safe drug depends on which contraindication applies.

subtopic_detail: Concealed abruption recognition
stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks presents in the middle of the night after a car passenger seat impact 3 hours ago. She reports continuous abdominal pain since the accident, one small gush of PV bleeding at home, and reduced fetal movements over the last hour.

On examination she is tender across the uterus with a hard tense abdomen. Speculum shows only a small amount of dark blood in the vagina. Her last morphology scan at 20 weeks documented a fundal placenta. CTG shows a fetal heart baseline of 100 with reduced variability and late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender and firm (Couvelaire-like); minimal external blood loss; cervix closed and soft on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (115-165); platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-400); fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (4.0-6.0 in pregnancy); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2); base excess -6
data_table.CTG: Baseline 100, reduced variability, recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cross-match blood, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM for fetal lung maturation
options.rationale: Antenatal steroids are given up to 34+6 weeks; at 36+4 they are not indicated. More importantly, this fetus cannot wait 4 hours - it is compromised now. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound to exclude placenta praevia before proceeding
options.rationale: Her 20 week morphology already documented a fundal placenta, and TV ultrasound is time consuming in a category 1 situation. Ultrasound is also poorly sensitive for abruption; delaying delivery for imaging in a compromised fetus worsens outcome. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and continuous CTG
options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia with late decelerations plus maternal DIC do not permit induction; there is no time and the CTG demands immediate delivery. Prostaglandin is contraindicated in this pattern. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and observe for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Magnesium neuroprotection is used before very preterm birth (under 30 weeks) and does not apply at 36+4. Observation for 30 minutes with fetal bradycardia and late decelerations delays delivery beyond the safe window. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Category 1 emergency caesarean section with major haemorrhage protocol activation
options.rationale: This is placental abruption with fetal compromise (late decelerations, bradycardia) and evolving maternal DIC (falling fibrinogen, rising INR, thrombocytopenia). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean (delivery within 30 minutes) with major haemorrhage protocol activation because both mother and baby are in extremis. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption after trauma classically presents with continuous abdominal pain, tender rigid uterus and disproportionately small external bleeding for the clinical picture (concealed haemorrhage). Fetal compromise plus maternal coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, high INR, thrombocytopenia) is a category 1 caesarean indication with major haemorrhage protocol activation.
key_points: Concealed abruption presents with pain and firm uterus but minimal external blood
Fetal bradycardia plus late decelerations plus maternal coagulopathy = category 1 caesarean
Category 1 timing target: delivery within 30 minutes of decision
MHP activation goes in parallel because DIC is already developing
explanation.pearls: The exam trap in abruption is doing an ultrasound to exclude praevia - the CTG has already made the call, and delay costs the baby.

sources.label: RANZCOG Category of urgency for caesarean statement

subtopic_detail: Magnesium toxicity recognition
stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 33+1 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia is on a magnesium sulfate infusion at 1 g per hour after a 4 g loading dose 3 hours ago. The bedside nurse calls you because she has become drowsy and complains of feeling weak.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has a normal blood pressure of 148/94 on labetalol infusion. Her patellar reflexes are absent bilaterally. Respiratory examination shows shallow breathing. She has an in-dwelling urinary catheter with 15 mL of urine in the last hour. Her booking creatinine was 68 micromol/L; today's is 128 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 66, BP 148/94, RR 8, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, weak, patellar reflexes absent bilaterally; shallow respiratory pattern
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 128 micromol/L (was 68 at booking); serum magnesium level pending; urine output 15 mL in last hour
data_table.Medications: Magnesium sulfate infusion 1 g per hour (loading 4 g given 3 h ago); labetalol infusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue magnesium at the same rate and add furosemide 40 mg IV to increase renal clearance
options.rationale: Continuing magnesium in the face of overt toxicity worsens respiratory depression and risks arrest. Furosemide is not the immediate rescue; magnesium must be stopped and calcium gluconate given first. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
options.rationale: This is magnesium toxicity with the classical sequence of loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression. Her rising creatinine and low urine output have caused magnesium accumulation. Immediate management is to stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 minutes as the specific antidote. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Halve the magnesium infusion to 500 mg per hour and repeat serum magnesium in 4 hours
options.rationale: Reducing the infusion without stopping is inadequate for overt clinical toxicity; loss of reflexes plus respiratory rate 8 requires immediate reversal, not dose adjustment. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intubation and mechanical ventilation for airway protection before further management
options.rationale: Intubation is a rescue if the respiratory depression persists after magnesium is stopped and calcium given; it is not the first action when a specific antidote is available and can restore respiratory drive within minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV for suspected opioid depression with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: There is no opioid in her medication list and her clinical picture (absent reflexes, weakness, respiratory depression on a magnesium infusion in AKI) is magnesium toxicity, not opioid. Naloxone would waste time. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in pregnancy proceeds in a predictable sequence: loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression then cardiac arrest. She has accumulated magnesium because of oliguria (15 mL in the last hour) and rising creatinine. The specific reversal is stopping the infusion and giving IV calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes. Monitor urine output and reflexes hourly, keep magnesium infusion at 0.5-1 g per hour, and reduce dose in renal impairment.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity sequence: reflex loss, respiratory depression, arrest
Renal impairment or oliguria (under 30 mL per hour) accumulates magnesium rapidly
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 min
Reduce infusion rate to 0.5 g per hour in renal impairment or reduced urine output
explanation.pearls: The safety net for magnesium is reflexes and urine output at the bedside - a nurse's reflex check every hour catches toxicity before the respiratory rate drops.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition
stem:
A 33-year-old G4P3 at 39+4 weeks has an artificial rupture of membranes for augmentation of established labour. Two minutes later she becomes restless, complains of feeling short of breath, then loses consciousness. Fetal heart rate drops to 60.

When you arrive her airway is patent with agonal respirations, there are no palpable peripheral pulses, and she has begun to bleed briskly from her IV cannulation site and around her mouth. The senior midwife has called an obstetric emergency and started chest compressions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 40 (transitioned from 118 in 60 seconds), BP unrecordable, SpO2 84 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, RR agonal, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Recent events: ARM 2 minutes ago; sudden collapse; brisk oozing from IV site and gums; fetal heart 60
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ROTEM pending; venous blood gas being drawn

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anaphylaxis to intravenous oxytocin with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Oxytocin anaphylaxis is very rare and typically produces urticarial rash, bronchospasm and hypotension without immediate DIC. There is no rash description here and the bleeding pattern does not match anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from thrombus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Pulmonary thromboembolism causes acute hypoxia and haemodynamic collapse but does not produce simultaneous rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy from IV and gum bleeding within minutes. The DIC-like coagulopathy is the AFE fingerprint. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

options.text: Eclampsia with seizure and hypoxia with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Eclampsia usually presents with a tonic-clonic seizure and post-ictal state, not the immediate coagulopathic bleeding pattern here. There is no BP surge history and the coagulopathy pattern does not fit eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Uterine rupture with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Uterine rupture in a G4P3 without a scarred uterus is possible but typically presents with abdominal pain, tenderness, loss of fetal station, and haemorrhagic shock without such rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy. The temporal link to ARM and the mucosal oozing point elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: The triad of sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and consumptive coagulopathy (oozing from puncture sites and mucous membranes) at the time of ARM or delivery is classical for amniotic fluid embolism (AFE). Diagnosis is clinical; treatment is supportive with immediate resuscitative caesarean if maternal arrest, massive transfusion protocol and ICU. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

explanation.summary: AFE is characterised by sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and coagulopathy occurring during labour, at ARM or delivery, or immediately postpartum. It is a clinical diagnosis; there is no bedside test. Management is supportive - airway, oxygen, resuscitative caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest, MHP activation, ICU. Mortality remains high despite treatment.
key_points: AFE triad: sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia, DIC
Temporal association with ARM, delivery, or immediate postpartum
Diagnosis is clinical; ROTEM will show consumptive coagulopathy but does not confirm AFE
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest if not already delivered
explanation.pearls: The AFE fingerprint is coagulopathy with bleeding from IV sites and mucous membranes appearing within minutes - PE does not do that.

subtopic_detail: Ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P0 with a prior right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy 3 years ago presents with 4 hours of severe left iliac fossa pain and syncope. Her serum bhCG is 8200 IU/L today. She was trying to conceive after unsuccessful IVF cycles and this is a spontaneous pregnancy.

On examination she has a distended tender abdomen with guarding and rebound in the left iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a left tubal 32 mm mass with fetal cardiac activity, and significant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She is now peripherally shut down.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/56, RR 26, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Peripherally shut down; peritonism left iliac fossa; guarding and rebound
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 8200 IU/L; Hb 88 g/L (115-165) (was 128 last week); group and screen underway; Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 32 mm mass with fetal cardiac activity; large volume free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.History: Prior right salpingectomy for ectopic 3 years ago; nil other surgical history; failed IVF cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management now?

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation in interventional radiology to control bleeding
options.rationale: UAE is used for postpartum haemorrhage refractory to medical management, arteriovenous malformations, and specific fibroid indications; it is not the treatment for ruptured tubal ectopic. Definitive surgical removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic left salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability and in ruptured ectopic because it is technically slower, has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate requiring MTX follow up, and same-tube recurrence approaches 20 percent - the very tube she is trying to preserve is now maximally damaged. IVF is her fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 and admission for observation
options.rationale: MTX is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, rupture, fetal cardiac activity, mass over 3.5 cm, and bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L. She fails all five of these criteria. MTX would delay definitive surgical control of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic left salpingectomy after major haemorrhage protocol activation
options.rationale: She has a ruptured left tubal ectopic with shock in her only remaining tube. Although salpingostomy might otherwise be preferred to preserve the only remaining tube, the RANZCOG evidence base shows salpingostomy has a 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic rate. In a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large ruptured mass, salpingectomy is safer and definitive; future fertility can be pursued via IVF. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Cross-match, resuscitate, and re-scan in 6 hours before deciding surgery
options.rationale: She has already ruptured and is shocked; the diagnosis is made and the operating theatre needs her now. Waiting 6 hours risks exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: This T14-flip scenario tests the historical-bilaterality inversion: the standard teaching that a prior contralateral salpingectomy should push you toward salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube is over-ruled by haemodynamic instability, rupture, mass over 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac activity and bhCG well above the MTX threshold. In this real-world constellation salpingectomy is safer, definitive, and IVF becomes her fertility route.
key_points: MTX absolute contraindications include instability, rupture, FCA, mass over 3.5 cm, bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L
Salpingostomy has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic
Haemodynamic instability trumps tube-preservation logic - salpingectomy is safer
Fertility via IVF is a legitimate downstream plan when both tubes are lost
explanation.pearls: The historical-bilaterality flip usually favours preservation, but rupture with instability inverts it back to salpingectomy - safety over sentiment.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate loading in renal impairment
stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents to your tertiary obstetric emergency department with a 4 hour history of frontal headache, epigastric pain, and one episode of visual flashing lights. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 and she had previously been well. She has no history of chronic kidney disease.

On arrival she is anxious with brisk reflexes and 3 beats of clonus at the ankles bilaterally. Uterus is soft with regular fetal movements felt by the mother. Cardiotocograph shows a normal reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. You have decided to commence magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and initiated antihypertensive treatment. IV access has been secured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 168/112, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; brisk reflexes with 3 beats of clonus; abdomen soft with fundal height 34 cm; no epigastric tenderness on palpation; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol; sodium 132 potassium 4.6 urea 8.2 creatinine 128 micromol/L; ALT 84 AST 78 platelets 118 x10^9/L; INR 1.1; uric acid 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 1 gram per hour with 4 hourly deep tendon reflex and urine output monitoring
options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends 4 g IV loading over 15-20 min then 1 g/hr maintenance for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia, with a reduced maintenance rate (1 g/hr rather than 2 g/hr) when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L. Deep tendon reflex loss and urine output under 100 mL over 4 hours trigger withholding. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 2 grams per hour with hourly reflex and urine output monitoring
options.rationale: The standard maintenance dose is 2 g/hr but this must be halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L to avoid toxic accumulation because magnesium is renally excreted. This patient has creatinine 128 micromol/L. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 6 grams intramuscularly plus 5 grams into each buttock with subsequent 5 grams intramuscularly every 4 hours per the Pritchard regimen
options.rationale: The Pritchard IM regimen is a historical alternative used where IV pumps are unavailable. In an AU tertiary setting the IV loading-plus-infusion regimen is standard because it allows real-time titration and monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Phenytoin loading 15 milligrams per kilogram intravenously over 30 minutes followed by 100 milligrams every 8 hours as an alternative anticonvulsant
options.rationale: Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate for eclampsia seizure prevention (Magpie and Collaborative Eclampsia Trial) and is no longer used as first-line. Magnesium is the SOMANZ standard. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Diazepam 10 milligrams intravenously over 2 minutes with observation for further seizures before considering magnesium sulfate infusion
options.rationale: Diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures unresponsive to magnesium; withholding magnesium in favour of diazepam prophylaxis is inappropriate and increases eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is severe pre-eclampsia with proteinuria, raised transaminases, thrombocytopenia, and neurological symptoms. SOMANZ recommends IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis at 4 g loading over 15-20 minutes followed by 2 g/hr maintenance, halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L because magnesium is renally cleared. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output. IM Pritchard regimen is a historical alternative and diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures.
key_points: SOMANZ MgSO4: 4 g load over 15-20 min then 1-2 g/hr maintenance
Halve maintenance to 1 g/hr when creatinine >100 micromol/L
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output for toxicity
Phenytoin and diazepam are not first-line for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: When creatinine rises above 100 micromol/L in severe pre-eclampsia, halve the magnesium maintenance to 1 g/hr; the loading dose stays 4 g.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline
RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic selection with contraindication
stem:
A 32-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 has just had an unassisted spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3800 gram baby after a labour of 14 hours. The third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units at delivery of the anterior shoulder. She has a booking blood pressure of 165/105, was diagnosed with chronic hypertension pre-pregnancy on labetalol, and has had blood pressures ranging 150-170 systolic through labour.

Within 5 minutes of placental delivery she has 900 mL of visible fresh red blood loss and the uterus feels soft on abdominal palpation. Vaginal examination reveals a bulky uterus with clots at the introitus and no vaginal or cervical tear identified. She has good IV access and the postpartum haemorrhage protocol has been activated with fluids running.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/62, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; uterus above the umbilicus and soft; no vaginal or cervical tear on inspection; no perineal haematoma
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 900 mL and ongoing; venous gas pH 7.36 haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128); coags awaited

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Intravenous ergometrine 250 micrograms as a slow push with cardiac monitoring in place and full uterotonic protocol continued
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes profound vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum blood pressures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intramuscular Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 international units and ergometrine 500 micrograms) with cardiac monitoring and continue full uterotonic protocol
options.rationale: Syntometrine contains ergometrine which is contraindicated in hypertension; giving it here risks hypertensive crisis and cerebrovascular accident. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units every 5 minutes up to 4 doses before escalation to any additional uterotonic
options.rationale: Repeat IM oxytocin doses without escalation to second-line uterotonics wastes time in an ongoing PPH; RANZCOG pathway is to start an oxytocin infusion (40 units in 1 L saline over 4 hours) then move to ergometrine or carboprost. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms plus intravenous tranexamic acid 1 gram over 10 minutes as combined pharmacotherapy before repeat oxytocin
options.rationale: Misoprostol 800 mcg (rectal or sublingual) is a fallback where injectable uterotonics are unavailable and is slower in onset; carboprost is preferred when it is available. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with bronchospasm precautions in place and repeat every 15 minutes up to 8 doses if bleeding continues
options.rationale: After oxytocin failure and where ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension, carboprost 250 mcg IM (Hemabate, F2-alpha prostaglandin) is the next-line uterotonic per RANZCOG PPH guidance. Bronchospasm precautions are needed. Doses may be repeated up to 8 total. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: This is a primary postpartum haemorrhage with atony after oxytocin. The RANZCOG uterotonic ladder is oxytocin (bolus then infusion), then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol. Ergometrine is CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension because of vasoconstriction and risk of hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum BP, so ergometrine (and Syntometrine which contains it) must be avoided; carboprost IM is the appropriate next-line uterotonic. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine (and Syntometrine) contraindicated in hypertension
Carboprost 250 mcg IM with bronchospasm precautions is next-line when ergometrine is contraindicated
TXA should be given but is haemostatic not uterotonic
explanation.pearls: In a PPH with chronic hypertension, skip ergometrine and go straight to carboprost; watch for bronchospasm in asthmatics.

subtopic_detail: Acute severe hypertension threshold and agent
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 30 plus 4 weeks with a known singleton pregnancy presents to your birth suite with a 3 hour history of persistent occipital headache. Booking blood pressure was 118/74 and she has been well since. She has no known drug allergies. She has been fasted for 6 hours in preparation for antenatal review.

On arrival to the birth suite the initial BP is 172/116, confirmed 15 minutes later at 168/114 with an appropriate cuff on the right arm. She is alert with no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, and no shortness of breath. Reflexes are 2+ without clonus. Bedside urinalysis shows protein 2+. Cardiotocograph shows a reactive trace with baseline 140 and moderate variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 168/114, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.7 C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Alert; reflexes 2+; no clonus; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles; abdomen soft with fundal height 30 cm and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis protein 2+; urine protein:creatinine ratio pending; sodium 138 potassium 4.4 urea 4.2 creatinine 74; ALT 32 platelets 220 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line agent to lower blood pressure?

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside titrated infusion at 0.3 micrograms per kilogram per minute with continuous arterial line monitoring for BP control
options.rationale: Nitroprusside is generally avoided in pregnancy because of cyanide accumulation risk in the fetus and requires ICU-level monitoring; it is reserved for refractory hypertensive emergency after other agents have failed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 milligrams to achieve rapid drop with cardiotocograph continuous throughout for fetal wellbeing monitoring
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is not recommended in pregnancy because uncontrolled rapid drops can cause fetal distress from placental hypoperfusion. Oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine at controlled doses are the SOMANZ options. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams as a slow push to reduce blood pressure and preload with careful reassessment of BP after 20 minutes
options.rationale: Furosemide is not a first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; it may worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia (which has capillary leak) and is reserved for pulmonary oedema. It does not treat the hypertension itself. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 milligrams and repeat blood pressure in 30 minutes with a second dose if systolic remains at or above 160
options.rationale: SOMANZ acute severe hypertension in pregnancy pathway lists oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate release (repeatable at 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg) as a first-line option alongside IV labetalol and IV hydralazine when BP is at least 160/110. Oral nifedipine is preferred when IV access is not needed for other reasons. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.text: Oral captopril 25 milligrams as first-line antihypertensive with a target of achieving a systolic below 140 within one hour of administration
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and cause fetal renal dysgenesis; they are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Captopril is not appropriate at any dose antenatally. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at least 160/110 on two readings 15 minutes apart) with likely new-onset pre-eclampsia (proteinuria). SOMANZ first-line agents for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy are oral nifedipine immediate release, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, all in stepped protocols. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided (risk of uncontrolled fetal distress), nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases, and ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated. Furosemide is not an antihypertensive in this setting.
key_points: SOMANZ severe HTN threshold: 160/110 on two readings 15 min apart
First-line options: oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, IV hydralazine
ACE inhibitors absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic)
Sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside avoided
explanation.pearls: For severe HTN in pregnancy at 160/110, oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release is a legitimate first move when IV access is not otherwise needed; sublingual is not the same drug in a different route.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline
RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy surgical option with contralateral history
stem:
A 32-year-old gravida 4 para 1 presents to your gynaecology emergency assessment unit at 6 plus 5 weeks by dates with 6 hours of left iliac fossa pain and moderate vaginal spotting. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy. She has been trying to conceive since and has undergone no assisted reproductive therapy.

She is haemodynamically stable with mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation without peritonism. Speculum examination shows a small amount of dark blood at the cervical os. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with a yolk sac but no fetal cardiac activity, and 40 mL of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She strongly wishes to preserve future fertility.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation with no peritonism; abdomen otherwise soft; speculum shows small amount of dark blood at os; bimanual with left adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 4200 IU/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; blood group A rhesus positive; venous gas pH 7.40 lactate 1.4 mmol/L; transvaginal ultrasound as described above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingostomy with removal of ectopic tissue and preservation of the left fallopian tube for potential future spontaneous conception
options.rationale: Although salpingostomy classically preserves fertility, this patient has a prior contralateral salpingectomy meaning the left tube is her only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube is 15-30 percent, so leaving a damaged tube in place risks a further ectopic in the only remaining tube. RANZCOG accepts salpingectomy in this situation to lower recurrence risk, with IVF as the future fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 milligrams per square metre single dose with weekly beta-hCG follow-up until confirmed less than 15 international units per litre
options.rationale: This ectopic has yolk sac (though no cardiac activity) and moderate free fluid; RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate require beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L (met), mass under 3.5 cm (met), no significant pain, no haemorrhage, and no fetal cardiac activity. Moderate free fluid and worsening pain move her outside methotrexate territory. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with removal of ectopic tissue and the left fallopian tube with counselling that future fertility will require in vitro fertilisation
options.rationale: The T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy means the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube (15-30 percent) after salpingostomy dominates the fertility calculus in this scenario; salpingectomy plus IVF has a better cumulative live birth outcome than salpingostomy with a high recurrence chance. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy in this specific scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Expectant management with 48 hour beta-hCG monitoring and clinic review in one week without surgical or medical intervention at this stage
options.rationale: Expectant management is only appropriate for asymptomatic patients with declining beta-hCG under 1000-2000 IU/L, minimal free fluid, and no adnexal mass. This patient has a 2.8 cm mass with yolk sac, moderate free fluid, and pain. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Laparotomy through a Pfannenstiel incision with left salpingectomy and inspection of the contralateral surgical site for adhesions
options.rationale: Laparotomy is unnecessary in a haemodynamically stable patient with an unruptured tubal ectopic; laparoscopy has lower morbidity, shorter recovery, and comparable outcomes. Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or extensive adhesions preventing laparoscopy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: This is the T14 historical-bilaterality flip: normally salpingostomy is chosen over salpingectomy to preserve fertility, but when the contralateral tube has already been removed the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent, which dominates the fertility calculus. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy plus IVF as the higher cumulative live birth pathway in this specific scenario. Methotrexate is excluded by the moderate free fluid and yolk sac features, and expectant management is excluded by the mass and pain.
key_points: T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy makes salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy
Recurrent ectopic risk in same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent
Methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage
Laparotomy reserved for haemodynamic instability
explanation.pearls: In an ectopic patient with prior contralateral salpingectomy, do NOT try to preserve the only remaining tube; take it and offer IVF, because a repeat same-tube ectopic can end that tube anyway.

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR sequence after failed McRoberts
stem:
A 33-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 with a booking BMI of 34 and diet-controlled gestational diabetes is delivering at 39 plus 5 weeks. She has just delivered the fetal head after a normal first stage and 45 minutes of active second stage. The head has retracted tightly against the perineum (turtle sign) and gentle downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. She is in the lithotomy position with an epidural.

The accoucheur has called for help and the emergency buzzer has been pressed. The clock has been started. McRoberts hyperflexion of the hips has been performed by two assistants for 30 seconds without effect, then combined with suprapubic pressure applied by the second assistant from the anterior shoulder side for a further 30 seconds, also without effect. The head has now been undelivered for 90 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air; fetal HR 100 with reduced variability
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign present; anterior shoulder impacted behind the pubic symphysis; no cord felt palpable; epidural block adequate
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Repeat McRoberts hyperflexion and suprapubic pressure for another minute with more forceful application by all available assistants before escalating further
options.rationale: Repeat cycles of the same manoeuvre waste time; the HELPERR pathway moves promptly to internal manoeuvres after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed. Fetal head-to-body delivery interval predicts acidosis and injury. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Deliver the posterior arm by inserting a hand along the fetal back and sweeping it across the chest to bring the posterior arm out first
options.rationale: Delivery of the posterior arm is the RANZCOG next step after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure fails; it converts the bisacromial diameter to the more favourable acromio-axillary and has the highest resolution rate of the internal manoeuvres. Rubin II and Woods screw are alternative internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Apply fundal pressure while continuing suprapubic pressure to overcome the impaction and deliver the anterior shoulder without episiotomy
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury risk. It should never be used. Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) is different. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Perform symphysiotomy under local infiltration to widen the pelvic outlet before attempting further shoulder manoeuvres or Zavanelli manoeuvre
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre in Australian obstetric practice after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; it carries significant maternal morbidity and is not the next step after McRoberts fails. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre replacing the head into the pelvis and proceeding immediately to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; skipping directly to it is inappropriate at this stage where internal manoeuvres have not yet been attempted. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: This is shoulder dystocia. The RANZCOG HELPERR pathway is Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres including Rubin II and Woods), Remove posterior arm, and Roll patient to all-fours. After McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed, delivery of the posterior arm is the next-highest-yielding internal manoeuvre. Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED and Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last resorts after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery fail.
key_points: HELPERR sequence for shoulder dystocia
After McRoberts plus SPP: internal manoeuvres or posterior arm delivery
Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED (worsens impaction, brachial plexus injury)
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last-resort
explanation.pearls: In shoulder dystocia after failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, do NOT repeat the same manoeuvre; move directly to the posterior arm which has the highest resolution rate.

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption vs praevia discrimination and management
stem:
A 31-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 33 plus 2 weeks presents to your regional birth suite with 2 hours of severe constant lower abdominal pain and moderate dark vaginal bleeding. She has had two previous uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her booking anatomy scan at 20 weeks reported a posterior fundal placenta with the lower edge well clear of the internal cervical os. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily and had a fall from a low horse this morning.

On arrival she is anxious with a firm tender uterus that palpates as woody hard on abdominal examination. She is unable to feel fetal movements over the last hour. Speculum examination has been deferred due to the known posterior placental position and abdominal tenderness. IV access has been secured with two large-bore cannulae and full antenatal haemorrhage protocol activated.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C; fetal HR 88 on doptone with prolonged decelerations
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen woody hard tender uterus at 34 cm; scant dark vaginal blood at introitus; no visible source outside vaginal orifice
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (booking 128); INR 1.4 fibrinogen 1.8 g/L; blood group A rhesus negative; Kleihauer-Betke pending; formal ultrasound pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer 250 micrograms of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin, transfuse two units of packed red cells, and admit for close observation with tocolysis
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in placental abruption because it can worsen bleeding and hide clinical deterioration. Anti-D and transfusion should be given but are supportive; the primary need is delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Perform digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before proceeding to expectant management with continuous cardiotocography and 6 hourly review
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination in undiagnosed antepartum haemorrhage before excluding praevia risks catastrophic bleeding; ultrasound must precede a digital exam. Expectant management is inappropriate given fetal compromise and maternal shock. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Give intramuscular corticosteroid for fetal lung maturation and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before category one caesarean section under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean should not be delayed for steroid or magnesium administration when there is severe abruption with fetal compromise; steroids given intraoperatively (which is common practice) do not delay delivery. Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated by the coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Continuous cardiotocography, bolus intravenous crystalloid, activate massive transfusion protocol and proceed to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: This is placental abruption (constant pain, woody uterus, dark blood, maternal shock, coagulopathy) with fetal compromise (fetal HR 88 with prolonged decelerations). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean when there is maternal or fetal compromise from abruption. Resuscitation and MTP activation occur in parallel with theatre transfer. GA is preferred over neuraxial when there is coagulopathy (fibrinogen 1.8, INR 1.4). (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

options.text: Await emergency transabdominal ultrasound scan to confirm placental location and grade the abruption before making a decision about mode and timing of delivery
options.rationale: Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption (misses up to 50 percent) and is not diagnostic; delaying delivery for imaging in the face of fetal bradycardia and maternal shock costs the baby. Clinical picture of abruption plus fetal compromise mandates immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

explanation.summary: The clinical picture (constant pain, woody uterus, dark bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, fetal bradycardia) is placental abruption with maternal and fetal compromise. RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean in this setting; resuscitation, MTP activation, and theatre transfer occur in parallel. GA is preferred over regional anaesthesia given the coagulopathy. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated before excluding praevia, ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption, and tocolysis is contraindicated.
key_points: Abruption + maternal/fetal compromise = category 1 caesarean
GA preferred if coagulopathy (fibrinogen <2 g/L, INR >1.4)
Ultrasound misses up to 50 percent of abruptions - do not delay for imaging
Tocolysis contraindicated in abruption
explanation.pearls: A woody hard tender uterus with dark PV bleeding and fetal bradycardia is abruption until proved otherwise; go to theatre with MTP activated, do not wait for ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: Second twin delivery with non-cephalic presentation
stem:
A 30-year-old gravida 2 para 1 at 37 plus 4 weeks with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is in your tertiary birth suite. Both twins were cephalic at 36 weeks. Twin one was delivered spontaneously vaginally 8 minutes ago after an uncomplicated first stage of labour, birth weight 2820 g, Apgars 8 and 9. The consultant obstetrician and neonatology team are present.

Ultrasound immediately after twin one delivery shows twin two now in a transverse lie with the back inferior and a longitudinal spine. Cardiotocograph of twin two shows a reassuring reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. The membranes of twin two are intact. She is comfortable with a working epidural and the birthing team has been briefed. Vital signs are within normal limits. The team has been briefed and options for intrapartum management have been thoroughly discussed antenatally.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 88, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air; twin 2 fetal HR 145 reactive with moderate variability
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft with palpable transverse fetal lie of twin 2, back inferior; cervix fully dilated; membranes intact; longitudinal spine confirmed on ultrasound
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound: transverse lie of twin 2 with back inferior; placenta not previa; amniotic fluid adequate; no cord presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mode of delivery for twin two?

options.text: External cephalic version to cephalic under continuous ultrasound guidance followed by amniotomy and spontaneous vaginal delivery of twin 2
options.rationale: External cephalic version of a second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres in this setting and risks umbilical cord accidents from a transverse position with intact membranes. Internal podalic version is the preferred approach in an experienced unit for non-cephalic second twin. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Amniotomy of twin 2 sac now and await spontaneous descent while continuous cardiotocography assesses fetal wellbeing over the next 60 minutes
options.rationale: Amniotomy without version in a transverse lie risks cord prolapse or arm prolapse; the fetus will not descend from a transverse position. Delaying delivery of the second twin beyond about 30 minutes also increases neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Immediate emergency category one caesarean section for twin 2 under regional anaesthesia after early counselling of the mother
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean of the second twin after vaginal delivery of the first carries substantial maternal morbidity (combined vaginal and caesarean recovery); it is reserved for cases where internal manoeuvres are not feasible or fetal compromise supervenes. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Internal podalic version and breech extraction with intact membranes broken as the fetal foot is delivered through the cervix
options.rationale: For a non-cephalic second twin at term in an experienced unit, internal podalic version with breech extraction (grasping a fetal foot and bringing it down before amniotomy) has better outcomes than ECV or immediate caesarean when the CTG is reassuring. This is the RANZCOG-endorsed approach when the accoucheur is experienced. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Commence oxytocin augmentation to encourage descent of twin 2 with amniotomy at the next contraction under regional block with continuous cardiotocography
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation for a transverse lie is not standard practice and will not correct the presentation. Amniotomy without version risks cord or arm prolapse from the transverse position. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: This is a twin two now in transverse lie after vaginal delivery of a cephalic twin one, with a reassuring CTG and intact membranes in a term dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy. RANZCOG endorses internal podalic version with breech extraction as the optimal approach in an experienced unit: the accoucheur grasps a fetal foot, brings it down, and performs breech extraction only breaking membranes at the last moment. This avoids the maternal morbidity of caesarean after vaginal delivery and has better outcomes than ECV, amniotomy without version, or awaiting spontaneous descent.
key_points: Internal podalic version + breech extraction is preferred for non-cephalic second twin
Break membranes as the foot is brought through, not before, to avoid cord prolapse
ECV of second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres
Delivery of twin 2 within 30 minutes of twin 1 minimises neonatal morbidity
explanation.pearls: For a transverse second twin with reassuring CTG at term, internal podalic version by an experienced accoucheur beats caesarean; keep the membranes intact until you have a foot through the cervix.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition and resuscitation
stem:
A 34-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 39 plus 2 weeks is having oxytocin augmentation for prolonged second stage. Ten minutes after artificial rupture of membranes she becomes acutely short of breath, agitated, and cyanotic. She then loses consciousness and becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse. The rhythm on the monitor is a narrow-complex PEA. She has no known medical or obstetric history. The baby's head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated.

The arrest team is called and CPR is commenced. The consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist, neonatology team, and haematology are on their way. There is early bright red PV bleeding estimated at 300 mL and increasing. Bedside coagulation testing reveals INR 3.2 and fibrinogen 0.6 g/L. Left lateral tilt has been applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal cardiac arrest, PEA on monitor, no palpable pulse; fetal HR 60 on doppler decreasing
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive; CPR in progress; cyanotic; fresh bright red PV bleed 300 mL and increasing; uterus soft; head at station +2 with cervix fully dilated
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care coags INR 3.2 fibrinogen 0.6 g/L; venous gas pH 7.10 lactate 8 mmol/L; haemoglobin 78 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Continue CPR and administer intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram then deliver the baby by perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes of arrest
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes is standard for maternal arrest at more than 20 weeks WHEN vaginal delivery is not imminent. Here the head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated; a category 1 assisted vaginal delivery (rotational forceps or ventouse) achieves delivery faster than caesarean and improves both maternal and fetal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG maternal collapse statement)

options.text: Continue CPR and administer intravenous fibrinogen concentrate 4 grams and cryoprecipitate as the primary resuscitation without delivering the baby immediately
options.rationale: Blood products are essential and should be given but delaying delivery is worse; delivery relieves aortocaval compression and dramatically improves resuscitation chances. Blood products and delivery happen together, not sequentially. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give a 30 millilitre per kilogram bolus of Hartmann's solution, and administer intravenous salbutamol 250 micrograms bolus to reverse bronchospasm
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not part of the AFE resuscitation algorithm; the mechanism is not primarily bronchospasm but multiorgan haemodynamic collapse and DIC. Fluid without blood products in massive haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give thrombolysis with alteplase 100 milligrams intravenously over 2 hours for presumed pulmonary embolism during pregnancy
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in a peripartum patient with already severe coagulopathy and active haemorrhage is catastrophic. The clinical picture is AFE (sudden collapse with DIC) not PE (which usually presents with unilateral leg findings, pleuritic pain, and different haemodynamics). (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

options.text: Continue CPR, give intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram, activate massive transfusion, and perform immediate assisted vaginal delivery by ventouse or forceps
options.rationale: This is amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac arrest AND imminent vaginal delivery (station +2, fully dilated). ANZCOR maternal cardiac arrest algorithm calls for delivery within 4-5 minutes to improve maternal circulation; when vaginal delivery is imminent, assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. MTP activation and standard ALS with adrenaline continue in parallel. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

explanation.summary: This is amniotic fluid embolism (sudden peripartum collapse with cardiac arrest and DIC after ARM). The ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest algorithm mandates delivery within 4-5 minutes to relieve aortocaval compression and improve circulation. When vaginal delivery is imminent (fully dilated, head at station +2), assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. Standard ALS (chest compressions, adrenaline 1 mg, defibrillation for shockable rhythms) and MTP activation with balanced blood products for DIC occur in parallel. Fluid alone worsens coagulopathy; thrombolysis is contraindicated with active haemorrhage.
key_points: AFE presents with sudden collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC
Delivery within 4-5 minutes of arrest improves resuscitation
Assisted vaginal delivery preferred if fully dilated and station +2 or lower
MTP with balanced blood products for the DIC; avoid crystalloid-only resuscitation
explanation.pearls: In maternal cardiac arrest with cervix fully dilated and head at station +2, an emergency ventouse or forceps beats perimortem caesarean because it delivers faster with less blood loss.

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in preterm labour
stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+2 weeks presents to your labour ward with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes. Vaginal examination shows the cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced. Membranes are intact. Her last GBS swab was negative at 26 weeks in her previous pregnancy; no GBS swab has been performed in this pregnancy. She has no penicillin allergy and no other risk factors for infection. Fetal heart rate is reassuring.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fully effaced, membranes intact; regular contractions every 4 minutes; fundus at 33 cm; presenting part cephalic at station -2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic decision for GBS prophylaxis?

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotics as her previous pregnancy swab was negative and there are no additional risk factors present in this pregnancy so far
options.rationale: A GBS swab from a previous pregnancy does not carry over; preterm labour without a current negative GBS status is treated as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Take a low vaginal and rectal swab now for GBS PCR and defer intravenous antibiotics until the result is available in approximately 4 hours from now
options.rationale: Delivery is imminent at 4 cm and four-minutely contractions; delaying antibiotics for a PCR result risks inadequate cover and PCR has variable turnaround times.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Give IV amoxicillin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every four hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily for broad-spectrum cover during her labour
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum cover including gentamicin is used for clinical chorioamnionitis, not intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a woman without infection features.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, treating preterm labour without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance treats preterm labour under 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive; benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g four-hourly is the regimen.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Give IV clindamycin 900 mg every eight hours until delivery, as clindamycin covers GBS reliably regardless of the culture status in this preterm patient
options.rationale: Clindamycin is used only when penicillin is contraindicated and only after confirming isolate susceptibility; up to 20 percent of GBS isolates in AU are resistant.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

explanation.summary: Preterm labour before 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status is managed as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin. The standard regimen is benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery. A prior pregnancy swab does not carry across. In true penicillin allergy cefazolin is used for low-risk anaphylaxis and clindamycin only if the isolate is confirmed susceptible.
key_points: Preterm labour without current negative GBS swab is treated as GBS positive
Prior pregnancy GBS swab does not carry over
Regimen: benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g Q4H until delivery
Clindamycin only if penicillin allergy AND susceptible isolate
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis), request GBS susceptibility on any available swab before defaulting to clindamycin; up to 20 percent of AU GBS isolates are clindamycin resistant and vancomycin becomes the alternative.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing for sensitising event
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 RhD-negative woman at 15 weeks gestation presents to your emergency department 4 hours after a moderate abdominal blow from a motor vehicle accident. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness but no vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a live fetus with normal fetal heart rate and no retroplacental clot. She is otherwise well. Her partner is RhD-positive and she is confirmed RhD-negative on her routine antenatal group and screen.

data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness, no vaginal bleeding, fundus not palpable abdominally at this gestation
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold: O-negative; antibody screen negative; ultrasound live fetus, no retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D dose and Kleihauer approach?

options.text: No anti-D immunoglobulin is required as there is no visible vaginal bleeding and ultrasound shows no retroplacental clot on this presentation today
options.rationale: Any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D regardless of visible bleeding; feto-maternal haemorrhage may occur without external signs.

options.text: Administer 250 IU (50 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now with no Kleihauer required at this gestation, then routine follow-up in clinic
options.rationale: 250 IU is the standard dose for sensitising events before 12 weeks; at 15 weeks the standard sensitising event dose is 625 IU, and Kleihauer is not required before 20 weeks.

options.text: Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and request Kleihauer to determine any additional dose required for the sensitising event today
options.rationale: Kleihauer is required at or after 20 weeks only; before 20 weeks a single standard dose reliably covers the expected feto-maternal haemorrhage volume.

options.text: Administer 1500 IU IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat 625 IU every 6 weeks until delivery in view of the trauma and the perceived ongoing risk
options.rationale: 1500 IU is the routine antenatal prophylactic dose given at 28 and 34 weeks; the sensitising event dose at this gestation is 625 IU, not 1500.

options.text: Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now, and Kleihauer testing is not required at gestations before 20 weeks
options.rationale: AU NBA advice is 625 IU IM anti-D for sensitising events from 12 weeks up to and including delivery; Kleihauer is not needed before 20 weeks as the standard dose covers likely feto-maternal haemorrhage.

explanation.summary: In an RhD-negative pregnant woman, any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D immunoglobulin. Before 12 weeks the dose is 250 IU IM; from 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU IM. Kleihauer testing is not required before 20 weeks because a single 625 IU dose neutralises any likely feto-maternal haemorrhage volume; at or after 20 weeks Kleihauer guides additional doses.
key_points: Any sensitising event triggers anti-D regardless of visible bleeding
Under 12 weeks 250 IU; from 12 weeks 625 IU IM
Kleihauer required only at 20 weeks or later
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 1500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Sensitising events include amniocentesis, external cephalic version, antepartum haemorrhage and abdominal trauma; give anti-D within 72 hours of the event but a dose given within 10 days still offers partial protection.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding endometrial thickness
stem: A 62-year-old woman who reached menopause at age 51 presents to your gynaecology clinic with one episode of light postmenopausal bleeding 2 weeks ago. She is not on hormone replacement therapy. Body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes. She has no vaginal atrophy on examination and no cervical lesion is visible. Her transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a smooth outline and no focal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 138/84, RR 16, temp 36.7 C, BMI 34 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: External genitalia normal, no vaginal atrophy, cervix healthy on speculum, no lesion; bimanual normal size uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrial thickness 6 mm, smooth outline, no focal lesion, ovaries normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.text: Arrange outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy to obtain histological diagnosis of the thickened endometrium seen at transvaginal ultrasound today
options.rationale: Endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with biopsy is the preferred AU approach when available, especially in obesity and diabetes.

options.text: Reassure and discharge with safety-net advice, since an endometrial thickness under 10 mm makes malignancy very unlikely in this postmenopausal patient population
options.rationale: The AU RANZCOG threshold to reassure without tissue is 4 mm or less; at 6 mm with risk factors of obesity and diabetes, tissue diagnosis is required for safety.

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 6 weeks to assess for persistent thickening of the endometrium before considering endometrial biopsy or referral for hysteroscopy
options.rationale: A delay of 6 weeks in a symptomatic postmenopausal woman with an above threshold endometrium is inappropriate; tissue diagnosis is needed now to exclude malignancy.

options.text: Trial 3 months of vaginal oestrogen cream and review symptoms and endometrial thickness at the end of the treatment period before further investigation
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen would not be given to a woman with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding and could worsen an occult endometrial cancer if present under the endometrium.

options.text: Refer for MRI pelvis to further characterise the endometrium and adnexa before deciding whether an endometrial biopsy is required for tissue diagnosis at all
options.rationale: MRI is not first line; it is used for staging once endometrial malignancy has been histologically confirmed, not for the initial diagnostic decision in postmenopausal bleeding.

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding with a transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred where available, particularly in women with high pretest probability such as obesity, diabetes, or Lynch syndrome. Blind pipelle sampling is acceptable when hysteroscopy is not immediately available.
key_points: PMB with endometrial thickness > 4 mm needs tissue diagnosis
Outpatient hysteroscopy plus biopsy preferred where available
Obesity, diabetes, unopposed oestrogen and tamoxifen raise pretest probability
Do not use vaginal oestrogen before diagnosis is made
explanation.pearls: In women with Lynch syndrome, endometrial cancer risk is high and screening should include annual endometrial biopsy and TVUS from age 35, not the 4 mm threshold applied to sporadic PMB.

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice in migraine with aura
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to your general practice for contraception advice. She has migraine with aura, described as bilateral scintillating scotoma lasting 30 minutes preceding a headache, occurring about once monthly. She smokes 5 cigarettes daily. She has regular menstrual cycles and no other cardiovascular risk factors. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/72. She wants long-acting reversible contraception.
