data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 118/72, RR 14, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Well woman, no focal neurology, cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 20 microgram and levonorgestrel 100 microgram taken daily for continuous cycle control
options.rationale: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to combined hormonal contraception at any dose due to ischaemic stroke risk associated with oestrogen exposure.

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device (52 mg) inserted for 5 years, providing highly effective progestogen-only long-acting reversible contraception without oestrogen exposure
options.rationale: Progestogen-only intrauterine contraception is UKMEC category 1 in migraine with aura; it is highly effective, long-acting, reversible and does not carry the oestrogen-related ischaemic stroke risk.

options.text: Combined transdermal patch delivering ethinylestradiol 20 microgram and norelgestromin 150 microgram daily for continuous contraceptive cover in the community
options.rationale: Any oestrogen-containing method is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura, regardless of the route of oestrogen administration used or the specific progestogen combined with it.

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks, starting today and continuing as long-term contraceptive cover through further clinic reviews
options.rationale: DMPA is UKMEC category 2 in migraine with aura and is a reasonable option, but is not as long-acting or as low-risk for bone loss and weight gain as a LNG-IUD.

options.text: Vaginal ring delivering ethinylestradiol 15 microgram and etonogestrel 120 microgram daily, replaced every 3 weeks with a hormone-free week to allow bleeding
options.rationale: The vaginal ring contains oestrogen and remains UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; the route does not change the ischaemic stroke risk assessment for combined hormonal methods.

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to any oestrogen-containing contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk; this includes combined oral pill, patch and vaginal ring at any dose. Progestogen-only methods are safe. The levonorgestrel intrauterine device is UKMEC category 1, highly effective and long-acting, and is the preferred option here. DMPA is acceptable but has other drawbacks compared with an IUD.
key_points: Migraine with aura: UKMEC 4 for any oestrogen-containing method
LNG-IUD is UKMEC 1 and preferred LARC in aura
Progestogen-only pill and DMPA are UKMEC 2
Route of oestrogen (oral, patch, ring) does not change the category
explanation.pearls: Aura features that trigger UKMEC 4 include any focal neurological symptom lasting under 60 minutes (visual, sensory, dysphasia); a nonspecific prodrome or postdrome without focal neurology is not aura.

subtopic_detail: Planned caesarean for placenta accreta spectrum
stem: A 36-year-old G4P3 woman with three previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta praevia at 32 weeks. MRI at 30 weeks shows features of placenta increta with focal loss of the retroplacental clear zone, bulging of placenta into bladder wall, and abnormal vascularity. She is stable with no bleeding. Delivery is being planned at your tertiary maternal-fetal medicine centre. She is fully counselled and has consented to caesarean hysterectomy if required.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 122/76, RR 14, temp 36.8 C, BMI 32
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundus 32 cm, cephalic, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: MRI 30 weeks: features of placenta increta; MSU negative; Hb 118, platelets 258; group and hold complete

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Planned classical caesarean under general anaesthesia at 39 weeks with immediate hysterectomy avoiding attempts at placental removal, with a 4 unit red cell cross-match
options.rationale: For placenta accreta spectrum, planned delivery is 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, not 39 weeks; delay to 39 weeks risks unscheduled bleeding and emergency surgery.

options.text: Continue expectant management with weekly ultrasound and plan for spontaneous labour with continuous fetal monitoring at term with a low threshold for emergency caesarean
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated with placenta praevia and accreta due to unmanageable haemorrhage risk; expectant management to term is unsafe in placenta accreta spectrum.

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, leaving placenta in situ, with MDT and IR standby and 4 to 6 unit cross-match
options.rationale: AU MFM guidance advises delivery between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, with an MDT including anaesthesia, urology, IR and blood bank; the placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy.

options.text: Planned lower segment caesarean at 37 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta and bimanual compression plus uterotonic infusion if uterine bleeding occurs
options.rationale: Attempted manual removal in placenta accreta causes catastrophic haemorrhage; the placenta must be left in situ during hysterectomy or conservative management is chosen.

options.text: Planned classical caesarean at 34 weeks with insertion of a Rusch balloon before uterine closure to allow later delivery of the placenta 6 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Delayed hysterectomy at 6 weeks is a conservative alternative in selected fertility-preserving cases; a Rusch balloon does not have a role and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard.

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is delivered by planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, in a tertiary centre with an MDT including obstetric anaesthesia, urology, interventional radiology and blood bank. Cross-match at least 4 to 6 units of red cells. The placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy; attempted removal causes catastrophic haemorrhage.
key_points: Planned delivery 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids
Do not attempt to remove the placenta at CS
MDT: MFM, anaesthesia, urology, IR, blood bank
Cross-match 4 to 6 units red cells minimum
explanation.pearls: For women declining hysterectomy who wish to preserve fertility, a Triple-P procedure or leaving the placenta in situ with methotrexate is an option, but with substantial infection and delayed bleeding risk.

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia antenatal management
stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 32 weeks has a transvaginal ultrasound today for a low-lying placenta, which has now migrated. However, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels running through membranes over the internal cervical os, confirming vasa praevia. She has had no bleeding, is asymptomatic and cervical length is 34 mm. Fetal movements are normal and fetal growth is at the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Fundus 32 cm, cephalic presentation, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: vasa praevia confirmed with fetal vessels overlying internal os, cervical length 34 mm, EFW 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antenatal management plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with delivery by elective caesarean at 39 weeks and expectant management until then, with fetal movement education for the mother
options.rationale: 39 weeks is too late; the risk of membrane rupture and fetal exsanguination rises after 34 weeks. Inpatient admission and steroids are usually recommended from around 32 weeks.

options.text: Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM twice 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 39 weeks unless she develops any bleeding beforehand
options.rationale: Waiting to 39 weeks after admission and steroids exposes the pregnancy to spontaneous rupture and fetal exsanguination; planned delivery is at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after steroids.

options.text: Outpatient management with weekly cardiotocography and TVUS until 37 weeks, at which point an elective caesarean is performed under regional anaesthesia after discussion
options.rationale: Outpatient management to 37 weeks exposes the pregnancy to risk of membrane rupture during transit; inpatient admission and earlier planned delivery are preferred.

options.text: Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM in two doses 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG supports inpatient admission around 32 weeks, antenatal steroids completing before 34 weeks, and elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture and haemorrhage can occur.

options.text: Immediate emergency caesarean at 32 weeks under general anaesthesia given the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage from any spontaneous membrane rupture that might occur
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 32 weeks exposes the neonate to unnecessary preterm complications; the risk-benefit balance favours planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after steroids.

explanation.summary: Confirmed vasa praevia requires planned inpatient admission around 32 weeks with a course of antenatal corticosteroids completed before 34 weeks. Elective caesarean is performed at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture of membranes can cause fetal exsanguination. Outpatient management to term risks membrane rupture in transit and is not standard AU practice. Immediate delivery at 32 weeks unnecessarily commits the neonate to preterm complications when planned delivery a few weeks later is safer.
key_points: Confirmed vasa praevia: admit around 32 weeks, steroids, deliver 34 to 36 weeks
Vaginal delivery contraindicated
Outpatient management to term is not standard
Emergency caesarean if any ROM or bleeding regardless of gestation
explanation.pearls: A 50 mL fetal bleed can exsanguinate a term fetus; do not wait for an abnormal CTG. If membranes rupture with bleeding, category 1 caesarean is warranted for suspected vasa praevia bleeding.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome grade and management
stem: A 34-year-old woman, day 8 after oocyte retrieval, presents to your emergency department with abdominal distension, oliguria and calf pain. She underwent IVF with 25 oocytes retrieved. She is dyspnoeic on exertion. Weight is up 4 kg since collection. On examination she has tense ascites and reduced air entry at the right lung base with dullness to percussion. Serum sodium 129, potassium 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/62, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, right pleural effusion clinically, calf oedema and tenderness left leg, no chest pain
data_table.Investigations: Na 129, K 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51, WCC 16, platelets 420; urine output 20 mL/hour over 6 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home on 3 litres oral fluids daily, oral cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly for 8 weeks, and a follow-up specialist appointment in the fertility clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Cabergoline is a preventative pre-trigger measure; this severe hospital-requiring presentation cannot be safely managed as an outpatient with oral therapy and follow-up.

options.text: IV furosemide 40 mg for the fluid overload plus 3 litres of normal saline over 6 hours to improve renal perfusion and correct the low urine output during observation
options.rationale: Furosemide worsens intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration in OHSS; loop diuretics are contraindicated in the third-space phase of the illness where extravascular fluid predominates.

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for suspected pulmonary embolism and proceed to CT pulmonary angiogram for further evaluation
options.rationale: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin is standard for severe OHSS; therapeutic dose is reserved for confirmed VTE and CT-PA is only warranted if suspicion is high, not from ascites-related dyspnoea alone.

options.text: Prescribe oral spironolactone 100 mg daily, restrict oral fluid intake to 800 mL per day and follow up as an outpatient in 3 days for repeat electrolyte assessment and review
options.rationale: Fluid restriction and diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and thrombotic risk in severe OHSS; outpatient care is inappropriate with haematocrit above 0.45 plus oliguria and tense ascites.

options.text: Admit for cautious IV crystalloid, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin, human albumin infusion for oncotic support, and ultrasound-guided paracentesis if respiratory compromise persists
options.rationale: Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration and effusion requires admission with careful crystalloid or colloid, VTE prophylaxis and paracentesis for symptomatic relief.

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration (haematocrit above 0.45) and pleural effusion requires hospital admission. Manage with cautious IV crystalloid or colloid to restore intravascular volume, human albumin as oncotic support, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin (severe OHSS is a strong VTE risk), and ultrasound-guided paracentesis for symptomatic ascites or effusion. Diuretics and fluid restriction are contraindicated as they worsen haemoconcentration and thrombosis.
key_points: Severe OHSS: admit, cautious IV fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Paracentesis for symptomatic tense ascites or effusion
Diuretics contraindicated in third-space phase
Cabergoline is a preventive measure, not a treatment at this stage
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline 0.5 mg daily started on the day of hCG trigger for 8 days reduces the incidence of moderate-to-severe OHSS by modulating VEGF-mediated vascular permeability.

subtopic_detail: Sheehan syndrome hormone replacement priority
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your emergency department 8 days postpartum after a delivery complicated by placental abruption with 2.8 L blood loss and 6 units red cell transfusion. Today she is drowsy, hypotensive, hypoglycaemic and hyponatraemic. She has failed to lactate. Random cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L. She is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 84/50, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent, temp 35.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds; breasts not lactating; no goitre, no adrenal skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, Na 122, K 4.1, glucose 2.6, Hb 92

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate hormone replacement order?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours first, IV 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious 3 percent saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia, then thyroxine after 24 hours
options.rationale: In panhypopituitarism, glucocorticoid replacement must precede thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis, along with dextrose for hypoglycaemia and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give IV levothyroxine 200 microgram now, followed by oral levothyroxine 100 microgram daily, then IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly to complete the replacement
options.rationale: Thyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in panhypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis by increasing metabolic demand on unreplaced cortisol; steroids must be given first.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours, avoid dextrose and hypertonic saline as these overcorrect the sodium too rapidly, and defer thyroxine replacement indefinitely to prevent rebound
options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs dextrose and severe symptomatic hyponatraemia at 122 warrants cautious hypertonic saline; deferring thyroxine indefinitely once cortisol is replaced is inappropriate.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give fludrocortisone 100 microgram orally daily as first-line steroid, then oral levothyroxine 100 microgram once the mineralocorticoid effect has been established over 24 hours
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency since aldosterone secretion is preserved via the RAAS; hydrocortisone is the correct first agent for the cortisol deficit.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give IV dexamethasone 8 mg and then perform a diagnostic short synacthen test before instituting any further hormone replacement therapy or dextrose or saline supplementation today
options.rationale: Delaying life-saving replacement to complete a synacthen test in a haemodynamically unstable postpartum woman is inappropriate; treat first and confirm the diagnosis later.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome from postpartum haemorrhage causes panhypopituitarism with hypocortisolism, hypothyroidism and central diabetes insipidus in some patients. The immediate priority is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours to prevent adrenal crisis, correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose, and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia. Thyroxine must be started after glucocorticoid replacement because unopposed thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis.
key_points: Hydrocortisone before thyroxine in panhypopituitarism
Dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia
Fludrocortisone not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency
Synacthen test and other confirmatory tests come after treatment
explanation.pearls: The classical Sheehan triad of failure to lactate, secondary amenorrhoea and postural symptoms may not appear until months after the causative haemorrhage; a low index of suspicion for hypopituitarism in postpartum fatigue and hyponatraemia is warranted.

sources.label: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis and initial management
stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 woman at 27+3 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic for her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test result. She had a healthy first baby weighing 3.6 kg. Her BMI is 29 kg/m2. She has no family history of type 2 diabetes and reports no polyuria or polydipsia. Her fasting venous plasma glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour post 75 g load is 9.8 mmol/L and 2 hour post load is 8.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 27 cm; symphysis-fundal height appropriate; fetal heart rate reassuring; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hr 9.8 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hr 8.1 mmol/L (<8.5); HbA1c 5.6 percent (<5.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that her OGTT is normal as only the fasting value is fractionally elevated and repeat the test in 4 weeks with the same 75 g load to confirm before making any diagnosis
options.rationale: AU ADIPS criteria require only one abnormal value, and her fasting glucose meets the threshold; repeating in 4 weeks delays management and increases fetal risk from ongoing hyperglycaemia.

options.text: Confirm gestational diabetes diagnosis, refer to the diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for structured education, capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily and dietitian review this week
options.rationale: AU ADIPS criteria diagnose GDM on any of fasting >=5.1, 1 hr >=10.0 or 2 hr >=8.5; her fasting of 5.4 exceeds the threshold so she meets diagnostic criteria and enters the standard care pathway.

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg orally twice daily immediately without lifestyle-first trial and arrange growth scan and umbilical artery Doppler in 2 weeks to evaluate fetal effects
options.rationale: AU pathway is lifestyle first for 1 to 2 weeks with glucose monitoring, adding metformin or insulin only if glycaemic targets are not met; jumping to metformin skips the standard trial period.

options.text: Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy, start basal insulin 0.2 unit/kg subcutaneously at night, arrange retinal screening and refer to endocrinology for postpartum management planning today
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by fasting glucose >=7.0, random >=11.1 or HbA1c >=6.5; her values do not meet the overt diabetes cut-offs so GDM management is appropriate.

options.text: Advise no further action until repeat OGTT at 34 weeks gestation and continue routine antenatal care, giving lifestyle advice only if that repeat test shows persistent glucose abnormality
options.rationale: Deferring diagnosis to 34 weeks misses 6 to 8 weeks of glycaemic control and increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia.

explanation.summary: Australian ADIPS criteria diagnose gestational diabetes on the 75 g OGTT if any one value meets: fasting >=5.1, 1 hour >=10.0 or 2 hour >=8.5 mmol/L. One abnormal value is sufficient. Initial management is structured education, self-monitoring of capillary glucose four times daily (fasting plus 2 hours post each main meal) and dietitian review, with metformin or insulin added within 1 to 2 weeks if targets are not met.
key_points: One value at or above ADIPS threshold diagnoses GDM in AU
Fasting 5.1, 1 hr 10.0, 2 hr 8.5 mmol/L are the cut-offs
Lifestyle plus glucose monitoring for 1 to 2 weeks first-line
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met on lifestyle
explanation.pearls: Postpartum 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks is mandatory as approximately 50 percent of women with GDM develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years; women should be counselled about this trajectory at diagnosis to reinforce postpartum follow-up.

subtopic_detail: External cephalic version criteria and timing
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+5 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic having been told at her 36 week ultrasound that her baby is now in a complete breech position. Estimated fetal weight is 2900 g on the 55th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume and a fundal posterior placenta. She had a normal vaginal birth at term 3 years ago. There is no scar, no significant medical history and no known bleeding disorder. She would like to explore all options for a vaginal birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 36 cm; presenting part breech, ballotable; no palpable engagement; cardiotocography reactive; no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: singleton, complete breech, EFW 2900 g (55th centile), amniotic fluid index 14 cm (normal), fundal posterior placenta, no praevia, no cord around neck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to offer?

options.text: Book elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as external cephalic version has a low success rate and is not routinely recommended in Australia for a first breech presentation at term today
options.rationale: ECV has approximately 50 percent success in AU cohorts and is offered routinely; skipping ECV without offer is not consistent with RANZCOG guidance and denies informed choice.

options.text: Attempt external cephalic version now at 36+5 weeks under regional anaesthesia with intravenous salbutamol tocolysis and continuous fetal monitoring before deciding on mode of birth
options.rationale: ECV timing is 37 weeks to allow spontaneous version, and salbutamol IV is not the AU tocolytic of choice; terbutaline SC is standard for ECV.

options.text: Recommend planned vaginal breech birth without external cephalic version as this is a multiparous woman with a proven pelvis and average fetal weight below the 4000 g cut-off
options.rationale: Vaginal breech birth is possible in selected women but ECV should be offered first as it converts to cephalic and lowers overall caesarean rate; jumping to VBB skips the safer first step.

options.text: Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks in a facility with immediate access to caesarean section, with tocolysis using terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously and CTG before and after the procedure
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance recommends ECV from 37 weeks in eligible women with tocolysis, CTG monitoring before and after, and immediate caesarean facilities; there are no contraindications in this scenario.

options.text: Refer for moxibustion therapy at 34 weeks and follow up scan at 38 weeks to confirm fetal position before further intervention or delivery decision on the mode of birth is made
options.rationale: Moxibustion evidence is weak and best used before 34 weeks; at 36+5 the priority is offering ECV at 37 weeks which has a stronger evidence base and is the AU-recommended intervention.

explanation.summary: External cephalic version should be offered to all women with a singleton breech presentation at 37 weeks in the absence of contraindications (praevia, uterine scar in some settings, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, fetal compromise, coagulopathy, antepartum haemorrhage). Success is approximately 50 percent and reduces caesarean rate. The procedure requires tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously, CTG monitoring before and after and access to caesarean facilities.
key_points: Offer ECV at 37 weeks in eligible women with breech
Success rate approximately 50 percent
Terbutaline 250 microgram SC tocolysis; CTG before and after
Must have immediate caesarean facilities available
explanation.pearls: In RhD-negative women, anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU IM is given after ECV regardless of outcome because ECV is a sensitising event; Kleihauer is performed if at 20 weeks or beyond to guide any additional dosing.

subtopic_detail: Primary PPH medical management sequence
stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 woman has just delivered a live term male infant weighing 3900 g vaginally after a normal labour. Third stage is being actively managed with 10 units IM oxytocin. Over the next 10 minutes she loses an estimated 900 mL of blood and continues to bleed briskly. On abdominal palpation the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus. Perineal examination shows no visible tears. Her pre-labour haemoglobin was 118 g/L (115 to 165) and she has no history of bleeding disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 108/60, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, boggy, above umbilicus; perineum intact; no visible cervical or vaginal tears on speculum inspection; bladder empty via catheter
data_table.Investigations: Cumulative EBL 900 mL and ongoing; IV access 2 x 16 gauge; group and screen taken; FBC and coagulation pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medical management step?

options.text: IV ergometrine 250 microgram slow bolus and IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes, uterine bimanual compression, warmed 500 mL crystalloid bolus and call for senior obstetric assistance
options.rationale: In a soft high uterus with ongoing atonic PPH after prophylactic oxytocin, next-line uterotonic is ergometrine plus IV TXA 1 g; bimanual compression, resuscitation and senior review complete the initial bundle.
source_refs: WOMAN trial and AU PPH pathway

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes and IM carboprost 250 microgram, then reassess uterine tone at 15 minutes before further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Magnesium is uterine relaxant and worsens atony; carboprost is a valid uterotonic but not the AU next-line before ergometrine plus TXA in an unallergic non-hypertensive woman.

options.text: IV metoclopramide 10 mg and IM syntocinon 10 unit repeat dose, reposition patient into the left lateral tilt and administer warmed Hartmann 1000 mL bolus over 10 minutes
options.rationale: A second oxytocin dose after prophylactic oxytocin is not first-line escalation; the next-line uterotonic is ergometrine and adding TXA within 3 hours of onset lowers mortality.

options.text: Transfer immediately to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and consideration of Bakri balloon insertion before any further pharmacological uterotonic escalation is initiated at this stage
options.rationale: Bakri balloon is appropriate after failed medical management; skipping the pharmacological escalation is not the AU recommended stepwise approach when brief medical measures have not been attempted.

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg and 2 units fresh frozen plasma empirically while awaiting group and hold result, before administering any additional uterotonic to address the ongoing atony
options.rationale: There is no indication for empirical vitamin K or FFP before coagulation results; the priority is uterotonic escalation with ergometrine plus TXA and mechanical measures.

explanation.summary: For atonic primary PPH after prophylactic oxytocin, the AU next-line uterotonic is ergometrine 250 microgram IV slow bolus with tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset. Carboprost 250 microgram IM is added if bleeding continues (contraindicated in asthma). Concurrent measures include bimanual uterine compression, bladder emptying, warmed IV crystalloid, group and crossmatch and senior obstetric review. Failed medical measures escalate to Bakri balloon then surgical control.
key_points: Ergometrine + TXA is next-line after prophylactic oxytocin
TXA reduces mortality if given within 3 hours (WOMAN trial)
Bimanual compression while pharmacological measures work
Bakri balloon after failed medical management before surgery
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, cardiac disease and Raynaud phenomenon; in these women carboprost is preferred if not asthmatic, or misoprostol 800 microgram sublingually is an alternative uterotonic.

sources.label: WOMAN trial and AU PPH pathway

subtopic_detail: HELLP - timing of delivery and MgSO4
stem: A 28-year-old G1 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation presents to your regional obstetric unit with 2 days of right upper quadrant pain and nausea. She had a normal 20 week anatomy scan and no known chronic hypertension. Her BP today is 162/108 mmHg on repeat measurement. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. She has one episode of visual scotoma but no headache. The fetal heart rate is reassuring on CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 162/108, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.8 C; fetal HR baseline 140 with accelerations
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no clonus but 4+ knee jerks; tender right upper quadrant; no peripheral oedema described; fundal height 33 cm; CTG reactive
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400), Hb 108 g/L (115 to 165), LDH 720 U/L (<250), AST 168 U/L (<40), ALT 156 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (<90), PCR 320 mg/mmol (<30), coagulation normal, film with schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit for conservative management with oral nifedipine 20 mg every 6 hours, twice daily CTG, expectant care until 37 weeks and delay delivery unless fetal or maternal deterioration
options.rationale: Expectant management to 37 weeks in HELLP with severe features is not recommended; delivery within 24 to 48 hours after steroids is the AU standard given ongoing maternal risk of stroke, DIC and eclampsia.

options.text: IV hydralazine 20 mg boluses every 20 minutes for BP control, plasma exchange to remove antibodies and platelet transfusion 1 pool prophylactically, without magnesium sulfate loading now
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is not first-line for HELLP unless progression to thrombotic microangiopathy is confirmed; magnesium is mandatory for eclampsia prophylaxis in severe features.

options.text: Commence IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: This is HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) with severe features (BP >=160/110, visual disturbance, brisk reflexes); magnesium seizure prophylaxis, BP control and expedited delivery after steroid loading are AU standard.

options.text: Emergency caesarean section within the next 30 minutes and IV furosemide 40 mg for BP control while transferring to theatre, without magnesium sulfate or antenatal corticosteroid administration
options.rationale: Fetal status is reassuring and betamethasone significantly reduces neonatal morbidity at 33 weeks; skipping magnesium raises eclampsia risk and furosemide is not the AU first-line antihypertensive here.

options.text: Start IV dexamethasone 10 mg twice daily as definitive HELLP therapy, expectant management for 7 days for maternal biochemical improvement and platelet count recovery before considering delivery
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not modify maternal outcome in HELLP; the definitive treatment is delivery, expedited within 24 to 48 hours after antenatal betamethasone at 33 weeks.

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome with severe features (BP >=160/110, headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, RUQ pain, evidence of end-organ damage) at 33+2 weeks requires IV magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour infusion for eclampsia prophylaxis, tight BP control with labetalol or hydralazine to <150/100, betamethasone for fetal lung maturity and delivery within 24 to 48 hours. Dexamethasone does not improve maternal outcomes. Mode of delivery is by obstetric indication.
key_points: HELLP with severe features triggers MgSO4 loading and BP control
Betamethasone before 34 weeks
Deliver within 24 to 48 hours; do not delay to term
Dexamethasone does not improve maternal HELLP outcomes
explanation.pearls: Watch for subcapsular liver haematoma when RUQ pain worsens with falling haemoglobin and platelet drop; urgent CT or MRI abdomen and multidisciplinary review with hepatobiliary surgery are essential, and hepatic rupture carries maternal mortality above 50 percent.

subtopic_detail: Preterm PROM with chorioamnionitis
stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 woman at 30+4 weeks presents to your maternity unit with 12 hours of a persistent watery loss and now 4 hours of uterine tenderness. Speculum confirms clear fluid pooling in the posterior fornix. She was admitted 3 days ago for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and has been on latency erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly. Her temperature 6 hours ago was 37.4 C. CTG shows a persistent baseline of 168 with reduced variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/68, RR 20, SpO2 99 percent, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender on palpation with mild guarding; clear amniotic fluid pooling on speculum; cervix appears long, closed on visual inspection; no offensive discharge; fetal HR 168 baseline, reduced variability
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10^9/L (4 to 11), CRP 82 mg/L (<5); high vaginal swab and blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Increase erythromycin to 500 mg every 6 hours, continue expectant management to 34 weeks and repeat inflammatory markers in 12 hours before deciding on antibiotic escalation or delivery
options.rationale: Once chorioamnionitis is clinically suspected, latency antibiotics are no longer appropriate; continued expectant care risks maternal sepsis and neonatal early-onset sepsis.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: IV paracetamol 1 g for maternal antipyresis, oral azithromycin 1 g single dose and expectant observation for 6 hours to see if maternal symptoms and fetal heart rate settle before intervention
options.rationale: Antipyresis and observation delay definitive treatment; chorioamnionitis is a maternal and fetal emergency requiring IV antibiotics and delivery, not oral macrolide alone.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy, discontinue latency antibiotic and continue expectant management for a further 48 hours to complete corticosteroid course before planning delivery
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis needs anaerobic and Gram-negative cover which ceftriaxone monotherapy does not reliably provide; standard AU regimen is ampicillin plus gentamicin (add metronidazole intrapartum or postpartum).

options.text: Start indometacin 100 mg per rectum tocolysis to allow completion of steroids over next 48 hours and defer delivery decision until fetal maturity is optimised and infection markers reassessed
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated when chorioamnionitis is present as it may worsen maternal sepsis and delay life-saving delivery.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Commence IV ampicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily, notify neonatal team, arrange delivery expedited within hours regardless of gestation and continue fetal monitoring
options.rationale: Maternal fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia and rising inflammatory markers on PPROM meet AU chorioamnionitis criteria; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and expedited delivery are indicated regardless of gestation.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Chorioamnionitis complicating PPROM is diagnosed by maternal fever plus one or more of maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, or purulent discharge with supporting rising inflammatory markers. Management is IV ampicillin plus gentamicin (metronidazole added intrapartum or postpartum for anaerobic cover), expedited delivery regardless of gestation and neonatal team notification. Tocolysis and expectant care are contraindicated once chorioamnionitis is suspected.
key_points: Fever + uterine tenderness + fetal tachycardia = chorioamnionitis
IV ampicillin + gentamicin (add metronidazole intrapartum) is AU standard
Deliver expeditiously regardless of gestation
Tocolysis contraindicated once chorioamnionitis suspected
explanation.pearls: Latency erythromycin (per ORACLE I) prolongs pregnancy in PPROM without chorioamnionitis; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to increased necrotising enterocolitis risk (per ORACLE II) despite being effective for maternal outcomes.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion recognition and management
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 3 hours ago. She has vomited twice and now feels the pain radiating to the right groin. She uses a Mirena for contraception and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one partner and has no fever. She had an ultrasound 2 months ago for pelvic pain that showed a right ovarian dermoid cyst measuring 6 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 99 percent, temp 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, no rebound; bimanual examination reveals a tender palpable right adnexal mass; cervical motion tenderness minimal; no free fluid clinically
data_table.Investigations: beta-hCG negative, urinalysis normal, WCC 12 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, transvaginal ultrasound: right ovary enlarged 8 cm with heterogeneous echoes, no arterial or venous Doppler flow demonstrated, left ovary normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous morphine 5 mg titrated to pain, cefotriaxone 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg IV for pelvic inflammatory disease, repeat ultrasound in 12 hours if pain does not settle
options.rationale: PID typically has fever, cervical motion tenderness, discharge and does not cause absent Doppler flow; treating as PID delays surgical detorsion and risks ovarian necrosis.

options.text: Emergency laparoscopy for detorsion and ovarian preservation with cystectomy after untwisting rather than oophorectomy, aiming to preserve ovarian function even if the ovary appears necrotic
options.rationale: The sudden severe pain, palpable enlarged ovary and absent Doppler flow on TVS are diagnostic of ovarian torsion; AU consensus favours detorsion and cystectomy even for dusky ovaries because most recover function.

options.text: Urgent CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to characterise the mass and exclude appendicitis before deciding on surgical intervention or continued observation over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: TVS has already shown absent Doppler flow in an enlarged ovary; CT delays definitive detorsion and adds radiation without changing the surgical indication.

options.text: Trial of conservative management with NSAID analgesia for 24 hours as many suspected torsions detorse spontaneously in young women with mobile adnexa and structurally normal contralateral pelvis
options.rationale: Delayed detorsion risks irreversible ovarian necrosis; even suspected torsion warrants urgent surgical exploration in AU pathways.

options.text: Perform emergency oophorectomy immediately if intraoperative findings demonstrate any dusky discolouration of the affected ovary as such ovarian tissue is invariably non-viable in this context
options.rationale: Contemporary evidence shows dusky ovaries frequently recover function after detorsion; oophorectomy is now reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy on frozen section.

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion classically presents as sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an enlarged tender adnexa and absent Doppler flow on transvaginal ultrasound. Any woman with these features requires emergency laparoscopy for detorsion. Contemporary AU practice favours ovarian preservation with cystectomy even for dusky-appearing ovaries, as most regain function; oophorectomy is reserved for confirmed necrosis or suspicion of malignancy.
key_points: Sudden pain + enlarged ovary + absent Doppler flow = torsion
Emergency laparoscopy is the standard next step
Detorsion preserves function even in dusky ovaries
Oophorectomy reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy
explanation.pearls: Ovarian torsion risk is highest with ovarian masses between 5 and 10 cm (very large masses are anchored, very small ones do not create torque); the underlying cyst should be removed after detorsion, ideally at the same procedure to reduce recurrence risk.

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion management
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman has just delivered a live term baby vaginally at your regional hospital following a normal labour with active third stage management using 10 units IM oxytocin. Two minutes after placental delivery she suddenly becomes shocked and complains of severe pelvic pain. On abdominal examination the uterine fundus is not palpable. On vaginal examination a bluish-purple bulging mass is seen at the introitus with the placenta still attached to it. Estimated blood loss is 800 mL and rising.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 82/48, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Absent uterine fundus per abdomen; bulging bluish-purple mass at introitus with placenta partially attached; brisk ongoing bleeding; peripheries cool with cap refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Group and crossmatch and coagulation urgent; 2 x 16 gauge IV; call for obstetric and anaesthetic teams; massive haemorrhage protocol activated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: IV syntocinon 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann as an infusion and IV ergometrine 500 microgram to restore uterine tone before considering manual replacement of the inverted uterus at any time
options.rationale: Uterotonics BEFORE replacement fix the inverted uterus in position by contracting the cervical ring; they are held until after successful replacement, then given to prevent recurrence.

options.text: Detach the placenta by cord traction with the assistance of an ergometrine bolus, then reposition the uterus using O'Sullivan hydrostatic pressure via 500 mL warmed saline into the vagina
options.rationale: Placental separation before replacement causes catastrophic bleeding; replace uterus with placenta attached first, then manage placenta after successful replacement.

options.text: Vaginal packing with a warm saline soaked pack, IV tranexamic acid 1 g and transfer to theatre for laparotomy with the Huntington procedure to replace the uterus abdominally under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Vaginal packing does not treat inversion; surgical replacement (Huntington or Haultain) is reserved for failed manual replacement, not first-line.

options.text: Immediate manual replacement of the uterus using Johnson manoeuvre with the placenta still attached, stop uterotonics, IV fluid resuscitation and prepare for tocolysis with terbutaline if replacement fails
options.rationale: Acute uterine inversion is a life-threatening emergency where the AU first-line manoeuvre is immediate manual replacement (Johnson) with the placenta in situ; delay allows a cervical ring to contract and makes replacement harder.

options.text: Blood transfusion 2 units O negative packed red cells and 1 g intravenous tranexamic acid immediately, then observe blood pressure response for 15 minutes before attempting any uterine intervention
options.rationale: Volume resuscitation is done concurrently, not sequentially before intervention; delay of 15 minutes worsens outcome. Replace uterus while resuscitating.

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare obstetric emergency presenting as sudden shock after delivery with an absent uterine fundus and a mass at the introitus. Immediate management is manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached, before uterotonics or attempted placental separation which cause further bleeding or make replacement impossible. Tocolysis with terbutaline may be needed if a cervical ring has formed. Uterotonics are given only after successful replacement.
key_points: Sudden shock after delivery with absent fundus = uterine inversion
Replace immediately with placenta still attached (Johnson manoeuvre)
Hold uterotonics until after successful replacement
Tocolysis with terbutaline if cervical ring prevents replacement
explanation.pearls: If manual replacement fails, escalate to O'Sullivan hydrostatic replacement (warm saline via douche in the vagina with the vulva sealed by an assistant); operative approaches (Huntington traction on round ligaments, Haultain posterior cervical incision) are last resorts requiring laparotomy under general anaesthesia.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition
stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 39+2 weeks is in the second stage of labour in your birth suite after a spontaneous onset of labour. Membranes ruptured spontaneously 3 hours ago with clear fluid. Just before the crowning of the head she suddenly develops severe agitation, breathlessness and coughs up frothy blood-tinged sputum. She rapidly loses consciousness. Cardiac output is barely detectable and the CTG shows a prolonged deceleration. There is no history of hypertensive disorder or anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 sinus, BP 62/40, RR 40 gasping, SpO2 78 percent room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, altered conscious state, frothy blood-tinged sputum from mouth; brisk vaginal bleeding starting; fetal HR baseline 60 sustained
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG sinus tachycardia; bedside echo: right ventricular dilatation with septal deviation into left ventricle; coagulation dispatched urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Call obstetric and anaesthetic MET, secure airway with rapid sequence intubation, high FiO2 ventilation, IV crystalloid resuscitation with vasopressor support and expedited operative delivery within minutes
options.rationale: This is classical amniotic fluid embolism (sudden hypoxia, hypotension, altered conscious state and coagulopathy peri-delivery); management is airway, oxygenation, vasopressor circulatory support and immediate delivery within 5 minutes to improve maternal and fetal outcome.

options.text: IV heparin 5000 unit bolus and CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm pulmonary embolus before starting anticoagulation and expediting delivery when imaging results are available
options.rationale: AFE typically causes consumptive coagulopathy with severe bleeding; heparin worsens haemorrhage and CT scan delay is fatal. Empirical treatment based on the classical triad is standard.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes and IV labetalol 20 mg bolus assuming eclampsia given the sudden collapse, seizure-like activity and rapid neurological deterioration
options.rationale: There is no hypertension, and the sudden hypoxia, RV dilatation on echo and coagulopathy fit AFE; magnesium is not the treatment and delays airway and circulatory rescue.

options.text: Vaginal pack with warmed saline soaked gauze and IV tranexamic acid 1 g monotherapy while continuing bag mask ventilation and awaiting theatre for elective caesarean under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated in shocked coagulopathic patient; airway must be secured with RSI and delivery expedited within minutes.

options.text: Immediate perimortem caesarean section without airway intervention or circulatory resuscitation to remove the fetus first as this alone will resolve the maternal cardiopulmonary compromise
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean is done after 4 minutes of arrest if ROSC not achieved, alongside continuous resuscitation; skipping airway and circulatory support in a shocked but not yet arrested woman is inappropriate.

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism presents peri-delivery with sudden hypoxia, cardiovascular collapse, altered consciousness and consumptive coagulopathy. Management is simultaneous ABC resuscitation with airway control by RSI, high-flow oxygen, vasopressor support, massive haemorrhage protocol for the coagulopathy and immediate expedited delivery (perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes if cardiac arrest). Empirical treatment based on classical triad; do not delay for confirmatory imaging.
key_points: Sudden hypoxia + collapse + coagulopathy peri-delivery = AFE
Secure airway (RSI), oxygen, vasopressors, MHP
Deliver immediately (perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes if arrested)
Do not delay for CT or heparin
explanation.pearls: Contemporary management includes early use of the A-OK bundle (atropine, ondansetron, ketorolac) which targets vagal, serotonin and thromboxane pathways implicated in AFE; discuss with a maternal-critical-care team early as ECMO may be considered in refractory cases.

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis
stem: You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 weeks who presents in early labour. She had a normal vaginal delivery at term two years ago. Her antenatal course has been unremarkable. A vaginal-rectal swab at 36+2 weeks was positive for Group B streptococcus. She has no drug allergies. Cervical examination reveals 4 cm dilated, 90% effaced, membranes intact. Contractions are every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds. Fetal heart rate baseline is 140 with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 140
data_table.Cervical exam: 4 cm dilated, 90% effaced, station -1, membranes intact
data_table.History: GBS positive vaginal-rectal swab at 36+2 weeks, no penicillin allergy, no previous GBS-affected infant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours until delivery for group B streptococcus prophylaxis
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve intrapartum tissue and cord blood concentrations sufficient to reduce early-onset GBS neonatal disease. Australian and CDC-based intrapartum protocols require IV therapy. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g at the start of the active labour phase
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not the recommended IAP agent and single dosing does not maintain adequate cord blood concentrations across the intrapartum period. Serial IV doses of benzylpenicillin are used. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until delivery for group B streptococcus prophylaxis
options.rationale: Clindamycin is reserved for women with severe penicillin allergy where the isolate has documented clindamycin susceptibility. In an unallergic woman, benzylpenicillin is first-line because of superior efficacy and narrower spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic GBS IAP)

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery
options.rationale: Australian RANZCOG guidance and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommend IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery for GBS-positive women without penicillin allergy, aiming for at least 4 hours of exposure before delivery to reduce early-onset GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and reassess if the maternal temperature rises above 37.8 degrees Celsius
options.rationale: GBS-positive status alone (not intrapartum fever) is the indication for IAP. Waiting for fever misses the window to reduce vertical transmission and early-onset neonatal disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Universal antenatal screening at 35 to 37 weeks or a risk-based approach identifies women needing intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. In a penicillin-tolerant woman with a positive antenatal swab, IV benzylpenicillin loading 3 g followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours is the RANZCOG-endorsed regimen. Adequate prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours between the first dose and delivery.
key_points: GBS positive swab at 35-37 weeks = IAP in labour or ROM at term
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
Cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours if non-severe penicillin allergy
Clindamycin only if severe pen allergy AND documented isolate susceptibility
explanation.pearls: Adequate IAP defined as at least one dose of benzylpenicillin 4 hours or more before delivery; shorter intervals still confer some but reduced benefit.

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G1P0 in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhoea and 3 days of intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort but no heavy bleeding. She has no significant medical history, no allergies, and lives locally with her partner. She works as a primary school teacher and is highly reliable for follow-up. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 26 mm right adnexal mass containing no embryonic pole, no cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG today is 4820 IU/L; a value 48 hours ago at another service was 4180 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed with minimal spotting
data_table.Investigations: bhCG 4820 IU/L today (was 4180 IU/L 48 h ago), Hb 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 258 x10^9/L, LFTs normal, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), transvaginal US 26 mm right adnexal mass without cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin every 48 hours in the outpatient setting
options.rationale: Expectant management is confined to a small subset with bhCG less than 1000 IU/L, a decreasing trend, no adnexal mass or cardiac activity, and no pain. This woman has a rising bhCG above 4800 IU/L with an adnexal mass and pain, so expectant management fails RANZCOG criteria. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
options.rationale: The RANZCOG threshold requiring surgical management is bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher, or the presence of cardiac activity, mass 3.5 cm or larger, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or unreliable follow-up. This woman meets none of the mandatory surgical triggers. Salpingectomy is also more invasive than methotrexate when the tube-sparing medical option remains available. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic salpingostomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
options.rationale: Salpingostomy has higher rates of persistent trophoblast and is largely reserved for cases where the contralateral tube is absent or diseased. Neither medical nor surgical thresholds mandate this approach for the current presentation. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Administer oral mifepristone 200 mg now followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 microgram 48 hours later
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is a medical termination regimen for intrauterine pregnancy and does not treat tubal ectopic. Trophoblast in the tube will continue to grow and risk rupture. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 beta-hCG monitoring
options.rationale: This woman meets Australian RANZCOG criteria for medical management with single-dose methotrexate: bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, haemodynamically stable, reliable for follow-up, no contraindications with normal baseline haematology, renal and liver function. Single-dose 50 mg per m2 IM is standard with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (expect >=15% fall from day 4 to day 7) and weekly bhCG thereafter. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable woman with a tubal ectopic pregnancy meeting RANZCOG criteria: bhCG less than 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, and no contraindications. Success rates approximate 85 to 90% with these thresholds. Failure of bhCG to fall by 15% between day 4 and day 7 triggers a second dose or surgical intervention.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, no cardiac activity, mass <3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, no CI
Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (>=15% fall required)
Surgical management mandated at bhCG >=5000 IU/L or cardiac activity or mass >=3.5 cm or instability
Contraindications include cytopenias, abnormal LFTs, creatinine >120, breastfeeding, hepatic or renal disease
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG >=5000 IU/L (not 3000). Methotrexate remains an option below 5000 with all other criteria met.

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause
stem: A 57-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with a 12-month history of vaginal dryness, dyspareunia and post-coital spotting. Her last menstrual period was 5 years ago. She had breast cancer at age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive) treated with mastectomy, chemotherapy and trastuzumab, with no evidence of recurrence and current oncology sign-off for symptom management. She is otherwise well. She has already trialled a non-hormonal water-based lubricant and a polycarbophil vaginal moisturiser three times weekly for 3 months with only partial relief. She has no urinary symptoms and speculum examination shows pale, thin vaginal walls with loss of rugae, no discharge, and healthy cervix. There is no bleeding after speculum removal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 130/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Vaginal walls pale, thin, loss of rugae, minor petechial contact bleeding, no ulceration or lesion; cervix visible, no discharge
data_table.History: Breast cancer age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive), post-chemo, oncology sign-off given for local symptom therapy, no VTE history, no current medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe estriol 0.03 mg vaginal pessary daily for 2 weeks then twice-weekly maintenance dosing
options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogens (estradiol 10 microgram tablets or estriol 0.03 mg pessaries) produce local mucosal restoration with minimal systemic absorption and are supported by the AMS and RANZCOG for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Recent evidence and IMS 2016 statement support use in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement after non-hormonal therapies fail. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Commence combined oral hormone therapy estradiol 1 mg plus micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Systemic hormone therapy is inappropriate for isolated genitourinary symptoms and carries risks even in ER-negative disease that are hard to justify when a low-dose local option addresses the symptom directly. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Commence oral ospemifene 60 mg daily and arrange in-person symptom review at 6 to 8 weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Ospemifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator not routinely available on the PBS in Australia and generally avoided in women with prior breast cancer because of uncertain breast safety. AMS advises against SERM use in breast cancer survivors. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Refer for fractional carbon dioxide vaginal laser therapy as first-line after moisturiser failure
options.rationale: Vaginal laser therapy is not first-line and lacks the evidence base for efficacy and safety endorsed by the AMS and TGA; the TGA issued a safety alert in 2018. Reserve for after trial of local estrogen with oncology input. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Refer for outpatient cervical biopsy plus office hysteroscopy to exclude endometrial pathology today
options.rationale: Post-coital spotting from a friable atrophic vagina with a normal cervix does not itself mandate hysteroscopy; if postmenopausal bleeding is truly unexplained after treatment of atrophy or if endometrium is thickened on ultrasound (>4 mm), then endometrial assessment is warranted. Directly biopsying without addressing the atrophic cause first is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG PMB)

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause with failure of non-hormonal therapy is treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen. Australian AMS guidance supports this option in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement. Systemic HRT is disproportionate for local symptoms and ospemifene is not first-line in Australia.
key_points: Non-hormonal moisturiser and lubricant trial is first-line for GSM
Vaginal estradiol 10 mcg tablet or estriol 0.03 mg pessary, daily loading then twice-weekly maintenance
Local estrogen is acceptable in most breast cancer survivors after oncology discussion
Vaginal laser therapy is not endorsed as first-line by AMS or TGA
explanation.pearls: Systemic absorption from low-dose vaginal estradiol tablets rarely exceeds baseline postmenopausal serum estradiol; onc consent still documented case-by-case.

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 31-year-old G3P2 at 32+1 weeks referred with confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes at 30 minutes ago. Speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor with pH-positive testing and negative ferning-alternative tests unnecessary. There is no bleeding, no chorioamnionitis features, and no maternal fever. Cervix is closed on visual inspection. Fetal HR 145 with normal reactivity. Ultrasound shows AFI 6 cm, singleton cephalic, EFW 1810 g (50th centile). She has no penicillin allergy and no other medical problems. Her previous two pregnancies delivered at term uneventfully.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum shows clear liquor pooling, closed visual cervix, no bleeding, no offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 9.4 x10^9/L (5.0-11.0), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), CTG reactive baseline 145 variability 10-25 bpm, AFI 6 cm, EFW 1810 g at 50th centile, GBS status unknown from this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Admit for expectant management to 37 weeks with betamethasone plus oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days
options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance for PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or fetal compromise is expectant management to prolong pregnancy, with corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2) for fetal lung maturity, erythromycin (avoid amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in this indication because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal in ORACLE I) for 10 days to prolong latency, and intrapartum GBS prophylaxis given unknown GBS status. Aim for delivery by 37+0 weeks to balance prematurity and infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Proceed to immediate category-1 caesarean section today for fetal safety given confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes
options.rationale: Delivery is triggered by infection, fetal compromise, placental abruption, or reaching 37 weeks. In its absence, expectant management until 37 weeks improves neonatal outcomes because prematurity below 34 weeks poses more risk than the current infectious threat. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Discharge home on oral azithromycin 1 g weekly with weekly outpatient obstetric ultrasound review until 37 weeks
options.rationale: Discharge home is not recommended for PPROM before 34 weeks because of the risk of rapid deterioration from chorioamnionitis, abruption or cord accident. Inpatient care with regular CTG and infection surveillance is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Commence intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin and induce labour with an oxytocin infusion titrated over 12 hours
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and induction are used when chorioamnionitis is diagnosed. In their absence at 32 weeks, expectant management is preferred to allow further fetal lung maturation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose immediately and defer antenatal corticosteroids for 48 hours of observation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours and gestation is less than 30 to 32 weeks; at 32+1 with no evidence of imminent delivery it is not routinely given. Steroids should not be deferred; they are given at diagnosis of PPROM 24 to 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or fetal compromise is managed expectantly to prolong pregnancy with antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days to reduce infection and delay delivery. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk (ORACLE I). Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is given empirically when GBS status is unknown at delivery. Delivery is planned by 37+0 weeks.
key_points: PPROM 24-33+6 weeks without infection: expectant management with steroids + 10 day erythromycin
Corticosteroids: betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 h apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x4 12 h apart)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate contraindicated in PPROM (NEC signal in ORACLE I)
Deliver by 37+0 to balance prematurity vs infection risk
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is loaded 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours at <30-32 weeks gestation.

subtopic_detail: Trial of labour after caesarean
stem: You are the antenatal clinic obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 36+3 weeks. Her first pregnancy ended in emergency classical vertical caesarean section at 30 weeks for placenta praevia with catastrophic haemorrhage and preterm PROM. The operation note confirms a classical upper-segment incision was made because the lower segment was poorly formed and inaccessible. Her current pregnancy is a singleton cephalic and has been uncomplicated. She has read about VBAC on the internet and is asking whether she can have a trial of labour to avoid another caesarean. She has no other medical or surgical history and no allergies. She is well engaged in shared decision-making and asks for a clear recommendation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 36 cm, cephalic presentation, longitudinal lie, engaged head not deep, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms singleton cephalic, EFW 2860 g at 50th centile, anterior placenta well away from previous scar, AFI 12 cm; operative note from prior CS confirms classical vertical upper-segment incision

lead_in: What would you FIRST recommend?

options.text: Support planned trial of labour after previous caesarean with continuous cardiotocography in the tertiary birthing suite
options.rationale: Trial of labour is contraindicated when the prior caesarean incision was classical (vertical upper-segment) because rupture risk approaches 10 to 12% versus <1% for low-transverse. RANZCOG advises against labour in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Recommend planned elective repeat caesarean section at 37+0 weeks after a shared-decision discussion of rupture risk
options.rationale: A prior classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean is an absolute contraindication to trial of labour because uterine rupture rate is 10 to 12% versus under 1% for a single low-transverse incision. RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks to reduce the risk of labour onset while balancing neonatal maturation. Shared decision-making is documented but the recommendation should be specific. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Perform elective repeat caesarean section today at 36+3 weeks under regional anaesthesia in a tertiary theatre
options.rationale: Elective delivery before 37+0 without a specific indication increases neonatal respiratory morbidity. Timing of elective repeat caesarean after classical incision is typically 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Manage expectantly with cervical scoring at 40 weeks and induction using dinoprostone if the cervix is unfavourable
options.rationale: Prostaglandin cervical ripening is contraindicated after prior classical caesarean because of markedly increased rupture risk. Expectant management to 40 weeks is inappropriate given rising labour probability. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Offer an external cephalic version with oxytocin augmentation because the placenta is implanted anteriorly today
options.rationale: The baby is already cephalic, and oxytocin augmentation in a prior classical caesarean is contraindicated. External cephalic version has no role for a cephalic-presenting fetus. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after caesarean is contraindicated when the prior incision was classical (vertical upper-segment), T-incision, or inverted-T because of a substantially higher uterine rupture risk (10 to 12% vs <1% for a single low-transverse scar). RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. Prostaglandin cervical ripening and oxytocin augmentation are contraindicated in prior classical caesarean pregnancies planned for delivery.
key_points: Prior classical (vertical upper-segment) CS = absolute contraindication to trial of labour
Rupture risk classical incision 10-12% vs low-transverse <1%
Elective repeat CS at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks after prior classical incision
Prostaglandin cervical ripening contraindicated after any prior CS scar (RANZCOG)
explanation.pearls: Other absolute contraindications to VBAC: prior uterine rupture, T-shaped or inverted-T scar, transverse lie or breech in labour, placenta praevia or accreta.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top 45 Birth After Caesarean Birth

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks referred by ambulance with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding 45 minutes ago. She has smoked 20 cigarettes per day throughout pregnancy and had gestational hypertension diagnosed at 34 weeks with labetalol 200 mg BD. She is haemodynamically stable. On examination the uterus is tender and firm with palpable contractions every 3 minutes, she has passed approximately 400 mL of dark red blood, cervix is 3 cm on speculum and admits one finger, and the placenta was previously confirmed fundal. CTG shows a baseline of 140, variability 10 to 25 bpm, moderate variable decelerations recovering to baseline, with no late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR baseline 140
data_table.Examination: Tender firm uterus with contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 s, cervix 3 cm on speculum, active moderate PV bleeding estimated at 400 mL
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (2-4), INR 1.1, group and hold sent, CTG reactive baseline 140 with recovering moderate variable decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a further loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously for eclampsia prophylaxis and monitor CTG for 4 hours
options.rationale: The primary problem here is placental abruption at term with active bleeding, contractions and non-reassuring fetal patterns tending to deteriorate. Delaying delivery for magnesium prophylaxis exposes both mother and fetus to further catastrophic haemorrhage. If gestational hypertension had progressed to severe pre-eclampsia with imminent eclampsia signs, magnesium would be part of management but does not delay delivery in an active abruption. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Give subcutaneous terbutaline 250 microgram as tocolysis to permit transfer to a tertiary obstetric centre now
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in active abruption because it may worsen bleeding and delay definitive delivery. It is not part of the management pathway. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Prepare for immediate category-1 caesarean, secure two large-bore intravenous cannulae, and cross-match four units
options.rationale: Suspected placental abruption at 36+4 weeks with active bleeding, tender firm uterus, contractions and fetal compromise warrants urgent delivery. At term or near-term with fetal or maternal compromise, this is by caesarean unless vaginal delivery is genuinely imminent. Two large-bore IV cannulae, cross-match, coagulation studies, MTP awareness (Hb 108, likely underestimates true loss, fibrinogen still normal but consumption risk is high) and neonatal team activation are the concurrent steps. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter, give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g, and reassess CTG in 30 minutes
options.rationale: TXA and urinary catheterisation are useful adjuncts, but a 30-minute wait for reassessment is unsafe in the presence of active abruption with fetal compromise and heavy loss. Delivery should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Commence an oxytocin infusion to augment labour and aim for vaginal delivery with continuous cardiotocography
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation in a bleeding, abrupting uterus at 3 cm cervical dilation without fetal head deep in the pelvis is dangerous and takes hours to achieve delivery. Category 1 caesarean is the safest route. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

explanation.summary: Suspected placental abruption near term with active bleeding, uterine tenderness and any fetal compromise mandates urgent delivery, usually by category 1 caesarean unless vaginal delivery is imminent. Two large-bore IVs, cross-match, coagulation studies, and readiness to activate the massive transfusion protocol are simultaneous. Fibrinogen is a sensitive marker of consumption and DIC risk. Neonatal team must be present.
key_points: Placental abruption at term with maternal or fetal compromise = urgent delivery, usually category 1 CS
Two large-bore IVs, cross-match 4 units, group + coagulation profile including fibrinogen
Fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage is an early trigger for cryoprecipitate
Tocolysis contraindicated in active abruption; oxytocin augmentation contraindicated when delivery is not imminent
explanation.pearls: Peripartum fibrinogen normally rises to 4-6 g/L; a fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage predicts progression to massive haemorrhage and is an early cryoprecipitate trigger.

subtopic_detail: Placenta accreta spectrum
stem: You are the fellow in a maternal-fetal medicine clinic at a tertiary referral hospital. A 36-year-old G4P3 at 30+2 weeks has been referred with placenta praevia on 20-week ultrasound. She has had 3 prior lower-segment caesarean sections and a dilation and curettage after a first-trimester miscarriage 2 years ago. Repeat greyscale and colour Doppler ultrasound at 30 weeks shows an anterior placenta covering the internal os with 2 large lacunae, a hypoechoic myometrial interface with the bladder wall of less than 1 mm in places, and increased subplacental vascularity. Bladder wall bulging is present. She has no antepartum bleeding today. She is asymptomatic. MRI has been booked for tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 30 cm, no abdominal tenderness, no palpable bladder, no active PV bleeding, cephalic presentation on Leopold's manoeuvre
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound anterior praevia covering os, 2 large lacunae, myometrium-bladder interface <1 mm, bladder-wall bulging, increased subplacental vascularity; MRI booked for tomorrow morning; haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 220 x10^9/L, group and antibody screen O positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with continuous cardiotocography and postpartum haemorrhage readiness in the birth suite
options.rationale: Placenta praevia with strong ultrasound features of placenta accreta spectrum absolutely contraindicates a vaginal delivery attempt because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Delivery is by planned caesarean at a tertiary centre. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)
