options.text: Plan lower-segment caesarean at 39+0 weeks by the on-call obstetrician after in utero transfer to a regional hospital
options.rationale: Placenta accreta spectrum requires multidisciplinary tertiary-centre management. Regional facilities without interventional radiology, cell salvage, immediate blood products and colorectal or urological backup are the wrong setting, and delivery timing at 39 weeks is too late. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan classical caesarean at 34+0 weeks with attempted piecemeal manual placental removal to avoid hysterectomy today
options.rationale: Attempted forced placental removal in placenta accreta spectrum precipitates massive haemorrhage. The standard approach when accreta is confirmed is caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ, or occasionally a conservative leave-in-situ approach in highly selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan elective preterm caesarean at 32+0 weeks with vertical skin incision without steroids or magnesium neuroprotection
options.rationale: Delivery at 32 weeks is earlier than recommended when the mother is stable and asymptomatic; RANZCOG recommends 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for suspected placenta accreta spectrum unless bleeding, contractions, or fetal compromise force earlier delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection should also be given for planned preterm delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan elective caesarean-hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team present
options.rationale: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum with strong ultrasound features and prior caesarean history should be delivered by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with a dedicated multidisciplinary team. Standard care includes antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, planned caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ (preferred to piecemeal removal), interventional radiology for possible internal iliac balloon occlusion, urology on standby for possible bladder involvement, cell salvage, and pre-optimisation of iron stores. RANZCOG endorses this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with strong antenatal ultrasound features (lacunae, myometrial thinning, bladder wall bulging, hypervascularity) in the setting of prior caesarean plus praevia is managed by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre. Multidisciplinary team includes maternal-fetal medicine, interventional radiology, urology, senior anaesthesia, neonatology and blood bank. Standard operative approach is caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ rather than attempted removal.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum: deliver 34+0 to 35+6 weeks by planned caesarean at tertiary centre
Multidisciplinary team: MFM, IR, urology, senior anaesthesia, senior neonatology, blood bank
Standard operation: caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ (do not attempt removal)
Pre-optimise iron; antenatal corticosteroids for preterm delivery; consider cell salvage
explanation.pearls: Sensitivity of ultrasound plus colour Doppler for placenta accreta approaches 90% in high-volume centres; MRI adds most value for suspected posterior placentation or when depth of invasion (percreta) is unclear.

subtopic_detail: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
stem: You are the maternal-fetal medicine registrar reviewing a 26-year-old primigravida at 20+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. She was booked at 12 weeks with chorionicity confirmed. Serial ultrasound today shows twin 1 with deepest vertical pocket (DVP) 2 cm, twin 2 with DVP 12 cm, twin 1 bladder not visualised over the 60-minute scan, twin 2 EFW 20% larger than twin 1, both twins with normal umbilical artery Doppler and normal middle cerebral artery Doppler, and normal ductus venosus Doppler in both twins. There is no evidence of fetal hydrops. She has no contractions, no bleeding, cervix is 34 mm on transvaginal ultrasound. She lives 3 hours drive from the nearest fetal therapy centre.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, twin 1 fetal HR 148, twin 2 fetal HR 152
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound monochorionic diamniotic twins, twin 1 DVP 2 cm with bladder not visualised for 60 minutes (donor), twin 2 DVP 12 cm (recipient), EFW discordance 20%, umbilical artery Doppler normal both twins, MCA Doppler normal both twins, ductus venosus Doppler normal both twins, no hydrops, cervix 34 mm
data_table.History: Primigravida, monochorionic diamniotic twins confirmed at 12 weeks, 3-hour drive from fetal therapy centre, no contractions or bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently today to a national fetal therapy centre for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
options.rationale: This is Quintero Stage II twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: oligohydramnios in donor (DVP 2 cm at 20 weeks; less than 2 cm is required for stage I; combined with non-visualised bladder over 60 minutes moves to Stage II), polyhydramnios in recipient (DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks). Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks is managed with fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses, which improves at least one twin survival from 33% (amnioreduction alone) to 76% (Eurofetus and Solomon trials). Australian fetal therapy is centralised at select tertiary centres and urgent referral today is essential to allow assessment and intervention within the treatable window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Perform therapeutic amnioreduction at the local hospital and continue serial ultrasound assessments every 2 weeks
options.rationale: Serial amnioreduction has substantially inferior outcomes to fetoscopic laser for Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks (Eurofetus trial: laser survival benefit sustained at 6 months). It is retained as a temporising measure only when laser is not available or the woman is beyond the treatable gestational window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Recommend expectant management with weekly ultrasound and no intervention until Doppler indices become abnormal
options.rationale: Once Quintero Stage II is reached, intervention improves outcomes substantially. Waiting for Doppler abnormalities allows progression to Stage III or IV where perinatal outcomes are markedly worse. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Discuss selective feticide of the donor twin now as the preferred first-line intervention at this gestation
options.rationale: Selective feticide is reserved for cases with impending demise of one twin or where laser is contraindicated or unsuccessful. It is not first-line when fetoscopic laser remains a treatment option. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Plan urgent delivery this week by caesarean section given the current Quintero staging and gestational age
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is not survivable. Delivery for TTTS is planned around 34 to 37 weeks after successful in utero treatment, unless earlier for obstetric or fetal reasons. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Quintero staging for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: Stage I (donor DVP <2 cm with recipient DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks), Stage II (bladder not visualised in donor for at least 60 minutes), Stage III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), Stage IV (hydrops in either twin), Stage V (in utero demise of one or both twins). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses at a fetal therapy centre. Eurofetus RCT showed superiority over amnioreduction.
key_points: Quintero Stage II TTTS: oligohydramnios donor, polyhydramnios recipient, donor bladder not visualised in 60 min
Fetoscopic laser ablation for Stage II or higher between 16-26 weeks is standard of care
Eurofetus RCT: laser at least one twin survival 76% vs amnioreduction 51%; better neurological outcomes at 6 months
Amnioreduction reserved for beyond treatable window or centre inaccessibility
explanation.pearls: Australian fetal therapy is centralised (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane) and referral is national; treating within Quintero Stage II or III before hydrops onset offers best neurodevelopmental outcomes.

subtopic_detail: New pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks referred by her midwife for elevated blood pressure of 168/108 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since morning and one episode of epigastric discomfort. There is no visual disturbance, no vaginal bleeding, and normal fetal movements. She has no prior hypertension, no chronic kidney disease, and no significant family history. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and she has bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. Fetal heart rate is 148 with reactive CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/108, pulse 92, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Urine: protein/creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (<30), no blood, no leukocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, load magnesium sulfate 4 g IV, admit for delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34+ weeks with severe hypertension, symptoms and heavy proteinuria requires acute BP control (IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours after corticosteroid completion is not required after 34+0. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Start oral labetalol 200 mg 12-hourly, admit for expectant management with twice weekly review
options.rationale: Severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia (>=160/110 mmHg) requires rapid IV or fast-acting oral treatment to lower BP within 15 to 30 minutes; oral labetalol 12-hourly is too slow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Perform an immediate category-1 caesarean section without acute BP control given severe hypertension present
options.rationale: Immediate delivery without prior BP control risks maternal stroke; acute treatment of severe hypertension precedes and continues through delivery. Vaginal delivery is not contraindicated when maternal and fetal condition allow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Discharge home with sublingual nifedipine 10 mg as required and midwife visit tomorrow morning for repeat BP
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous BP drop and is not used in pre-eclampsia; discharge is unsafe given severe features (BP, symptoms, proteinuria) requiring inpatient monitoring and delivery planning. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Give IV furosemide 40 mg for oedema and start oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Furosemide is not first line and reduces already contracted intravascular volume in pre-eclampsia. Methyldopa is safe in pregnancy but its onset is slow and unsuitable for severe hypertension requiring rapid control. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP >=160/110, symptoms, heavy proteinuria) at or beyond 34 weeks requires acute BP control with IV labetalol or hydralazine, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis (4 g IV load then 1 g/hour), and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are not indicated after 34+0 weeks. Vaginal delivery is preferred when maternal and fetal status allow. Continuous CTG and strict fluid balance limited to 80 mL/hour reduce pulmonary oedema risk.
key_points: Severe BP threshold: >=160/110 mmHg treated with IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine 5 to 10 mg
Magnesium sulfate loading 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Delivery within 24 to 48 hours at or beyond 34+0 weeks with severe features
Fluid restriction 80 mL/hour to avoid pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Target BP after treatment is 140 to 150 / 80 to 100 mmHg to avoid placental hypoperfusion; overshoot toward normotension in a chronically hypertensive placenta can cause acute fetal distress.

subtopic_detail: Aspirin prophylaxis for pre-eclampsia
stem: You are the GP obstetric shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at her booking visit at 10+3 weeks. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by pre-eclampsia at 33 weeks requiring preterm delivery. She has chronic hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily and a BMI of 33. She has no bleeding disorder, no aspirin allergy, and no history of peptic ulcer disease. She is a non-smoker. Her BP today is 132/84 with urine dipstick clear.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 132/84, pulse 78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, weight 88 kg
data_table.History: Previous PET at 33 weeks, chronic HTN on labetalol, BMI 33, no aspirin allergy, no peptic ulcer
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 umol/L (45-90), no proteinuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic recommendation?

options.text: Defer aspirin until 20+0 weeks when placental circulation matures and start at a dose of 75 mg once daily
options.rationale: Aspirin started after 16+0 weeks has substantially reduced benefit for PET prevention because trophoblast invasion is largely complete. Starting between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks gives maximal benefit. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Start aspirin 150 mg oral at night from 12+0 weeks and continue until 36+0 weeks gestation completed
options.rationale: SOMANZ and RANZCOG recommend low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, current evidence favours 150 mg) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36 to 37 weeks in women with one or more high-risk factors (prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes) OR two or more moderate risk factors. This patient has two high-risk factors. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Prescribe elemental calcium 1.5 g daily as first-line prevention instead of aspirin due to safety profile
options.rationale: Calcium supplementation reduces PET risk primarily in women with low dietary calcium intake. In an Australian setting with adequate calcium intake, aspirin is the preferred prophylaxis in high-risk women. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Advise conservative dietary sodium restriction to below 2 g per day and no pharmacological prophylaxis required
options.rationale: Sodium restriction does not reduce PET risk and may worsen intravascular volume depletion. This patient has clear indications for aspirin prophylaxis given prior PET plus chronic HTN. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Prescribe enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily throughout pregnancy for placental insufficiency prevention
options.rationale: LMWH is not indicated for PET prevention alone; its use in pregnancy is for VTE prophylaxis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Aspirin is the correct choice for PET prophylaxis in this patient. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, 150 mg preferred) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36+0 weeks reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia by approximately 60 percent when started in early pregnancy in high-risk women. High-risk factors include prior PET, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, pre-existing diabetes, and autoimmune disease. Two or more moderate risk factors (nulliparity, age >=40, BMI >=35, family history, IVF, multiple pregnancy interval) also indicate prophylaxis. The window is critical: starting after 16 weeks loses much of the benefit.
key_points: Start aspirin 100 to 150 mg at night between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks
Continue until 36+0 weeks (stop before delivery to reduce bleeding risk)
High-risk indication: prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, diabetes, autoimmune disease
Calcium supplementation is second line in low-dietary-calcium populations
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 150 mg reduces preterm PET by approximately 62 percent (ASPRE trial 2017); the effect at term PET is smaller. Timing (before 16+0) matters more than dose within the 100 to 150 mg range.

subtopic_detail: Moderate hyperemesis gravidarum
stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 26-year-old primigravida at 9+2 weeks with 5 days of persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. She has lost 3.8 kg (5.2 percent of pre-pregnancy weight). She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no diarrhoea, no vaginal bleeding, and no dysuria. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones and specific gravity 1.030 with no leukocytes or nitrites. Bedside ultrasound confirms a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dates with no adnexal mass. She has already tried oral ginger with no benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Na 133 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Cl 92 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 umol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.48, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urine ketones 3+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Discharge on oral pyridoxine 40 mg TDS plus doxylamine 25 mg nocte with GP review the following morning
options.rationale: This patient has severe dehydration, hypokalaemia, ketonuria and metabolic alkalosis; discharge is unsafe. Admission for IV rehydration is warranted before oral therapy is likely to work. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Give IV 5 percent dextrose 1 L over one hour then metoclopramide 10 mg IV before considering discharge from ED
options.rationale: Dextrose without preceding thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in prolonged vomiting. Normal saline with potassium is preferred first, and thiamine must be given before any glucose load. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Admit for IV normal saline with added potassium and give thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose containing fluid
options.rationale: Moderate to severe hyperemesis with dehydration and hypokalaemia requires IV rehydration with normal saline (avoid dextrose containing solutions initially) plus potassium replacement. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Add pyridoxine plus doxylamine and second-line antiemetic (ondansetron or metoclopramide) as pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for two weeks as first-line steroid therapy for refractory presentation today
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered only after failure of stepped pharmacotherapy including pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron and metoclopramide, and are avoided before 10 weeks due to a small oral cleft signal. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Order urgent MRI brain to exclude posterior fossa lesion before any antiemetic therapy is commenced overnight
options.rationale: There are no neurological signs or atypical features to suggest raised intracranial pressure; investigations for secondary causes are reserved for unusual features. Empiric treatment for hyperemesis is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe hyperemesis gravidarum (PUQE >=13, weight loss >5 percent, ketonuria, electrolyte disturbance) requires admission for IV rehydration with normal saline plus potassium and stepped antiemetic therapy: pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron (first trimester use is now considered safe in most guidance), metoclopramide. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory disease after 10 weeks.
key_points: IV normal saline with potassium; avoid initial dextrose without prior thiamine
Thiamine 100 mg IV before any glucose load in prolonged vomiting
Stepped antiemetics: pyridoxine + doxylamine, then ondansetron or metoclopramide
PUQE score categorises severity (mild <7, moderate 7 to 12, severe >=13)
explanation.pearls: Ondansetron in the first trimester carries a small absolute cardiac malformation signal (approximately 3 additional cases per 10,000 exposures) balanced against the harms of untreated severe hyperemesis; RANZCOG considers benefit outweighs risk with informed consent.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency in third trimester
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 30-year-old G3P2 at 30+1 weeks referred with tiredness and a haemoglobin of 92 g/L on routine bloods. She has previously tried oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for the past 4 weeks but describes intolerable epigastric pain and constipation and admits to non-adherence for the last 2 weeks. She has no bleeding, no chronic disease, and no known haemoglobinopathy. Iron studies confirm iron deficiency. Her booking Hb was 116 g/L and she has no thalassaemia trait. She is not Rh negative.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Hb 92 g/L (110-140), MCV 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 ug/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8 percent (20-40)
data_table.History: Failed oral ferrous sulfate (intolerance), 30+1 weeks, no bleeding, no haemoglobinopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase oral ferrous sulfate to 325 mg three times daily and add ascorbic acid 500 mg to enhance absorption
options.rationale: Recent evidence favours alternate day dosing over multiple daily doses (hepcidin rise blocks absorption). She has documented intolerance; escalating is unlikely to succeed and IV iron is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer for a two unit packed red blood cell transfusion this week to correct haemoglobin promptly for delivery
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia (Hb <70), haemodynamic compromise, or ongoing bleeding. Hb 92 with iron deficiency responds to IV iron with lower risk than transfusion. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Recommend dietary iron increase alone with red meat, leafy greens, and legumes daily and repeat FBE at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Dietary iron alone cannot correct established iron deficiency anaemia at 30 weeks with ferritin 8 in the required timeframe before delivery. Active replacement is required. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a single IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion of 1000 mg over 15 minutes as an outpatient day case
options.rationale: IV iron is indicated for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy after 13 weeks when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when rapid replenishment is needed (>28 weeks with anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose is convenient and effective; ferric derisomaltose (Monofer) is an alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Start intramuscular iron sucrose 200 mg daily for 5 doses at the local community pharmacy over the coming week
options.rationale: Intramuscular iron is not routinely used in pregnancy (staining, pain, unreliable absorption). Iron sucrose IV requires multiple visits; ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose allow single-dose replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: IV iron in pregnancy is indicated after the first trimester when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when replenishment before delivery is needed (typically >28 weeks with iron deficiency anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes and ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg allow single-dose replacement; iron sucrose requires multiple 200 mg doses. Anaphylaxis risk is very low with modern formulations but resuscitation facilities must be available. Oral iron alternate day dosing improves absorption over daily dosing (hepcidin biology).
key_points: IV iron indications: oral failure, intolerance, non-adherence, need for rapid correction >28 weeks
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes as single outpatient dose
Ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg alternative (higher single dose cap)
Transfusion reserved for Hb <70 or haemodynamic compromise
explanation.pearls: Hypophosphataemia after ferric carboxymaltose is common (approximately 40 percent) and may cause fatigue or bone pain; check phosphate 2 to 4 weeks post-infusion if symptomatic. Ferric derisomaltose has lower hypophosphataemia risk.

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria at 14 weeks
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor reviewing a 27-year-old primigravida at 14+2 weeks. Her routine midstream urine culture returned pure growth of Escherichia coli at 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, trimethoprim, and amoxicillin. She has no urinary symptoms, no fever, no back pain, and no vaginal discharge. She has no drug allergies, no G6PD deficiency, no chronic kidney disease, and is not currently on any regular medications. She has never had a UTI before this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSU: E. coli 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, trimethoprim, amoxicillin
data_table.History: 14+2 weeks, no symptoms, no G6PD, no CKD, no allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days with folic acid 5 mg daily due to interference with folate metabolism
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonism, neural tube defect signal) and generally not used in pregnancy unless no alternative. At 14 weeks it is second choice. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Fosfomycin 3 g single sachet orally taken on an empty stomach with 200 mL of water at bedtime for optimal effect
options.rationale: Fosfomycin single dose is an option in non-pregnant women but is not first line in Australian pregnancy guidance where 5 to 7 day treatment courses are recommended. Nitrofurantoin remains first line in the second trimester. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Wait for symptoms to develop before treating and repeat MSU at 20 weeks to confirm bacteriuria persists longer
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy warrants treatment because up to 30 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis without therapy, and bacteriuria is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days as first-line therapy because E. coli sensitivity is confirmed here
options.rationale: Amoxicillin resistance in community E. coli is around 50 percent even with reported susceptibility on some panels; nitrofurantoin or cefalexin are preferred first-line agents in pregnancy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days and repeat MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis (60 percent risk if untreated) and preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin is first line in the second trimester (avoid at term and near delivery due to neonatal haemolysis risk). Duration is 5 to 7 days and a test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks later. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated because 20 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis and there is an association with preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is first line in the second trimester; cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is an alternative. Nitrofurantoin is avoided at term (34 weeks onward) and near delivery because of neonatal haemolysis risk. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester due to folate antagonism. A test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks after treatment.
key_points: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO 6-hourly for 5 days first line in second trimester
Avoid nitrofurantoin from 34 weeks onward (neonatal haemolysis)
Test of cure MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: In G6PD deficiency, nitrofurantoin causes haemolysis at any gestation. In this cohort choose cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days or amoxicillin plus clavulanate 500/125 mg 8-hourly (based on susceptibility) instead.

subtopic_detail: Complete molar pregnancy follow-up
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 25-year-old G1P0 following suction curettage yesterday for a confirmed complete hydatidiform mole diagnosed on ultrasound (snowstorm appearance) with a pre-operative beta hCG of 285,000 IU/L. Histology has confirmed complete mole. She is otherwise well, no bleeding, and observations are normal. She is not on any contraception and asks about future pregnancy plans. She reports her partner is very keen for a family soon.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: beta hCG 285000 IU/L pre-op, Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Preoperative USS: snowstorm appearance, no adnexal mass, no theca lutein cysts, empty uterus post-evacuation on today's scan

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan?

options.text: Serial serum beta hCG weekly until three negative results then monthly for 6 months, effective contraception advised
options.rationale: Complete mole surveillance is weekly serum beta hCG until three consecutive normal results then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or condoms; avoid IUD until hCG normal) prevents pregnancy that would confound hCG surveillance and delay recognition of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Discharge with GP follow-up if any bleeding recurs; no formal hCG monitoring required after evacuation is complete
options.rationale: Surveillance is essential to detect GTN, which affects 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and 1 to 5 percent of partial moles. Missing follow-up delays chemotherapy for treatable disease. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Start prophylactic methotrexate 50 mg IM weekly for 8 weeks as chemoprophylaxis to reduce recurrence risk
options.rationale: Prophylactic chemotherapy is not routinely recommended; surveillance identifies those needing treatment and avoids unnecessary chemotherapy in most patients. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Insert copper intrauterine device today to provide long-acting reversible contraception during monitoring
options.rationale: IUD insertion is deferred until beta hCG has normalised, as insertion trauma and rare uterine perforation of residual disease raise concerns about persistence detection and haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Arrange staging CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis this week to exclude metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
options.rationale: Staging imaging is performed when GTN is diagnosed (plateau or rise in hCG, histological features) not routinely after evacuation of a mole with expected declining hCG. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

explanation.summary: After suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, serum beta hCG is monitored weekly until three consecutive normal results, then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or barrier) is used to prevent pregnancy that would confound surveillance; IUD is avoided until hCG is normal. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops in 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and requires methotrexate or actinomycin D. Referral to a specialist GTD service is recommended.
key_points: Weekly beta hCG until 3 normal results then monthly for 6 months (complete mole)
Partial mole: weekly until 3 normal then discharge
Effective contraception during surveillance; avoid IUD until hCG normal
15 to 20 percent of complete moles develop GTN needing chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: FIGO criteria for GTN after mole: hCG plateau over 4 measurements 3 weeks apart, hCG rise >=10 percent over 3 measurements 2 weeks apart, hCG persisting >=6 months after evacuation, or histological choriocarcinoma.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins timing of delivery
stem: You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 34+0 weeks with an uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. Fortnightly ultrasound surveillance since 16 weeks has shown concordant growth, normal Dopplers, no TTTS features, and both amniotic sacs with normal fluid volumes. Both twins are cephalic-cephalic. She is asymptomatic. She had a spontaneous vaginal delivery in her first pregnancy at term. She has no significant medical history and no contraindication to vaginal birth. Cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Ultrasound today: Both twins cephalic, EFW 2100 g and 2150 g (concordant), normal Dopplers, no TTTS, AFI both sacs normal, cervix 32 mm
data_table.History: MCDA twins, uncomplicated, prior SVD at term, no medical comorbidity

lead_in: What is the recommended timing and mode of delivery?

options.text: Elective delivery at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks with vaginal birth if leading twin cephalic and no contraindications
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends delivery of uncomplicated MCDA twins between 36+0 and 36+6 weeks because of the increased stillbirth risk beyond 37 weeks. Vaginal birth is appropriate when the leading twin is cephalic and there are no obstetric or fetal contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue expectant management to 39+0 weeks and induce at that point if no spontaneous labour has yet occurred
options.rationale: Continuing beyond 37 weeks in MCDA twins increases perinatal mortality. The stillbirth risk in monochorionic pregnancy rises earlier than in dichorionic, so delivery is planned earlier. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Deliver by elective caesarean section at 37+0 weeks regardless of presentation because of monochorionicity alone
options.rationale: Monochorionicity alone is not an indication for caesarean when both twins are appropriately grown and the leading twin is cephalic. Vaginal birth is preferred when feasible. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Elective delivery at 38+0 weeks by induction of labour matching the recommended timing for dichorionic twin sets
options.rationale: Dichorionic twins are delivered at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; monochorionic diamniotic at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; monochorionic monoamniotic by caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Elective delivery at 32+0 weeks with antenatal steroids and neonatal team present as monoamniotic protocol applies
options.rationale: Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) twins are delivered by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks. MCDA are delivered later (36+0 to 36+6). Confusing the two chorionicities is a common error. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Delivery timing in twins is guided by chorionicity: dichorionic diamniotic at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; monochorionic diamniotic at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; monochorionic monoamniotic by caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. Mode of delivery is guided by presentation and fetal status; vaginal birth is appropriate when the leading twin is cephalic and there are no contraindications. Continuous CTG in labour and early recourse to caesarean for the second twin are standard. Second twin non-cephalic delivery may be by breech extraction or internal podalic version with an experienced operator.
key_points: MCDA delivery 36+0 to 36+6 weeks (uncomplicated)
DCDA delivery 37+0 to 37+6 weeks (uncomplicated)
MCMA delivery by caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks with steroids
Vaginal birth if leading twin cephalic and no contraindications
explanation.pearls: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in MCDA/MCMA for early detection of TTTS, TAPS and sIUGR; DCDA scans 4-weekly. Discordance >20 percent EFW warrants closer surveillance and consideration of delivery.

subtopic_detail: Decreased fetal movements at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 34+3 weeks who has attended day assessment because of reduced fetal movements over the past 12 hours; previously her baby was very active. She reports no bleeding, no leaking, no pain, and is otherwise well. She has no significant obstetric history and had normal 20 week anomaly ultrasound and normal growth scans. She has no medical comorbidity. Symphysis-fundal height is 34 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, longitudinal lie, cephalic, SFH 34 cm, no bleeding
data_table.History: Decreased fetal movements 12 hours, otherwise well, 34+3 weeks, no risk factors

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Reassure and discharge home with fetal movement chart and advice to return if concerns persist next 24 hours
options.rationale: RANZCOG (and PSANZ Safer Baby Bundle) recommend CTG plus growth ultrasound after any episode of decreased fetal movements at or beyond 28 weeks; discharge without assessment misses fetal compromise. Kick charts are no longer routinely recommended. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

options.text: Continuous CTG for at least 20 minutes and arrange a growth and Doppler ultrasound within 24 hours
options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance on decreased fetal movements is CTG for 20 minutes minimum plus consideration of ultrasound for growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical Doppler within 24 hours if this is the first episode or with any risk factors. The Safer Baby Bundle standardises this response. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

options.text: Arrange immediate category-1 caesarean section this hour on the basis of the maternal report alone without CTG
options.rationale: Delivery is triggered by evidence of fetal compromise on CTG or ultrasound, not by the symptom alone. Empirical delivery exposes mother and baby to preterm and surgical risks unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

options.text: Advise a large sugary drink, lie on left side, and recount movements over 2 hours before any medical assessment
options.rationale: Provocative measures (sweet drinks, side-lying) are not evidence based and delay assessment. Present-day RANZCOG guidance is prompt CTG and imaging as needed. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

options.text: Empirical betamethasone dose today and elective induction of labour in 48 hours for suspected placental dysfunction
options.rationale: Steroids and delivery are not empirically triggered by decreased fetal movements alone. Assessment must confirm fetal compromise or growth restriction before this pathway is chosen. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

explanation.summary: Decreased fetal movements at or beyond 28 weeks warrant prompt assessment with continuous CTG for at least 20 minutes plus ultrasound for growth, amniotic fluid volume, and Doppler within 24 hours (particularly if this is a first episode or there are risk factors). Kick charts are not routinely recommended. The Safer Baby Bundle (PSANZ) standardises response and has been associated with reduced stillbirth rates in Australia. Recurrent DFM prompts consideration of delivery from 39+0 weeks even if surveillance is reassuring.
key_points: CTG for at least 20 minutes plus ultrasound within 24 hours
Kick charts not routinely recommended
Safer Baby Bundle standardises response to reduce stillbirth
Recurrent DFM: consider delivery from 39+0 weeks
explanation.pearls: Perception threshold for fetal movement counts varies widely; the pattern change (a definite decrease from a previously active baby) is more predictive than an absolute number. Sudden increase in vigorous movement also warrants assessment (uncommonly associated with cord accident).

subtopic_detail: Rhesus D negative routine prophylaxis
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor reviewing a 24-year-old primigravida at 27+5 weeks. Her booking blood group is O RhD negative with a negative antibody screen. She has had no antenatal bleeding, no invasive procedures, and no external cephalic version. She has no other medical problems. Partner blood group is unknown. Her booking bloods are otherwise normal. She has no allergies to blood products and no previous exposure to anti-D immunoglobulin.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Booking bloods: Group O RhD negative, antibody screen negative, no sensitising events, no procedures
data_table.History: Primigravida, 27+5 weeks, no bleeding, partner group unknown, no prior anti-D exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Give a single anti-D 1500 IU dose at 34 weeks only, with no antenatal dose earlier and no post-delivery dose
options.rationale: The single-dose regimen gives 1500 IU at 28 weeks, not 34 weeks. A post-delivery dose adjusted by Kleihauer is essential if baby is RhD positive to prevent sensitisation from fetomaternal haemorrhage at birth. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

options.text: Only give anti-D post-delivery if baby is RhD positive; no antenatal prophylaxis if there is no sensitising event
options.rationale: Routine antenatal anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks (or single 1500 IU at 28 weeks) reduces sensitisation from silent fetomaternal haemorrhage. This is standard care in Australia irrespective of sensitising events. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

options.text: Give anti-D 625 IU intramuscular at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, plus at delivery if baby is RhD positive
options.rationale: Australian NBA guidance for RhD negative non-sensitised women is routine anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks (two-dose regimen; a single 1500 IU dose at 28 weeks is an alternative). Post-delivery dose is given within 72 hours if baby is RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer. Additional doses are given after sensitising events. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

options.text: Determine paternal RhD group first and withhold anti-D if the father is proven to be RhD negative on testing
options.rationale: Paternal group is not reliable enough to alter management because paternity may be uncertain and cell-free fetal DNA typing is not yet routine in Australia. Prophylaxis is given based on maternal RhD alone. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

options.text: Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular now and repeat every 4 weeks throughout pregnancy for maximum sensitisation prevention
options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is used for first-trimester sensitising events; routine antenatal prophylaxis in the second half of pregnancy is 625 IU or single 1500 IU. Monthly dosing is not standard. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

explanation.summary: Routine anti-D prophylaxis for RhD negative non-sensitised women in Australia is 625 IU IM at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks (two-dose regimen), or a single 1500 IU dose at 28 weeks. Post-delivery dose within 72 hours if baby is RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer for fetomaternal haemorrhage. Additional doses for sensitising events: 250 IU IM for events before 12 weeks, 625 IU for events 12 to 20 weeks, and 625 IU with Kleihauer testing for events after 20 weeks.
key_points: Routine: 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks OR single 1500 IU at 28 weeks
Post-delivery: within 72 hours if baby RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer
First trimester sensitising event: 250 IU
Sensitising event 12 to 20 weeks: 625 IU
explanation.pearls: Kleihauer estimates fetal cells per 5 mL maternal blood; additional anti-D 125 IU per mL of fetomaternal haemorrhage above 6 mL. For large FMH give IV anti-D preparations for faster absorption if available.

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia first-line manoeuvres
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite when a 32-year-old G3P2 at 40+2 weeks in spontaneous labour delivers the head of an appropriately grown baby but no restitution occurs and the head retracts against the perineum (turtle sign) with no further progress despite maternal effort during the next contraction. She had no gestational diabetes and estimated fetal weight was 3600 g. She has no known coagulopathy and epidural is in situ providing analgesia. There is no cord prolapse and CTG has been reassuring throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Intrapartum: Full dilation reached 40 min ago, head delivered 30 seconds ago, turtle sign, no restitution
data_table.Fetal: Reassuring CTG until delivery of head, EFW 3600 g, no cord prolapse

lead_in: What is the correct first-line manoeuvre?

options.text: Immediate category-1 caesarean section after replacement of the head using the Zavanelli manoeuvre technique
options.rationale: Zavanelli (cephalic replacement and caesarean) is a last-resort manoeuvre after failed conventional efforts. First-line is McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Apply vigorous fundal pressure downward on the maternal abdomen at the height of the next uterine contraction
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture. Suprapubic pressure (above the symphysis directed toward the anterior shoulder) is used. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Perform immediate midline episiotomy first and pull firmly on the fetal head to complete delivery without further steps
options.rationale: Episiotomy alone does not resolve shoulder dystocia (a bony problem) and downward traction risks brachial plexus injury. Manoeuvres to disimpact the shoulder are required. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Ask the mother to flex both hips and knees onto her abdomen (McRoberts position) and apply suprapubic pressure now
options.rationale: The HELPERR mnemonic starts with H (call for Help), E (evaluate for episiotomy), L (Legs into McRoberts), P (suprapubic Pressure), E (Enter manoeuvres: Rubin II, Woods screw), R (Remove posterior arm), R (Roll onto all fours). McRoberts alone or with suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of dystocias. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Start an oxytocin infusion to strengthen contractions and encourage additional pushing effort by the mother now
options.rationale: Augmenting contractions does not overcome a bony impaction and risks worsening injury. The problem requires positional and manual manoeuvres, not more contractions. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is managed using the HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs into McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips to abdomen), suprapubic Pressure (downward and lateral toward the anterior shoulder to disimpact from symphysis), internal Enter manoeuvres (Rubin II rotation of anterior shoulder, Woods screw of posterior shoulder), Remove posterior arm, Roll onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre). McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of cases. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy, or Cleidotomy are last resort. Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic: Help, Evaluate, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter, Remove, Roll
McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of cases
AVOID fundal pressure (worsens impaction, uterine rupture risk)
AVOID downward traction on fetal head (brachial plexus injury)
explanation.pearls: Time is critical to reduce hypoxic injury and Erb's palsy risk; document minutes from head delivery, manoeuvres attempted with times, staff present, and cord gases postnatally. Debrief and formal clinical review afterward reduces medicolegal risk.

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening at age 25
stem: You are the GP seeing a 25-year-old woman for her first cervical screening test since turning 25. She is sexually active, has been vaccinated against HPV as a schoolgirl, has no abnormal bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no known immunosuppression. She has never had cervical screening before because she declined uptake at prior GP visits. She has no HIV, no transplant, and no chronic immunosuppressive therapy. She is not pregnant. She asks whether she can self-collect the sample.

data_table.History: 25 years old, HPV vaccinated, sexually active, no symptoms, first CST, no immunosuppression, not pregnant
data_table.Vital signs: unremarkable
data_table.Preference: Self-collection acceptable to patient if offered

lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening plan?

options.text: Perform a Pap smear cytology every 2 years from age 21 onwards continuing throughout the reproductive years
options.rationale: The Australian program switched from Pap cytology every 2 years to primary HPV testing every 5 years for ages 25 to 74 in December 2017. Cytology alone is no longer the primary screening test. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Test HPV plus reflex liquid-based cytology and continue every 12 months regardless of the first result obtained here
options.rationale: Reflex cytology is only triggered by an HPV-positive result (except HPV 16 or 18 which triggers direct colposcopy). Annual screening is not recommended in a healthy vaccinated 25 year old. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Screening is not required until age 30 because she has completed the HPV vaccination schedule as a schoolgirl
options.rationale: HPV vaccination reduces but does not eliminate cervical cancer risk (vaccines cover 9 high-risk types but not all). Screening starts at 25 regardless of vaccination status. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Colposcopy referral as the initial screening approach since she has never had any prior cervical screening test
options.rationale: Colposcopy is not a screening test; it is used for triage of HPV-positive results (particularly types 16/18) or after abnormal cytology. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Offer HPV self-collection or clinician-collected sample; if HPV negative next screen in 5 years time
options.rationale: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program (NCSP) uses primary HPV testing every 5 years for women aged 25 to 74. Since July 2022, self-collection has been available to all screening participants; it is analytically equivalent to clinician-collected samples for HPV testing. Return interval is 5 years if HPV negative. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program screens women aged 25 to 74 with primary HPV testing every 5 years. Self-collection has been available to all screening participants since July 2022 and is analytically equivalent to clinician-collected samples for HPV testing (but does not allow reflex cytology on the same sample, requiring recall for cytology if HPV positive not 16/18). HPV 16 or 18 positive triggers direct colposcopy referral; other HR HPV positive triggers reflex cytology on the sample. Exit test at 70 to 74 if two consecutive normal screens.
key_points: Primary HPV test every 5 years, ages 25 to 74
Self-collection available to all since July 2022
HPV 16/18 positive: direct colposcopy
Other HR HPV positive: reflex cytology
explanation.pearls: Self-collected samples require recall for a clinician-collected sample if HPV positive (not 16/18) because cytology cannot be performed on self-collected specimens. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women are strongly encouraged to participate in screening; self-collection may improve engagement.

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding first-line therapy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 35-year-old woman with 12 months of heavy menstrual bleeding causing flooding on 3 to 4 days of each cycle, requiring 2-hourly pad change and passing clots. She has no intermenstrual bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no pelvic pain. Cervical screening is up to date and negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus with no fibroids, polyps, or endometrial thickening. FBE shows Hb 106 g/L with ferritin 12. She has completed her family (2 children), takes no medications, and has no VTE history. Bimanual examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Bloods: Hb 106 g/L (115-155 female), ferritin 12 ug/L (30-200), TSH normal, coagulation screen normal
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic USS: normal uterus, endometrial thickness 6 mm, no polyps, no fibroids, no ovarian mass
data_table.History: Family complete, no VTE, no smoking, no migraine with aura, cervical screening up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 52 mg) as first-line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause
options.rationale: NICE and RANZCOG recommend the LNG-IUS (Mirena 52 mg) as first-line for HMB without structural cause when contraception is acceptable. It reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 95 percent, corrects anaemia, and offers 5 years of contraception. Other options (tranexamic acid, COCP) are second line if LNG-IUS declined. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

options.text: Endometrial ablation as first-line surgical management before any trial of medical or hormonal therapy is undertaken
options.rationale: Ablation is second line after failed medical therapy in HMB without structural cause. Medical therapy (LNG-IUS first) is preferred initial treatment. Ablation is not contraceptive and pregnancy after ablation is high risk. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive treatment because it eliminates the possibility of recurrence entirely
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but is a last resort after failed medical and less invasive surgical options. It is not first-line for HMB with normal uterus and completed family. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

options.text: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg oral daily and expectant management with review in 12 months when anaemia has resolved
options.rationale: Iron replacement is important adjunct but does not treat the HMB. Waiting 12 months delays effective therapy while ongoing bleeding perpetuates anaemia. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

options.text: GnRH agonist depot injection for 6 months to induce medical menopause followed by expectant observation only
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are used short-term before surgery or to control severe symptoms; they cause menopausal symptoms and bone loss so long-term use requires add-back HRT. They are not first-line for uncomplicated HMB. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

explanation.summary: First-line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause and where contraception is acceptable is the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 52 mg, Mirena), which reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 95 percent and provides 5 years of highly effective contraception. Alternatives include tranexamic acid 1 g PO 6-hourly on bleeding days (non-hormonal, non-contraceptive), COCP (contraceptive), and cyclic oral progestogens (higher failure rate). Endometrial ablation and hysterectomy are second-line surgical options after failed medical therapy. Structural cause (fibroid, polyp, adenomyosis, malignancy) is excluded before assuming primary HMB.
key_points: LNG-IUS first line for HMB without structural cause
Tranexamic acid 1 g QID during bleeding: non-hormonal alternative
Ablation second line after medical failure
Hysterectomy is definitive last resort
explanation.pearls: Endometrial biopsy is indicated in HMB with age >=45, persistent bleeding despite treatment, or risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen use, family history of Lynch syndrome).

subtopic_detail: Contraception initiation after birth
stem: You are the GP seeing a 30-year-old woman at 3 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her second child. She is exclusively breastfeeding and is going well with lactation. She wants effective contraception before returning to sexual activity. She has no VTE history, is a non-smoker, has BMI 26, no migraine, and no hypertension. Her preference is for a hormonal oral option rather than an intrauterine device. She is not experiencing depression symptoms.

data_table.History: 3 weeks postpartum, exclusive breastfeeding, previous SVD, no VTE, non-smoker, no migraine, BMI 26
data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 118/74, pulse 74
data_table.Preference: Oral hormonal contraception preferred over LARC or barrier

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting now to give effective ovulation suppression during breastfeeding period
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC/AUMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) until 6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding, and category 3 (risks usually outweigh benefits) from 6 weeks to 6 months in breastfeeding women, because of VTE risk and reduced milk supply. Not appropriate here. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

options.text: Progestogen-only pill (POP) can start today; category 1 or 2 for breastfeeding at any time from 21 days postpartum
options.rationale: Progestogen-only methods (POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS) can be started from 21 days postpartum in breastfeeding women; UKMEC/AUMEC category 1 to 2. They do not affect breast milk supply or contain estrogen. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

options.text: Barrier method only until 6 months postpartum and no hormonal contraceptive during exclusive breastfeeding period
options.rationale: Progestogen-only methods are safe from 21 days postpartum in breastfeeding women. Barriers alone have higher failure rates. Lactational amenorrhoea method has strict criteria and only lasts 6 months. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

options.text: Insert copper intrauterine device today at the GP appointment even though she has expressed preference for oral option
options.rationale: Copper IUD can be inserted from 4 weeks postpartum but she has stated a preference for oral hormonal contraception. POP meets her needs. IUD insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks postpartum is associated with increased expulsion. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

options.text: Depo-Provera injection today then combined oral contraceptive from 6 months postpartum after weaning is completed
options.rationale: DMPA is a reasonable option but she prefers oral. Progestogen-only pill fits her preferences and can start today. Complex sequencing is not needed. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception timing depends on breastfeeding status and time from birth. Combined hormonal contraception is category 4 until 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (VTE risk plus milk supply) and category 3 from 6 weeks to 6 months breastfeeding; category 3 until 3 weeks and category 2 from 3 to 6 weeks postpartum in non-breastfeeding women. Progestogen-only methods (POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS) are category 1 to 2 from 21 days postpartum regardless of breastfeeding. Copper IUD from 4 weeks (or immediately post-placenta with expulsion risk).
key_points: COC: category 4 breastfeeding < 6 weeks; category 3 breastfeeding 6 weeks to 6 months
POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS: from 21 days postpartum any status
Cu IUD or LNG-IUS: from 4 weeks postpartum (or immediately post-placenta)
LAM alone: only if <6 months, exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic
explanation.pearls: Fertility returns approximately 6 weeks after birth in non-breastfeeding women; earlier fertility return is possible so contraception should be discussed before discharge from hospital, not left to the 6 week check.

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage at 8 weeks with fetal heart present
stem: You are the GP seeing a 28-year-old primigravida at 8+3 weeks with 2 days of light painless per vaginal bleeding. Speculum shows a closed cervix and mild dark bleeding, no products of conception seen. She has no fever, no severe pain, and no dizziness. Transvaginal ultrasound today confirms an intrauterine pregnancy with a live embryo, CRL consistent with 8+2 weeks and fetal heart rate 154 bpm. She has no significant medical history and no Rh negative blood group. Vital signs are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Closed cervix, mild dark bleeding, no adnexal tenderness, no products seen
data_table.Ultrasound: IUP with live embryo CRL 8+2, FHR 154 bpm, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Empiric progesterone 400 mg pessary twice daily until 16 weeks as suggested by PRISM trial in every case here
options.rationale: PRISM trial supports vaginal progesterone in women with threatened miscarriage AND previous miscarriage(s); benefit in first-episode threatened miscarriage without prior loss is small. Empiric use in every case is not recommended in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

options.text: Bed rest for 2 weeks with no work attendance and daily transvaginal ultrasound scans to monitor pregnancy status
options.rationale: Bed rest does not reduce miscarriage rates and daily ultrasounds provide no additional useful information. Neither is recommended. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

options.text: Expectant management with return advice for increased bleeding, severe pain, or reduced pregnancy symptoms today
options.rationale: Threatened miscarriage with a live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound has approximately 95 percent chance of continuing when the fetal heart rate is confirmed at 8 weeks. Management is expectant with safety-net advice. Anti-D is not required in the first trimester unless there is a specific sensitising event (surgical management, therapeutic termination, ectopic surgery). (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

options.text: Suction curettage this afternoon to prevent progression to inevitable miscarriage and complete the pregnancy loss
options.rationale: There is a live pregnancy on ultrasound; there is no indication for surgical intervention. Threatened miscarriage with live embryo continues in 95 percent of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

options.text: Empirical anti-D immunoglobulin injection today because she has had per vaginal bleeding in first trimester
options.rationale: The patient is not Rh negative so anti-D is not required. Anti-D in the first trimester is given for RhD negative women only after specific sensitising events (miscarriage requiring surgical management, therapeutic termination, ectopic surgery, chorionic villus sampling). (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage is per vaginal bleeding in pregnancy with a closed cervix and a live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. When fetal heart is present at 8 weeks, approximately 95 percent of pregnancies continue. Management is expectant with safety-net advice (increasing bleeding, severe pain, faintness, fever, or loss of pregnancy symptoms). Progesterone is considered in women with a history of previous miscarriage (PRISM trial). RhD negative women receive anti-D 250 IU IM only after specific first-trimester sensitising events, not for spontaneous bleeding alone.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage with live IUP at 8 weeks: ~95 percent continue
Expectant management with safety-net advice
Progesterone only if history of previous miscarriage(s)
Anti-D in T1 for RhD negative only after specific sensitising events
explanation.pearls: Beta hCG serial testing (48-hour doubling) is used when ultrasound is inconclusive; a rise of at least 53 percent over 48 hours is expected in viable IUP under 6+3 weeks. Above discriminatory hCG (2000 IU/L) an intrauterine sac should be visible on TVUS.

subtopic_detail: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 27-year-old woman at 22+1 weeks with 4 days of vulval itch, thick white discharge, and superficial dysuria. Speculum reveals typical thick white curd-like discharge with erythema and no cervical motion tenderness. She has no fever, no pelvic pain, and no risk factors for STI. She has no known allergies and has no history of recurrent thrush. She has previously used oral fluconazole for the same symptoms outside of pregnancy without adverse effect. Point-of-care wet prep shows budding yeast; pH 4.2; no clue cells; no trichomonads.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema, thick white curd-like discharge, no CMT, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Wet prep: Budding yeast present; pH 4.2; no clue cells; no trichomonads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose repeated once after 72 hours as it worked previously without adverse effect
options.rationale: Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy: any-dose exposure is associated with a small spontaneous abortion signal and 400 mg/day plus exposure with tetralogy of Fallot and other malformations. Topical treatment is preferred throughout pregnancy. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

options.text: Oral itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for a single day and abstain from intercourse for one week completely
options.rationale: Oral azoles including itraconazole are category B3 in pregnancy and generally avoided. Topical clotrimazole is preferred and effective. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

options.text: Intravaginal boric acid 600 mg pessary daily for 14 days as antimicrobial therapy in pregnancy for the itch
options.rationale: Boric acid is contraindicated in pregnancy (embryotoxicity and no reliable safety data). It is reserved for resistant non-albicans species in non-pregnant patients. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

options.text: Clotrimazole 100 mg intravaginal pessary at night for 6 nights and clotrimazole 1 percent cream to vulva as needed
options.rationale: In pregnancy, topical imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole) are first line for vulvovaginal candidiasis; a 7-day course (100 mg nightly or 200 mg for 3 nights) is preferred because pregnancy-related recurrence is common with shorter courses. Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy because of cardiac malformation and spontaneous abortion signals. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

options.text: Betamethasone valerate 0.05 percent cream applied twice daily to the vulva for symptom relief as monotherapy today
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid alone does not treat candidiasis; it will worsen the infection and provides only transient symptom masking. Antifungal is required. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

explanation.summary: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy is treated with topical imidazoles (clotrimazole 100 mg pessary nightly for 6 nights, or 200 mg for 3 nights, plus vulval cream). Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy because of miscarriage and cardiac malformation signals (particularly at doses of 400 mg per day or more). Recurrence is common in pregnancy; a longer 7-day course is preferred over single-dose or 3-day therapy. Recurrent (>=4 episodes per year) or resistant candidiasis prompts culture and sensitivity because non-albicans species (glabrata, krusei) require different agents.
key_points: Topical clotrimazole pessary 100 mg nightly for 6 nights (or 200 mg x 3 nights) in pregnancy
Avoid oral fluconazole and other oral azoles in pregnancy
Longer course preferred in pregnancy due to recurrence risk
Culture if recurrent or resistant (non-albicans species need different treatment)
explanation.pearls: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (>=4 episodes per year) outside of pregnancy is treated with induction (fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses) then maintenance (fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months). This regimen is not used in pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Chronic hypertension in early pregnancy on ACE inhibitor
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor seeing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 8+2 weeks with chronic hypertension diagnosed 2 years ago. She has been taking perindopril 5 mg daily with good control. She reports BP is running 128/82 at home. She had a prior term delivery without complication before starting perindopril. She has no proteinuria, no cardiac or renal disease, and no other medications. She wants to know whether her medication is safe in pregnancy and whether it should continue.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.History: Chronic HTN 2 years on perindopril 5 mg, prior term SVD, no proteinuria, no CKD, no other meds
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 68 umol/L (45-90), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), no proteinuria on dipstick

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.text: Continue perindopril at the current dose because it is providing good BP control and pregnancy is well established
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, IUGR and neonatal hypotension, and are contraindicated in second and third trimester; first trimester exposure carries cardiac and CNS malformation signals. Cease as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Continue perindopril in the first trimester and switch to labetalol at the start of the second trimester exposure
options.rationale: ACEi carry first-trimester malformation signals (cardiac, CNS), so early switch is preferred. Continuing exposure through T1 adds unnecessary risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Stop perindopril and start hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg orally daily as first-line pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive
options.rationale: Thiazides are generally avoided in pregnancy because they reduce plasma volume and can worsen placental hypoperfusion; first-line pregnancy antihypertensives are labetalol, methyldopa, and slow-release nifedipine. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Stop perindopril and start atenolol 50 mg orally daily as long-term beta blocker for pregnancy-safe control
options.rationale: Atenolol is associated with IUGR and is generally avoided in pregnancy. Labetalol is a preferred alpha and beta blocker with a better fetal safety profile. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Stop perindopril today and start labetalol 100 mg orally twice daily titrated to BP with methyldopa alternative
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated across pregnancy; cease at diagnosis of pregnancy and switch to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive: labetalol first line, methyldopa alternative, nifedipine slow release as third option. Target BP is <140/90 in chronic HTN in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, IUGR, and neonatal hypotension in the second and third trimesters, and carry cardiac and CNS malformation signals in the first trimester. Cease at pregnancy confirmation. First-line pregnancy antihypertensives are labetalol (100 to 400 mg BD or TDS), methyldopa (250 to 500 mg TDS), and nifedipine slow release (30 to 60 mg daily). Target BP in chronic HTN in pregnancy is <140/90 (CHIPS trial supports tight control). Atenolol is avoided (IUGR). Thiazides reduce plasma volume.
key_points: ACEi and ARBs contraindicated across pregnancy; cease at confirmation
First line: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine SR
Target BP <140/90 in chronic HTN in pregnancy (CHIPS)
Avoid atenolol (IUGR) and thiazides (volume depletion)
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 100 to 150 mg nocte from 12 to 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia risk by ~60 percent in high-risk women (chronic HTN, prior PET, CKD, autoimmune, diabetes). This patient has a clear indication.

subtopic_detail: Suspected choledocholithiasis at 26 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar consulted about a 30-year-old G1 at 26+3 weeks admitted with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and pale stools. She has no fever, no rigors, and remains haemodynamically stable. Bloods show cholestatic LFT rise with markedly raised bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound shows a distended common bile duct 10 mm with a suspected distal stone; no acute cholecystitis; multiple small gallstones present in the gallbladder. She is not septic and observations are normal. She has no allergies and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Imaging: CBD 10 mm distended, suspected distal stone, multiple gallstones in GB, no cholecystitis, no ductal dilatation intrahepatic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management step?

options.text: Arrange MRCP for diagnostic confirmation; if choledocholithiasis confirmed, proceed to ERCP with lead shielding
options.rationale: MRCP is safe in pregnancy (no ionising radiation) and diagnostic for CBD stones. If confirmed, ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is performed with lead shielding of the fetus and minimised fluoroscopy time. Interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned, ideally in T2 (safest window). (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

options.text: Proceed directly to open cholecystectomy and common bile duct exploration today under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Direct surgery without confirming CBD stone is unnecessary. MRCP is diagnostic and non-invasive; ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is preferred for CBD stones in pregnancy. Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned after ERCP, ideally in second trimester. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the most appropriate first imaging to evaluate the biliary tree and stones
options.rationale: CT exposes the fetus to ionising radiation and is less sensitive than MRCP for CBD stones. MRCP is preferred as the non-radiation alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

options.text: Conservative management with IV antibiotics and analgesia for 2 weeks until postpartum ERCP after birth
options.rationale: Delaying treatment risks ascending cholangitis, pancreatitis, and sepsis. ERCP is safe in pregnancy with lead shielding. Definitive treatment should not wait until after birth if choledocholithiasis is confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

options.text: Immediate delivery by category-2 caesarean section to allow definitive surgical management of the biliary disease
options.rationale: Delivery is not required for choledocholithiasis; it is treated with ERCP in pregnancy. Preterm delivery for a non-obstetric surgical condition adds unnecessary neonatal risk. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

explanation.summary: Suspected choledocholithiasis in pregnancy is investigated with MRCP (no ionising radiation) and treated with ERCP plus sphincterotomy under fluoroscopy with lead shielding of the fetus if confirmed. Interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned, ideally in the second trimester (T2 is the safest window: T1 has organogenesis concerns; T3 has surgical access and preterm labour risk). Delay of definitive treatment risks cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis. Uncomplicated biliary colic can be managed conservatively but recurrent symptoms indicate cholecystectomy.
key_points: MRCP first line (no ionising radiation) for suspected CBD stones in pregnancy
ERCP with lead shielding for confirmed choledocholithiasis
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy ideally in T2 (safest window)
Do not delay treatment (cholangitis, pancreatitis risks)
explanation.pearls: Gallstone disease is 2 to 3 times more common in pregnancy due to elevated estrogen (increased cholesterol saturation) and reduced gallbladder motility (progesterone). Ursodeoxycholic acid does not resolve established stones but is used in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy for symptom relief.

subtopic_detail: Suspected uterine rupture during VBAC
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar attending a 34-year-old G2P1 with previous lower-segment caesarean section undergoing trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC) at 40+2 weeks. She is at 8 cm dilatation on epidural analgesia with an oxytocin augmentation running. She reports sudden severe suprapubic pain that persists between contractions. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm sustained for 3 minutes. On abdominal examination, the presenting part is no longer felt at the previously reached station and there is fresh vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically borderline.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Intrapartum: Prior LSCS, 8 cm on oxytocin, sudden severe pain persisting between contractions, station lost, fresh PV bleed
data_table.Fetal: Prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm, no recovery for 3 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue oxytocin at current rate and give tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously to relieve uterine hypertonus
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not appropriate when rupture is suspected. Oxytocin must be stopped and delivery expedited. Terbutaline would delay definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Stop oxytocin, resuscitate with fluids and cross-match, arrange emergency category-1 laparotomy for suspected rupture
options.rationale: The clinical picture (sudden severe pain, station loss, fresh bleeding, prolonged deceleration, maternal instability, prior CS) is highly suggestive of uterine rupture. Immediate actions: stop oxytocin, IV fluid resuscitation, cross-match blood, call for senior support, and proceed to emergency category-1 laparotomy for delivery and repair or hysterectomy. Uterine rupture in TOLAC occurs in approximately 0.5 to 1 percent of trials of labour. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Perform urgent bedside ultrasound to rule out placental abruption before proceeding to any operative delivery decision
options.rationale: Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis and time to delivery is critical for fetal survival. Delaying for imaging risks fetal death and maternal exsanguination. Move to laparotomy on clinical grounds. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Attempt instrumental vaginal delivery with forceps to expedite delivery while operating theatre is being prepared for use
options.rationale: At 8 cm dilatation instrumental delivery is not possible (requires full dilatation). Suspected rupture with a high station and haemodynamic instability requires laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Give IV bolus antibiotic prophylaxis and observe for 30 minutes to see whether the CTG spontaneously recovers back
options.rationale: Observation delays essential treatment. Prolonged decelerations without recovery within a few minutes, in the context of suspected rupture, mandate immediate laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)
