explanation.summary: Uterine rupture during TOLAC is a life-threatening emergency for mother and baby. Classical features include sudden severe suprapubic pain persisting between contractions, loss of station, fresh vaginal bleeding, prolonged fetal heart rate deceleration, maternal haemodynamic compromise, and cessation of contractions. Immediate management: stop oxytocin, IV resuscitation, cross-match 4 units, call for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, and proceed directly to category-1 laparotomy. At laparotomy the fetus is delivered rapidly and the uterus repaired if feasible, or hysterectomy performed for uncontrolled haemorrhage.
key_points: Uterine rupture: sudden severe pain, station loss, fresh PV bleed, prolonged deceleration, maternal collapse
Immediate: stop oxytocin, IV resuscitation, cross-match, cat-1 laparotomy
Do NOT delay for imaging or tocolysis
Risk in TOLAC ~0.5 to 1 percent; classical CS scar precludes VBAC
explanation.pearls: Prior classical (vertical) caesarean, T- or J-incision, or fundal uterine surgery (myomectomy involving cavity) are contraindications to VBAC because of much higher rupture risk (4 to 9 percent for classical vs 0.5 to 1 percent for LSCS).

subtopic_detail: Suspected magnesium sulfate toxicity
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia commenced on IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose followed by an infusion at 1 g/hour 6 hours ago. She now reports blurred vision, generalised weakness, and difficulty in swallowing. Nursing staff report she has become drowsy in the last 15 minutes. Deep tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally. Respiratory rate is 8 per minute. She has a background of stage 2 CKD (creatinine 130 umol/L) that was known before admission. Urine output has been 15 mL over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 62, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 8, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, absent DTRs bilaterally, diaphragmatic weakness on inspection, oliguria
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 158 umol/L (from baseline 130), potassium 4.4, magnesium level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue magnesium at current rate and give naloxone 400 mcg IV to reverse suspected opioid respiratory depression cause
options.rationale: The features are consistent with magnesium toxicity, not opioid effect. Naloxone will not reverse magnesium and continuing infusion will worsen toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Increase IV fluid rate to 250 mL/hour and continue magnesium at reduced 0.5 g/hour rate for continued PET prophylaxis
options.rationale: Fluid loading in pre-eclampsia risks pulmonary oedema (contracted intravascular volume with capillary leak). Continued infusion at any rate in toxicity is unsafe until level is known and toxicity resolved. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion, give 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 10 minutes, and check serum magnesium
options.rationale: Loss of DTRs, respiratory depression (RR <12), and drowsiness in a patient on magnesium sulfate suggest toxicity, especially given reduced renal clearance (CKD, worsening creatinine, oliguria). Immediate actions: stop the infusion, give calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV over 10 minutes as physiological antagonist, and check serum magnesium urgently. Support ventilation if respiratory arrest. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Give IV furosemide 40 mg to increase magnesium excretion and reduce serum level over the next 2 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Furosemide can cause further volume depletion and does not immediately reverse toxicity. Calcium gluconate is the direct antagonist. Furosemide is used cautiously only after infusion is stopped and antidote given. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Initiate haemodialysis with vascular access placed via femoral vein this hour for magnesium removal from bloodstream
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for severe refractory toxicity with anuria not responding to conservative measures. Stopping infusion, calcium gluconate, and supportive care are first line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate toxicity occurs at serum levels above 3.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2 to 3.5 mmol/L). Progressive signs: loss of DTRs (>3.5), respiratory depression (>5), cardiac conduction delay and arrest (>7). Renal impairment reduces clearance and increases toxicity risk. Immediate management: stop infusion, give 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 10 minutes as antagonist, check serum magnesium, monitor respiration and cardiovascular status, support airway and ventilation if needed. Adjust dose in renal impairment (halve maintenance to 0.5 g/hour and check levels every 4 hours).
key_points: Toxicity signs: loss of DTRs, RR <12, drowsiness, cardiac conduction changes
Immediate: stop infusion, calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV
Renal impairment: halve maintenance rate and check levels every 4 hours
Therapeutic range 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; toxicity >3.5 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Fetal magnesium exposure at delivery can cause neonatal hypotonia, respiratory depression, and hyporeflexia; alert the neonatal team if delivery occurs within 24 hours of infusion. Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis is loaded at 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion; some protocols use 5 g IM to each buttock plus 5 g IM every 4 hours (Pritchard regimen).

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta at 45 minutes with brisk bleeding
stem: You are the obstetric registrar attending a 28-year-old G3P2 at 40+1 weeks who delivered vaginally 45 minutes ago after active management of the third stage (oxytocin 10 units IM given, controlled cord traction attempted). The placenta remains undelivered, cord traction has been unsuccessful, and there is now brisk PV bleeding estimated at 800 mL. The uterus is deviated to the right and feels boggy. She has a functioning epidural in situ from labour. She is haemodynamically stable but observations are trending toward tachycardia. IV access is patent with a 16 gauge cannula and cross-match sent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus deviated right, boggy on palpation, cord in situ, brisk PV bleeding, placenta not delivered
data_table.Third stage: 45 min elapsed, oxytocin 10 U IM given, CCT unsuccessful, estimated 800 mL blood loss

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give an intraumbilical vein injection of oxytocin 20 units in 20 mL saline via the placental cord to deliver the placenta
options.rationale: Intraumbilical vein oxytocin has been studied but has limited evidence of benefit and is not first line when there is active bleeding. Manual removal is the definitive treatment when the placenta has not delivered at 30 to 60 minutes with active bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Wait another 30 minutes for spontaneous separation while giving IM ergometrine to encourage delivery of the placenta
options.rationale: Ergometrine causes uterine contraction that can trap the placenta and worsen bleeding. Waiting further with active haemorrhage delays essential treatment. Manual removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Perform bimanual uterine compression and give a further oxytocin 10 units IM before considering surgical intervention
options.rationale: Bimanual compression is for atonic PPH after placenta is delivered. Uterus cannot involute with placenta in situ. Manual removal is the correct intervention. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Empty the bladder, transfer to theatre for manual removal under spinal or epidural top-up, IV oxytocin infusion, and give prophylactic antibiotics
options.rationale: Retained placenta at 30 minutes with active bleeding requires manual removal under regional (spinal or epidural top-up) or general anaesthesia. Empty the bladder first (distension impairs uterine contraction), give IV oxytocin infusion to maintain uterine tone, prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole) as intrauterine manipulation is being performed, and cross-match blood. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Proceed to emergency subtotal hysterectomy as definitive haemorrhage control since manual removal has not been attempted
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is a last-resort for uncontrollable haemorrhage after manual removal, bimanual compression, uterotonics, tranexamic acid, and Bakri balloon fail. It is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined as failure to deliver the placenta within 30 minutes of active management of the third stage (or 60 minutes of physiological management). If bleeding is active, manual removal is required earlier. Management: empty bladder, transfer to theatre, regional (spinal or epidural top-up) or general anaesthesia, manual removal, IV oxytocin infusion, prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole), tranexamic acid 1 g IV, cross-match blood, and inspect for retained products. Placenta accreta spectrum is suspected if the placenta will not separate manually.
key_points: Retained placenta: >30 min after active management (or 60 min with physiological)
Manual removal in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia
Empty bladder, IV oxytocin, prophylactic antibiotics, TXA 1 g IV
Suspect placenta accreta if placenta will not separate manually
explanation.pearls: Umbilical cord blood collection for cord gases is standard whenever there is intrapartum concern (CTG changes, meconium, shoulder dystocia); an arterial pH <7.0 or base excess <-12 supports significant intrapartum hypoxic-ischaemic injury for medicolegal documentation.

subtopic_detail: Aspirin failure with new severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36-year-old G3P1 (with a prior pre-eclampsia and prior stillbirth at 34 weeks) at 32+1 weeks. She has been on aspirin 150 mg from 13 weeks. She has developed BP of 172/112 mmHg, severe headache, and epigastric pain over 24 hours. Bloods show a rapid rise in creatinine and low platelets. Urine protein/creatinine ratio is 350 mg/mmol. CTG is currently reactive. She has no HELLP features on LFTs. Estimated fetal weight is 1650 g on today's ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 172/112, pulse 96, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 108 umol/L (from baseline 68), ALT 42 U/L (<35), LDH 245 U/L (135-225), urate 0.48 mmol/L (0.15-0.35)
data_table.Fetal: CTG reactive, EFW 1650 g, umbilical Doppler normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Discharge on oral labetalol 400 mg TDS with community midwife review every 3 days until symptoms improve here
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP >=160/110, severe symptoms, low platelets, rising creatinine, heavy proteinuria) is not managed as outpatient. Immediate inpatient care with acute BP control, magnesium sulfate, and delivery planning is required. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Continue expectant management with weekly clinic review until 37 weeks then induce labour if symptoms have resolved
options.rationale: Expectant management to 37 weeks is not safe with severe pre-eclampsia features. Maternal risk (stroke, HELLP, eclampsia, renal failure) mandates earlier delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Emergency category-1 caesarean section within 30 minutes without acute BP control or magnesium sulfate loading first
options.rationale: Delivery is planned within 24 to 48 hours after corticosteroids and BP stabilisation. Cat-1 CS without pre-op BP control risks maternal stroke. Cat-1 is reserved for imminent maternal or fetal risk (eclamptic seizure, abruption, non-reassuring CTG). (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Stop aspirin immediately as it has failed to prevent pre-eclampsia and start high-dose prednisolone 40 mg orally daily
options.rationale: Aspirin is stopped for delivery to reduce bleeding risk. Prednisolone is not treatment for pre-eclampsia; corticosteroids in this context are for fetal lung maturity (betamethasone or dexamethasone). (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg (repeat every 10 min), IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, deliver in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 32+ weeks: acute BP control (IV labetalol 20 to 80 mg or IV hydralazine 5 to 10 mg), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2 24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturity as under 34 weeks, and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours (after steroids complete) balancing maternal deterioration against preterm morbidity. Aspirin does not eliminate PET, only reduces incidence. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Aspirin prophylaxis reduces pre-eclampsia risk by approximately 60 percent in high-risk women but does not eliminate it. New severe pre-eclampsia at 32+ weeks despite aspirin requires immediate inpatient management: acute BP control (IV labetalol or hydralazine to target <160/110 avoiding overshoot below 140/90), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if under 34 weeks, strict fluid balance (80 mL/hour max), and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours (after corticosteroid completion where feasible).
key_points: Severe PET features: BP >=160/110, symptoms, heavy proteinuria, low platelets, rising creatinine
Acute BP control (IV labetalol or hydralazine); target <160/110 not below 140/90
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if <34 weeks; deliver within 24 to 48 hours
explanation.pearls: PlGF/sFlt-1 ratio has entered clinical use in some centres for triage of suspected PET; a low ratio (<38) has strong negative predictive value for PET within 1 week, allowing safer outpatient monitoring.

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia with bleed at 32 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit for a 32-year-old woman at 32+3 weeks who has a small volume of bright red vaginal bleeding after a bowel motion. She had a second trimester scan reporting a low-lying velamentous cord insertion with a vessel crossing the internal os, confirmed on transvaginal imaging at 26 weeks. She is not contracting. Membranes are intact. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 with normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations. Speculum shows a small amount of fresh blood at the cervix, os closed.

She has completed one course of betamethasone at 28 weeks for a prior bleed. She is haemodynamically stable and asking whether she can go home given the bleeding has stopped.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Bloods: Hb 116 g/L (110-140), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), Kleihauer negative, group and hold on file
data_table.Imaging: confirmed vasa praevia with vessel over internal os, cord insertion velamentous, placental edge 3 cm from os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with twice weekly CTG and outpatient scan, plan caesarean at 39 weeks after any further bleed
options.rationale: Outpatient management after a sentinel bleed is unsafe because rupture of membranes causes fetal exsanguination in minutes; the woman must be in a facility able to expedite delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Admit until delivery, give a second course of betamethasone, plan elective caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks
options.rationale: Confirmed vasa praevia with a sentinel bleed at 32 weeks warrants inpatient admission until delivery, a rescue course of corticosteroids for lung maturity, and planned caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks to pre-empt catastrophic fetal exsanguination if membranes rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Perform an immediate category-1 caesarean now because any bleeding with vasa praevia is a fetal emergency
options.rationale: The CTG is normal and the bleed is small and settled; immediate delivery at 32 weeks carries avoidable prematurity risk when planned delivery at 34 to 35 weeks after steroids is achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Admit for observation for 48 hours then discharge if no further bleeding, plan vaginal delivery at 37 weeks
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is absolutely contraindicated in confirmed vasa praevia because membrane rupture during labour causes catastrophic fetal haemorrhage from the exposed vessel. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Discharge with prescribed magnesium sulfate at home for neuroprotection and plan caesarean at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given peripartum in facility, not as home therapy, and cannot mitigate the acute exsanguination risk of vasa praevia with a herald bleed. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is fetal blood vessels running through membranes over the cervical os. A herald bleed with confirmed vasa praevia is an admission indication because membrane rupture causes fetal death within minutes from exsanguination. The plan is inpatient corticosteroids and planned caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks. Outpatient management or vaginal delivery is unsafe.
key_points: Confirmed vasa praevia plus any bleed equals admission until delivery
Elective caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks is standard timing after corticosteroids
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in vasa praevia
Rescue steroids appropriate if prior course was more than 7 days ago and delivery anticipated within 7 days
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends delivery at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for confirmed vasa praevia; rescue betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart if last course over 7 days prior and delivery expected within 7 days.

subtopic_detail: Early-onset severe FGR with absent end-diastolic flow at 30 weeks
stem:
You are the maternal-fetal medicine registrar assessing a 34-year-old primigravida at 30+1 weeks with a small-for-gestational-age fetus first noted at the 28-week scan. Her repeat growth scan today shows estimated fetal weight less than the third centile, abdominal circumference less than the third centile, and umbilical artery Doppler showing absent end-diastolic flow across three consecutive cycles. Middle cerebral artery pulsatility index is at the fifth centile with a cerebroplacental ratio of 0.9. Amniotic fluid index is 6 cm. Ductus venosus a-wave is present and positive.

Her blood pressure is 128/82, urine dipstick shows no protein. Cardiotocograph is reactive with normal variability. She has completed a course of betamethasone at 28 weeks. Bloods including bile acids and pre-eclampsia screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 152
data_table.Doppler: UA absent end-diastolic flow, MCA PI 5th centile, CPR 0.9, DV a-wave positive
data_table.Growth: EFW <3rd centile, AC <3rd centile, HC 10th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue outpatient weekly Doppler until 34 weeks then deliver by planned caesarean with corticosteroid cover
options.rationale: Outpatient monitoring is inadequate once UA end-diastolic flow is absent because deterioration to DV changes or CTG loss can occur within days; inpatient surveillance is required. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

options.text: Deliver by category-2 caesarean today after magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection because absent EDF alone at 30 weeks mandates delivery
options.rationale: UA absent EDF alone without DV a-wave reversal or CTG decompensation does not mandate delivery before 32 weeks; premature intervention increases neonatal morbidity more than continued surveillance. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

options.text: Admit for daily CTG plus twice weekly Doppler surveillance and plan delivery at 32 weeks if ductus venosus a-wave becomes absent or reversed
options.rationale: Isolated UA absent end-diastolic flow with a positive DV a-wave at 30 weeks allows brief inpatient surveillance because DV a-wave reversal or CTG abnormality is the accepted trigger for delivery before 32 weeks; empirical delivery now exposes to prematurity morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

options.text: Give a second course of betamethasone now and induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin for delivery within 48 hours
options.rationale: Induction is inappropriate because severe early-onset FGR tolerates labour poorly; if delivery is indicated, caesarean is safer. Rescue steroid decision is separate and does not itself mandate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

options.text: Start low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin to improve placental perfusion, review in a week
options.rationale: Aspirin and heparin have no role in reversing established severe FGR; the intervention is surveillance and timely delivery, not late placental therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

explanation.summary: Early-onset severe FGR with absent UA end-diastolic flow but preserved DV a-wave and reactive CTG at 30 weeks is managed by inpatient surveillance. Delivery is triggered by DV a-wave becoming absent or reversed, spontaneous decelerations, computerised CTG short-term variation loss, or reaching 32 weeks. Delivery earlier than 32 weeks for UA changes alone increases prematurity morbidity without survival benefit.
key_points: UA absent EDF alone: inpatient surveillance until 32 weeks or DV decompensation
DV a-wave reversal or absence: deliver even before 32 weeks
Caesarean is the mode of choice for severe early-onset FGR
Magnesium neuroprotection given peripartum below 30 weeks (some centres 32)
explanation.pearls: TRUFFLE trial data: DV a-wave changes and computerised CTG STV are the triggers; before 32 weeks deliver on DV reversal, from 32 weeks deliver on UA absent EDF alone.

subtopic_detail: Impacted fetal head at full dilation caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar taking a category-1 caesarean for a 32-year-old at 39+4 weeks who has been fully dilated for two hours and pushing for 90 minutes. Fetal head is at spines +2 in the occipito-posterior position, cephalic. She has been contracting strongly. A cardiotocograph shows a prolonged deceleration to 60 for 5 minutes despite scalp stimulation and stopping oxytocin.

In theatre you make a lower segment transverse incision but find the fetal head deeply impacted in the pelvis and cannot dislodge it with the operator's fingers from above. An assistant attempts to push the head up from below via the vagina without success. Two minutes have passed since delivery of the incision.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78, SpO2 99% on room air, fetal heart rate 60 (prolonged deceleration)
data_table.Progress: second stage 2 hours, active pushing 90 minutes, station spines +2, OP position, caput++, moulding++
data_table.Operative: lower segment transverse uterine incision made, head impacted deep in pelvis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously to relax the uterus and reattempt head disimpaction
options.rationale: Tocolysis with terbutaline is not for impacted head at caesarean; it may add maternal tachycardia and delays definitive delivery when reverse breech extraction is available. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

options.text: Extend the lower segment incision inferiorly with scissors to allow more room and deliver the head with forceps
options.rationale: Extending the uterine incision inferiorly risks bladder injury, extension into the cervix or vagina and heavy bleeding; upward J or T extension is the accepted rescue if space is needed, but reverse breech extraction should be attempted first. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

options.text: Ask the assistant to push harder from below using the whole hand until the head disimpacts and can be delivered abdominally
options.rationale: Vaginal push-up has already failed and prolongs delivery interval; continuing prolongs fetal hypoxia, and reverse breech extraction is faster and less injurious. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

options.text: Deliver the fetus by reverse breech extraction, grasping a foot and delivering as breech through the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Reverse breech extraction (Patwardhan or foot-first through the uterine incision) is the preferred manoeuvre for a deeply impacted head at caesarean because it avoids extending the uterine incision inferiorly and shortens delivery interval versus repeated failed head disimpaction. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

options.text: Perform a classical vertical uterine incision above the impacted head and deliver by rotating the fetus in utero
options.rationale: Classical incision commits the woman to caesarean in future pregnancies and carries higher morbidity; upward J extension is preferred if the lower incision is inadequate, and reverse breech extraction remains the first-line manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

explanation.summary: A deeply impacted head at caesarean in the second stage is a recognised obstetric emergency with maternal (uterine tears, bladder injury, PPH) and neonatal (hypoxia, skull fracture) risks. Reverse breech extraction, grasping a foot and delivering by breech extraction through the uterine incision, is faster and safer than repeated head disimpaction attempts. Vaginal push-up may work but should not be persisted with. Extending the uterine incision inferiorly risks bladder and cervical injury.
key_points: Reverse breech extraction is first-line for impacted head at caesarean
Do not extend uterine incision inferiorly (bladder and cervix at risk)
Upward J or T extension acceptable if more space needed
Avoid classical incision unless nothing else works
explanation.pearls: MODIFY trial (2024, UK) supports reverse breech extraction; RANZCOG endorses it as first-line manoeuvre. Prepare Patwardhan technique in advance for anticipated deep transverse arrest cases.

subtopic_detail: Suspected amniotic fluid embolism intrapartum
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called for a woman who has collapsed on the labour ward. She is a 34-year-old at 39+6 weeks who had artificial rupture of membranes 15 minutes ago for augmentation. Immediately afterwards she developed sudden severe shortness of breath, complained of feeling terrified, and lost consciousness. She had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds.

She is now on oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather, blood pressure 65/32, pulse 148 with peripheral cyanosis, oxygen saturations 84 percent, CTG shows fetal bradycardia at 60 bpm. The airway is patent. Her uterus is soft with a trickle of dark blood from the vagina that is not clotting on the drape.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 65/32, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 84% on 15 L/min, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 60
data_table.Recent event: ARM 15 minutes ago, sudden dyspnoea, seizure 90 seconds, now unconscious
data_table.Bleeding: trickle of non-clotting dark blood per vaginam, uterus soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Perform an urgent bedside echocardiogram before initiating any treatment to confirm right heart strain and pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Delaying resuscitation for imaging in a periarrest woman is unsafe; bedside echocardiography may be done during resuscitation if it does not interrupt life-saving treatment. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

options.text: Give IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus for seizure control then plan urgent caesarean under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Magnesium is for eclamptic seizures with hypertension and proteinuria; this presentation is anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy with shock and coagulopathy, requiring resuscitation and consideration of perimortem caesarean, not magnesium as first step. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

options.text: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV and syntocinon infusion 40 units in 500 mL, transfer directly to theatre for caesarean
options.rationale: Uterotonics and tranexamic acid may be part of PPH management but do not address the primary cardiorespiratory collapse of AFE; airway, breathing, circulation, and perimortem caesarean if in arrest take priority. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

options.text: Administer IM adrenaline 0.5 mg for suspected anaphylaxis to latex or antibiotics and observe for response
options.rationale: This is not anaphylaxis to a known trigger; it is amniotic fluid embolism, a distinct anaphylactoid syndrome. Adrenaline may be needed as an inotrope in cardiac arrest but IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis alone is inadequate. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

options.text: Call arrest team, secure airway with CPR if pulseless, activate massive transfusion, and prepare perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes if no ROSC
options.rationale: The presentation is consistent with amniotic fluid embolism causing cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, seizure and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy; management is resuscitation with perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if cardiac arrest occurs, aggressive product replacement for coagulopathy, and inotropic and airway support. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a clinical diagnosis of sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, hypoxia, seizure, and DIC in labour or early postpartum. Management is aggressive resuscitation with airway, breathing, circulation, blood products for coagulopathy, and perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of cardiac arrest to improve maternal survival and enable resuscitation. Mortality remains high despite optimal care.
key_points: Triad: cardiorespiratory collapse, DIC, altered mental state or seizure in labour
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest
Early massive transfusion activation for DIC (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets)
Vasopressors and inotropes for cardiovascular support; ECMO if available
explanation.pearls: SMFM AFE registry criteria: acute cardiorespiratory arrest or hypotension with respiratory compromise; DIC within 30 min; onset during labour or within 30 min of delivery; no fever above 38 C.

subtopic_detail: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with severe bile acids
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 36+1 weeks referred by her GP with two weeks of intense generalised itch worse at night, particularly on palms and soles, no rash. She has no jaundice, no right upper quadrant pain, and no history of hepatobiliary disease.

Her bloods show total bile acids 118 micromol/L (fasting reference less than 10 micromol/L), ALT 168 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 22 micromol/L (less than 21), gamma-GT 34 U/L (less than 45). Coagulation is normal. Fetal movements are perceived normally and CTG this morning is reactive with normal variability. Estimated fetal weight is on the 45th centile. Hepatitis screen and autoimmune liver screen are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: bile acids 118 micromol/L (<10), ALT 168 U/L (<35), bilirubin 22 micromol/L (<21), gamma-GT 34 U/L (<45), INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily and continue conservative management until 39 weeks for spontaneous labour
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid modestly reduces maternal itch but does not reduce stillbirth risk; continuing to 39 weeks in severe ICP with bile acids over 100 exposes the pregnancy to the stillbirth window. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

options.text: Plan induction of labour at 35 to 36 weeks now because bile acids over 100 micromol/L confer a marked stillbirth risk from 36 weeks
options.rationale: Peak bile acids of 100 micromol/L or greater are associated with a significant stillbirth risk that increases at 36 weeks and beyond; RCOG and RANZCOG guidance is delivery at 35 to 36 weeks for severe intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

options.text: Perform an urgent category-1 caesarean today because bile acids over 100 mandate immediate delivery
options.rationale: Immediate delivery today is not required; the excess stillbirth risk climbs sharply from 36 weeks onward, allowing time to plan induction and complete corticosteroid cover if needed before 34+6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

options.text: Give a course of antenatal betamethasone and plan expectant management with weekly CTG until 38 weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not routinely indicated at 36+1 for lung maturity and expectant management to 38 weeks is not consistent with the elevated stillbirth risk of severe ICP. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

options.text: Prescribe rifampicin 300 mg twice daily to reduce itch and defer delivery until 39 weeks after normal weekly Doppler surveillance
options.rationale: Rifampicin is a second-line itch therapy in refractory cases and Doppler surveillance does not predict the acute stillbirth event in ICP; deferring delivery in severe ICP is not standard. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed on itch (often palms and soles) plus elevated serum bile acids. Severity is stratified by peak bile acids: mild (below 40), moderate (40 to 99), and severe (100 or greater). Severe ICP is associated with a substantially increased stillbirth risk that becomes marked from 36 weeks. Delivery timing is 35 to 36 weeks for severe ICP, 36 to 37 for moderate, and 37 to 38 for mild.
key_points: Bile acids 100 or more equals severe ICP; deliver at 35 to 36 weeks
Moderate ICP (40 to 99): deliver at 36 to 37 weeks
Mild ICP (10 to 39): deliver at 37 to 38 weeks
UDCA reduces itch but not stillbirth (PITCHES trial)
explanation.pearls: Ovadia meta-analysis (Lancet 2019): stillbirth risk rises steeply once peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L, particularly beyond 36 weeks; ursodeoxycholic acid does not eliminate this risk.

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion at third stage
stem:
You are the labour ward registrar called for a woman collapsed after vaginal delivery. She is a 30-year-old para 2 who delivered a 4.1 kg baby 5 minutes ago. The midwife applied controlled cord traction to deliver the placenta but immediately noted the woman becoming pale and tachycardic. On examination the woman is diaphoretic and confused. On abdominal palpation the uterine fundus is no longer palpable. A dark red vascular mass is visible protruding from the vagina with the placenta attached. There is heavy bleeding.

An 18-gauge IV is in situ, syntocinon 10 units IM has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: fundus non-palpable abdominally, red vascular mass at introitus with placenta attached, heavy bleeding
data_table.Access: 18-gauge IV in right hand, syntocinon 10 units IM given post-delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediately replace the fundus with a cupped hand (Johnson manoeuvre) leaving placenta attached, then remove placenta after reduction
options.rationale: Rapid manual replacement of the fundus (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached is the immediate first-line for uterine inversion; delay allows a constriction ring to form making replacement harder and haemorrhage worse. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

options.text: Remove the placenta manually first because retained placenta perpetuates the inversion, then attempt fundal replacement
options.rationale: Removing the placenta before replacing the uterus dramatically worsens blood loss; the placenta acts as a partial haemostatic tamponade until reduction is achieved. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

options.text: Start an oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 500 mL to contract the uterus and stop the bleeding, then attempt reduction after 15 minutes
options.rationale: Uterotonics before reduction cause a contraction ring that traps the inverted fundus and makes replacement impossible; uterotonics are used AFTER successful reduction. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

options.text: Insert a Bakri balloon into the visible inverted mass and inflate with 500 mL saline for uterine tamponade of bleeding
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is not indicated in the inverted uterus and delays definitive reduction; balloons may be used after reduction if atony persists. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

options.text: Transfer directly to theatre for immediate laparotomy and Huntington procedure without any attempt at vaginal reduction
options.rationale: Surgical reduction (Huntington or Haultain) is reserved for failed manual reduction; the first step is immediate bedside manual replacement, which succeeds in most cases. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

explanation.summary: Uterine inversion is a life-threatening obstetric emergency causing haemorrhage and neurogenic shock disproportionate to blood loss. Immediate treatment is bedside manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached, before uterotonics harden a constriction ring. Uterotonics and placental removal follow reduction. Failed manual reduction warrants theatre, tocolysis to relax the uterus, hydrostatic reduction, or surgical (Huntington or Haultain) procedures.
key_points: Immediate Johnson manoeuvre with placenta attached
Do NOT give uterotonics BEFORE reduction (creates constriction ring)
Do NOT remove placenta before reduction
Failed reduction: theatre with tocolysis (terbutaline or GA)
explanation.pearls: Neurogenic shock in inversion is out of proportion to blood loss (vagal traction on infundibulopelvic ligament); IV fluid resuscitation and atropine may be needed alongside reduction.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman referred by her GP with three episodes of light postmenopausal vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks. She is 12 years postmenopausal, has never used hormone replacement therapy, and has a body mass index of 34. She has hypertension on ramipril and type 2 diabetes on metformin. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal. Pelvic examination shows an atrophic vulva and vagina, cervix appears normal, small amount of old blood in the vault, no adnexal masses.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 8 mm with heterogenous echo pattern and increased vascularity on colour Doppler. Ovaries are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound: endometrial thickness 8 mm, heterogenous echotexture, increased vascularity on Doppler, ovaries normal
data_table.History: 62 years, BMI 34, T2DM, never HRT, cervical screening current and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform outpatient Pipelle sampling in clinic and manage further only if malignancy is found on that specimen
options.rationale: Pipelle sampling alone can miss focal lesions and polyps; a negative Pipelle in the setting of thickened heterogenous endometrium still warrants hysteroscopy to exclude focal pathology. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to see whether the endometrial thickness changes before proceeding to biopsy
options.rationale: Deferring histology in postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium above 4 mm risks missing endometrial cancer, which is present in roughly 10 percent of postmenopausal bleeding presentations. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy under general or local anaesthesia to sample the endometrium histologically
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness of 4 mm or greater requires histological sampling; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the reference standard, particularly with heterogenous echo pattern that raises suspicion of endometrial cancer. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Start topical oestrogen for atrophic vaginitis and review symptoms in 8 weeks before further investigation
options.rationale: Attributing postmenopausal bleeding to atrophy without histological exclusion of malignancy is unsafe when the endometrial thickness is above 4 mm with a heterogenous pattern. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Arrange staging CT abdomen and pelvis and cancer antigen 125 to assess for advanced malignancy first
options.rationale: Staging imaging and tumour markers are for confirmed malignancy; histological diagnosis via hysteroscopy and biopsy must come first to justify any staging workup. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer, which underlies roughly 10 percent of cases. Transvaginal ultrasound triages: thickness below 4 mm and homogenous has very low cancer risk; thickness 4 mm or more or heterogenous, focal, or vascular pattern requires tissue sampling. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the reference standard because Pipelle sampling misses focal lesions.
key_points: PMB plus ET at or above 4 mm equals histology
Hysteroscopy plus directed biopsy is standard, superior to Pipelle for focal lesions
Risk factors: obesity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, T2DM, PCOS, nulliparity, Lynch syndrome
Do not attribute PMB to atrophy without excluding malignancy
explanation.pearls: Endometrial thickness 4 mm is the RANZCOG cut-off (some international bodies use 5 mm). Persistent PMB with normal biopsy still warrants repeat sampling given up to 10% Pipelle miss rate.

subtopic_detail: Complex adnexal mass with elevated risk of malignancy index
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with three months of increasing abdominal distension and early satiety. She is 8 years postmenopausal and has no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Abdominal examination reveals mild ascites and a palpable pelvic mass. On bimanual examination the mass is fixed, irregular, and non-tender.

A transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound shows a 9 cm right adnexal mass with solid and cystic components, thick septations greater than 3 mm, papillary projections, and increased vascularity. There is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum CA-125 is 320 kU/L (below 35). Her Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) is well above 200.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 128/80, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound: right adnexal mass 9 cm, solid and cystic, septations >3 mm, papillary projections, vascular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange oral tranexamic acid and repeat imaging in 6 weeks to observe for change before intervention
options.rationale: Delaying management in a postmenopausal complex mass with elevated CA-125 risks progression; there is no role for surveillance in a highly suspicious mass. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

options.text: Arrange percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy of the mass to obtain histological diagnosis before referral
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected ovarian primary risks tumour spillage and upstaging; diagnosis is by surgical excision with intraoperative frozen section in specialist centres. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy locally with washings and biopsies to establish diagnosis before onward referral
options.rationale: Diagnostic laparoscopy outside a specialist centre in high-risk masses may complicate later staging and risks incomplete surgical cytoreduction; direct referral to a gynae-oncology unit is preferred. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team for planned surgery in a specialist centre with staging capability
options.rationale: Postmenopausal complex adnexal mass with elevated CA-125 and RMI above 200 has a high probability of ovarian malignancy; centralised surgery in a gynae-oncology centre with staging capability improves survival compared with generalist surgery. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

options.text: Commence neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel and refer at completion for interval debulking
options.rationale: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a valid option for advanced ovarian cancer but the decision is made by the gynae-oncology multidisciplinary team after diagnostic workup, not initiated in the referring service. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

explanation.summary: Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = U score x menopausal status x CA-125) triages adnexal masses. RMI above 200 identifies women at high risk of ovarian cancer who should have surgery in a specialist gynae-oncology centre because centralised care with complete staging improves survival. Percutaneous biopsy or generalist laparoscopy of a suspicious primary risks spillage and suboptimal staging.
key_points: RMI above 200 equals gynae-oncology referral
Postmenopausal, complex, solid or cystic mass with papillary projections raises suspicion
Do not biopsy a suspected ovarian primary percutaneously
Centralised surgery in specialist centres improves 5-year survival
explanation.pearls: RMI ultrasound score: 1 point each for multilocular, solid areas, bilateral, ascites, metastases (max 4). U=1 if 1 feature; U=3 if 2+ features. RMI = U x menopause (1 pre, 3 post) x CA-125.

subtopic_detail: MRI-confirmed increta with planned delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetric consultant reviewing a 36-year-old G4P3 at 33+0 weeks with two prior caesareans and an anterior placenta praevia. Ultrasound at 28 weeks showed multiple placental lakes, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, and bridging vessels crossing the bladder wall. MRI at 32 weeks confirms placenta increta with focal areas suspicious for percreta into the posterior bladder. She is asymptomatic today but reports a single small self-limited PV spot last week. The tertiary maternal-fetal medicine unit and interventional radiology are available on site.

She asks about the safest timing and mode of delivery given her prior counselling that she wants no further pregnancies.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 120/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 235 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L (3.7-6.2), group and crossmatch 4 units on standby
data_table.Imaging: MRI increta with focal percreta signs into posterior bladder, no fetal growth restriction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks in a specialist MDT theatre with IR standby
options.rationale: RANZCOG and international consensus recommend planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks for suspected accreta spectrum, in a specialist centre with an MDT ready and blood on standby to minimise haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

options.text: Expectant care to 37+0 weeks then elective caesarean with attempted placental removal in the local unit
options.rationale: Waiting to 37 weeks in confirmed accreta risks an unplanned haemorrhage; attempted placental removal at delivery causes massive bleeding and is contraindicated in the increta or percreta setting. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

options.text: Induce vaginal birth at 34+0 weeks after corticosteroids because the placenta may separate spontaneously later
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta praevia and accreta spectrum because cervical dilation over an adherent placenta produces uncontrolled haemorrhage requiring emergency laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

options.text: Elective classical caesarean at 36+0 weeks with placenta left in situ and outpatient methotrexate follow-up
options.rationale: Leaving placenta in situ is a conservative option only for women who want future fertility and accept infection and delayed haemorrhage risk; it is not first line when the woman has completed her family. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

options.text: Emergency category-1 caesarean today because a single antepartum bleed indicates imminent placental separation
options.rationale: A single small self-limited bleed with normal maternal and fetal status does not mandate immediate delivery; escalating to category-1 loses the benefit of planned MDT setup and additional steroid maturation. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with increta or percreta requires planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks in a specialist centre with a multidisciplinary team on site. Attempted placental removal at caesarean is contraindicated because it triggers massive haemorrhage. Vaginal birth is contraindicated when placenta praevia coexists. Conservative in situ management is reserved for women wanting future fertility who accept the risks.
key_points: Suspected PAS with increta or percreta needs MDT delivery at 34 to 35 weeks
Do not attempt placental removal at caesarean when PAS is confirmed
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in coexisting placenta praevia
In situ conservative management only when fertility preservation is wanted
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends planned delivery at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks for suspected PAS; two units of packed red cells crossmatched with four on immediate standby, cell salvage available, and IR balloon occlusion catheters considered for percreta into bladder.

subtopic_detail: Quintero stage III at 20 weeks in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional unit assessing a 27-year-old G1 at 20+2 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. Fortnightly surveillance scanning today shows twin one deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm with an empty bladder, and twin two deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm with a full bladder. Twin one umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow. Twin two shows a reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus. Both twins are alive with normal biometry and no structural anomaly. Cervical length is 34 mm.

The woman is well. The nearest tertiary fetal medicine unit performing fetoscopic laser is 4 hours by air.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 122 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400), group A positive on file
data_table.Imaging: MCDA twins, twin one DVP 1.4 cm bladder empty UA AEDF, twin two DVP 9.2 cm bladder full DV reversed a-wave, cervix 34 mm closed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Weekly amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac at the regional unit until viability at 24 weeks
options.rationale: Amnioreduction alone is inferior to fetoscopic laser for stage II and above TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks and should not delay referral to a laser centre. (Source: ISUOG TTTS Guideline)

options.text: Urgent transfer today to the tertiary fetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
options.rationale: Quintero stage III TTTS at 16 to 26 weeks has best survival with fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses, and delay worsens outcomes; urgent transfer to a laser-capable centre is standard care. (Source: ISUOG TTTS Guideline)

options.text: Selective feticide of the donor twin by cord occlusion at the regional unit under ultrasound guidance
options.rationale: Selective reduction is a last-line option when laser fails or is technically impossible, and should not be offered as first step in a viable stage III pregnancy with laser available. (Source: ISUOG TTTS Guideline)

options.text: Give corticosteroids and admit for continuous CTG monitoring until spontaneous delivery in the coming days
options.rationale: Steroids and monitoring are inappropriate at 20 weeks (previable) and do not address the underlying vascular anastomoses driving TTTS; laser therapy targets the pathology. (Source: ISUOG TTTS Guideline)

options.text: Reassure and repeat the scan in 2 weeks because Quintero stage III often improves spontaneously without treatment
options.rationale: Untreated stage III TTTS carries a very high mortality for both twins and does not resolve spontaneously; a two week delay would risk both fetuses. (Source: ISUOG TTTS Guideline)

explanation.summary: TTTS in monochorionic twins is diagnosed by oligohydramnios in the donor sac (DVP under 2 cm) and polyhydramnios in the recipient (DVP over 8 cm before 20 weeks). Quintero stage III adds abnormal Doppler in either twin. Between 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser photocoagulation is superior to amnioreduction. Urgent transfer to a laser-capable centre saves both twins. Untreated stage III TTTS has very high dual mortality.
key_points: TTTS diagnosis: DVP under 2 cm donor plus over 8 cm recipient before 20 weeks
Quintero stage III adds abnormal UA, DV or umbilical vein Doppler
Fetoscopic laser is first line for stage II and above between 16 and 26 weeks
Untreated stage III TTTS has around 80 to 90 percent dual mortality
explanation.pearls: ISUOG uses DVP over 8 cm before 20 weeks and over 10 cm after 20 weeks for the polyhydramnios threshold; laser survival is around 65 percent for both twins and 88 percent for at least one twin, compared with under 30 percent survival with expectant management for stage III.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent early pregnancy loss with confirmed APS in the current pregnancy
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 33-year-old G4P0 at 8+2 weeks. She has had three consecutive first trimester miscarriages between 6 and 9 weeks. Non-pregnant workup showed persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart, negative anticardiolipin and negative beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies. She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism and no systemic lupus features. Her current pregnancy is confirmed viable on ultrasound with a fetal heart rate of 142.

She is asking what treatment during this pregnancy will maximise her chance of a live birth.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (110-140), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 umol/L (45-90), APTT prolonged and not correcting on mixing (lupus anticoagulant pattern)
data_table.Imaging: single intrauterine pregnancy 8+2 weeks, cardiac activity present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this pregnancy?

options.text: Therapeutic dose enoxaparin twice daily plus aspirin plus hydroxychloroquine for the whole pregnancy
options.rationale: Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for prior VTE or catastrophic APS, not for obstetric APS with recurrent early loss and no thrombosis history; hydroxychloroquine is not standard first line here. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

options.text: Low dose aspirin 100 mg daily alone with no anticoagulant, reserving heparin for prior VTE only
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inferior to aspirin plus LMWH for live birth in obstetric APS with recurrent miscarriage; heparin is added regardless of VTE history in this indication. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

options.text: Low dose aspirin 100 mg daily started now plus prophylactic dose enoxaparin daily throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Obstetric APS with recurrent early pregnancy loss is treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from confirmation of pregnancy; combination therapy improves live birth rates over aspirin alone. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

options.text: Warfarin bridged with enoxaparin from 12 weeks to term to prevent placental thrombosis in APS
options.rationale: Warfarin is teratogenic between 6 and 12 weeks and crosses the placenta at term causing fetal haemorrhage; it is contraindicated in obstetric APS in pregnancy. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

options.text: Prednisolone 20 mg daily plus low dose aspirin from now until 20 weeks then wean and continue aspirin
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve live birth in obstetric APS and add gestational diabetes and preterm delivery risk; they are not part of first-line management. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

explanation.summary: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent early pregnancy loss is treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from confirmation of a viable pregnancy through to delivery and postnatally. Combination therapy improves live birth rates compared with aspirin alone. Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for prior VTE or catastrophic APS. Warfarin is contraindicated in early and late pregnancy.
key_points: Obstetric APS with recurrent early loss: aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from viability
Aspirin alone is inferior to combination therapy for live birth
Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and unsafe near term
Continue LMWH postnatally for 6 weeks as per standard prophylaxis rules
explanation.pearls: RCOG Green-top 17 defines obstetric APS as three or more consecutive losses under 10 weeks, one or more fetal deaths at or over 10 weeks, or one severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks, plus persistent aPL antibodies 12 weeks apart; enoxaparin 40 mg daily is the standard prophylactic dose in booking weight under 90 kg.

subtopic_detail: Severe hypertension 190/125 with seizure prophylaxis before delivery at 35 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 35+0 weeks who arrived with a headache and one episode of vomiting. Blood pressure on two readings 15 minutes apart is 192/126. She has a normal reflex examination with no clonus. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 148 with reduced variability but no decelerations. Her booking pressure was 118/72. Her platelets are 96 and her ALT is 128. Proteinuria is 3 plus on dipstick.

The consultant is on their way and has agreed to birth by caesarean today. You must start the medical priorities now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 192/126, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: Hb 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 128 U/L (5-40), creatinine 92 umol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), fibrinogen 3.8 g/L (3.7-6.2)
data_table.Imaging: cephalic presentation on portable ultrasound, estimated fetal weight 2450 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 500 mg loading dose plus oral clonidine and admit for observation and 6 hourly reassessment
options.rationale: Oral agents act too slowly for severe hypertension over 160/110 in the acute setting; IV agents and immediate magnesium prophylaxis are indicated before urgent delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

options.text: Immediate caesarean under general anaesthetic before any antihypertensive or magnesium sulfate is started
options.rationale: Uncontrolled severe hypertension at induction of general anaesthesia risks maternal stroke; blood pressure control and magnesium loading should be initiated before or in parallel with theatre transfer. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

options.text: IV furosemide 40 mg to offload preload plus sublingual nifedipine because renal function is deteriorating
options.rationale: Furosemide is not indicated in pre-eclampsia unless there is pulmonary oedema; sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated because of unpredictable severe blood pressure drops. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus now with repeat dosing plus magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g per hour
options.rationale: Severe hypertension over 160/110 requires rapid IV antihypertensive therapy and concurrent magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis before delivery in severe pre-eclampsia; both are started immediately in parallel. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

options.text: Phenytoin 15 mg per kg IV load for seizure prophylaxis, then transfer for caesarean when blood pressure settles
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for eclampsia prophylaxis and treatment; phenytoin has higher seizure recurrence and no maternal or perinatal benefit over magnesium. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension of 160/110 or above in pre-eclampsia requires rapid IV antihypertensive therapy with labetalol or hydralazine, alongside magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, before or in parallel with delivery. Sublingual nifedipine is unsafe. Magnesium is superior to phenytoin. Furosemide is only for pulmonary oedema. Both mother and fetus benefit from timely blood pressure control and magnesium therapy before theatre.
key_points: Severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia is over 160 systolic or over 110 diastolic
IV labetalol 20 mg boluses or hydralazine 5 mg boluses are first line
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g per hour infusion for 24 hours postnatally
Do not use sublingual nifedipine because of unpredictable BP drops
explanation.pearls: SOMANZ target is BP under 160/110 within 30 to 60 minutes; magnesium toxicity signs are loss of patellar reflex then respiratory depression, reversed with calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV over 10 minutes.

subtopic_detail: Severe grade with ascites and haemoconcentration after IVF retrieval
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman in ED, day 6 after IVF oocyte retrieval with 22 eggs collected. She reports progressive abdominal distension, nausea, reduced urine output, and dyspnoea on lying flat. Examination shows a tense abdomen with dullness to flank percussion, respiratory rate 24, and mild bilateral pitting oedema. She has no fever or vaginal bleeding. She had a fresh embryo transfer two days ago and a positive pregnancy test today. She is on no anticoagulant.

Her fertility unit clinician has asked for admission and initial management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/72, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 168 g/L (110-140), haematocrit 0.52 (0.35-0.45), white cells 16.2 x10^9/L (4-11), creatinine 118 umol/L (45-90), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)
data_table.Imaging: large volume ascites on bedside ultrasound, enlarged ovaries 9 cm bilateral, small right pleural effusion on chest X-ray

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start IV albumin infusion 25 percent 100 mL 6 hourly as sole volume expander plus oral fluid restriction
options.rationale: Albumin is not superior to crystalloid in OHSS and is not first line; oral fluid restriction worsens hypovolaemia and renal perfusion in an already haemoconcentrated patient. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

options.text: Discharge on oral fluids and outpatient follow up because ongoing pregnancy will resolve OHSS spontaneously
options.rationale: Ongoing pregnancy extends and worsens OHSS due to endogenous hCG; severe OHSS with haemoconcentration and dyspnoea requires admission not discharge. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

options.text: Give IV furosemide 40 mg to relieve dyspnoea and ascites, hold anticoagulation until diuresis achieved
options.rationale: Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and thrombosis risk in OHSS by removing intravascular volume; they are not first line. Withholding LMWH increases VTE risk further. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

options.text: Emergency laparotomy for ovarian decompression and drainage of ascites in theatre under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgery on OHSS ovaries is reserved for torsion, rupture with haemorrhage, or ectopic pregnancy; ovaries are friable and elective decompression is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

options.text: Admit for IV crystalloid replacement, prophylactic enoxaparin daily, strict fluid balance, and paracentesis if symptomatic
options.rationale: Severe OHSS requires inpatient care with judicious volume expansion for haemoconcentration, LMWH thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis for symptomatic ascites; targets are haematocrit under 0.45, urine output over 30 mL per hour, and symptom relief. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS presents with haemoconcentration, ascites, oliguria, and dyspnoea after ovarian stimulation, worsened by ongoing pregnancy through endogenous hCG. Admission for careful IV crystalloid replacement, LMWH thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis for symptomatic ascites is standard. Diuretics and elective surgery are contraindicated. Albumin has no proven benefit over crystalloid.
key_points: Severe OHSS features: HCT over 0.45, oliguria, ascites, dyspnoea, VTE risk
Admission plus IV crystalloid, LMWH prophylaxis, symptomatic paracentesis
Avoid diuretics, they worsen haemoconcentration and VTE risk
Surgery only for torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Ongoing pregnancy prolongs and worsens OHSS through endogenous hCG; RANZCOG suggests LMWH prophylaxis for at least the duration of clinical OHSS and up to 12 weeks gestation in severe cases with haemoconcentration.

subtopic_detail: 45 minute retention with heavy bleeding requiring theatre manual removal
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite 45 minutes after a normal vaginal birth of a 3200 g infant at term. Active management was used with oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery. The placenta remains undelivered and controlled cord traction has not succeeded. Estimated blood loss is now 900 mL and ongoing. The woman is haemodynamically borderline with a pulse of 108 and blood pressure 102/64. She has a spinal already sited. The consultant is 15 minutes away. Bladder was catheterised at delivery.

The theatre coordinator confirms an emergency theatre is ready.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 102/64, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L (110-140), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (3.7-6.2), 4 units red cells and 2 units FFP on standby
data_table.Imaging: no separation signs, cord in situ, empty bladder confirmed on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to theatre now for manual removal of placenta under spinal top-up with syntocinon 40 units IV in 500 mL
options.rationale: Retained placenta beyond 30 minutes with heavy ongoing bleeding needs prompt theatre transfer for manual removal under regional anaesthetic and an oxytocin infusion; delaying increases haemorrhage and infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Give ergometrine 250 mcg IM at the bedside and continue attempted cord traction for another 30 minutes
options.rationale: Ergometrine may worsen placental entrapment and does not remove a retained placenta; sustained cord traction without separation risks uterine inversion and cord avulsion. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Attempt umbilical vein oxytocin injection of 30 units in saline at the bedside instead of theatre transfer
options.rationale: Umbilical vein oxytocin has weak evidence and is not the standard next step when haemorrhage is ongoing; definitive management is manual removal in theatre. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Insert a Bakri balloon vaginally and inflate to 500 mL to tamponade bleeding before removing the placenta
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is used after removal of the placenta for atonic bleeding; inserting a balloon over a retained placenta is not appropriate management. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Wait one further hour with slow oxytocin infusion and no other intervention because delivery is common by 2 hours
options.rationale: Delaying beyond an hour with heavy ongoing bleeding is unsafe; timely manual removal reduces blood loss and morbidity in retained placenta with active haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Retained placenta at 30 minutes with ongoing bleeding, or at 60 minutes without bleeding, is an indication for manual removal in theatre under regional or general anaesthetic with a concurrent oxytocin infusion. Sustained cord traction risks uterine inversion. Ergometrine may entrap the placenta. Balloon tamponade is used for atony after removal.
key_points: Retained placenta plus PPH at 30 minutes needs theatre manual removal
Give syntocinon 40 units in 500 mL crystalloid over 4 hours after removal
Ergometrine may cause placental entrapment and is avoided until placenta out
Prophylactic antibiotics at manual removal reduce endometritis
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends a single dose IV cefazolin 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg at manual removal; risk of uterine inversion rises with sustained cord traction and fundal pressure without confirmed separation signs.

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks without infection, timing of delivery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 admitted with PPROM at 32+2 weeks confirmed on speculum pooling and positive amnisure. She is 24 hours in with no contractions. Maternal observations are normal, CTG is reactive, and there are no clinical signs of chorioamnionitis. She has completed betamethasone 24 hours ago and is on oral erythromycin. Group B strep swab is pending.

She asks how long she should stay pregnant and what will trigger delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 138
data_table.Bloods: Hb 116 g/L (110-140), white cells 10.8 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (under 5), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: cephalic presentation, deepest vertical pool 1.6 cm, normal Doppler indices

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Expectant care with inpatient surveillance until 37+0 weeks then induction of labour if not already delivered
options.rationale: Expectant care beyond 34 weeks in PPROM increases chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis risk without meaningful neonatal benefit; planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks is preferred with 34 as the earliest routine threshold in some guidelines. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

options.text: Expectant care with inpatient surveillance to 36+0 weeks then plan delivery, sooner if infection or fetal distress
options.rationale: Between 34 and 37 weeks, planned delivery is preferred over expectant care to reduce chorioamnionitis; RANZCOG suggests delivery by 36 to 37 weeks with earlier delivery for infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

options.text: Induce labour today at 32+3 weeks because further latency increases sepsis risk beyond neonatal benefit
options.rationale: At 32 weeks with no infection, prematurity risk still outweighs latency risk; delivery before 34 weeks is not indicated without infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

options.text: Discharge home with weekly clinic review and instructions on symptom monitoring for infection or bleeding
options.rationale: Outpatient management of PPROM is not standard in Australia because chorioamnionitis and cord accident risk requires inpatient CTG and observation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

options.text: Start tocolysis with nifedipine and give a second course of betamethasone to prolong latency to 39 weeks
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated in PPROM without contractions and does not improve neonatal outcomes; a second steroid course is a rescue given only if delivery is anticipated in the next 7 days. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly with inpatient surveillance, corticosteroids, and erythromycin, provided no infection or fetal compromise. Delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier for infection or non-reassuring CTG. Tocolysis is not indicated. Outpatient care is not standard. GBS chemoprophylaxis is added at delivery.
key_points: PPROM 24 to 34 weeks: expectant with steroids and erythromycin 250 mg 4 times daily 10 days
Deliver by 36 to 37 weeks, earlier for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise
Tocolysis not indicated in PPROM without contractions
Inpatient care standard because of chorioamnionitis and cord accident risk
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG PPROM Statement recommends erythromycin 250 mg orally 4 times daily for 10 days; magnesium sulfate neuroprotection for anticipated preterm delivery under 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy risk with number needed to treat around 60.

subtopic_detail: Second trimester dilatation with prolapsed membranes at 22 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G3P0 at 22+3 weeks who presents with painless pressure. Speculum shows cervix dilated to 3 cm with membranes hourglassing into the vagina. She has no bleeding, no contractions, and no fever. She had a mid-trimester loss at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy and a preterm birth at 26 weeks in her second. There is no evidence of infection on blood tests. Fetal biometry is normal for gestation.

She asks whether anything can prolong the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (under 5), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: single viable fetus 22+3 weeks, cephalic, cervix funnelled with membranes prolapsed into vagina, normal Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate delivery at 22+3 weeks after magnesium neuroprotection because prognosis is otherwise dismal
options.rationale: 22+3 weeks is periviability and expectant management with rescue cerclage in the absence of infection can extend gestation meaningfully; immediate delivery discards potential viability. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

options.text: Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly and expectant care because cerclage is contraindicated after cervical dilation
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone is for short cervix on ultrasound, not for dilated cervix with prolapsed membranes; rescue cerclage is a valid option in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

options.text: Offer rescue cervical cerclage under regional anaesthetic after counselling on risks and prognosis today
options.rationale: Rescue cerclage between 16 and 27+6 weeks with dilated cervix and no infection or contractions can prolong pregnancy and improve neonatal survival; NICE and RANZCOG support offering it after counselling. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

options.text: Arabin pessary placement alone with outpatient review at the local unit and no admission or antibiotics
options.rationale: Pessary evidence is mixed and inferior to cerclage in dilated cervix with prolapsed membranes; outpatient management at this stage is unsafe due to imminent labour risk. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

options.text: Give IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and antibiotics but no cerclage because membranes are prolapsed
options.rationale: Prolapsed membranes without rupture are not an absolute contraindication to rescue cerclage; refusing cerclage on that basis alone forgoes the intervention with best chance to prolong pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

explanation.summary: Rescue cervical cerclage between 16 and 27+6 weeks is offered for painless cervical dilation with prolapsed membranes in the absence of infection, ruptured membranes, contractions, or fetal compromise. It can prolong pregnancy by several weeks and improve neonatal survival. Progesterone treats a short cervix on ultrasound. Pessary evidence is weaker than cerclage for this indication.
key_points: Rescue cerclage: cervix dilated, membranes prolapsed, no infection or labour, 16 to 27+6 weeks
Vaginal progesterone is for short cervix on scan, not dilated cervix
Absolute contraindications: infection, ruptured membranes, active labour, fetal compromise
Counsel about risks of infection and iatrogenic membrane rupture
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG cites rescue cerclage prolonging gestation by around 4 to 6 weeks on average and increasing 34-week delivery from around 20 to over 60 percent; McDonald technique is standard, avoid Shirodkar in the emergency setting.

sources.label: NICE Preterm Labour and Birth NG25

subtopic_detail: Painless bleed at 32 weeks with an unknown placental site
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an outer metropolitan hospital reviewing a 33 year old G3P2 at 32 plus 3 weeks who presents with a single episode of painless bright red vaginal bleeding of around 200 mL after intercourse 1 hour ago. She has no contractions and reports normal fetal movements. Her booking ultrasound at 20 weeks reported a low placenta but a follow-up scan was cancelled by the patient. Blood group is O positive and no antibodies. Her previous births were vaginal at term with no complications.

On arrival she is calm and haemodynamically stable and the CTG is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9
data_table.Abdominal examination: soft non-tender uterus, fetus longitudinal with cephalic presentation, no palpable contractions
data_table.CTG: baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140 pregnancy), platelets 232 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 5.1 g/L, group and hold sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment step?

options.text: Perform a gentle bimanual digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before any imaging
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound because it can precipitate torrential haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)
