options.text: Give a stat course of steroids with IV oxytocin infusion to induce labour and expedite delivery given the bleed
options.rationale: There is no indication for expedited delivery in a haemodynamically stable mother with reassuring CTG at 32 weeks before the placental site is defined; oxytocin risks massive haemorrhage if praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Arrange transabdominal followed by transvaginal ultrasound to locate the placenta before any digital examination
options.rationale: Painless antepartum haemorrhage with a documented low placenta at 20 weeks and no repeat scan must be evaluated with ultrasound; transabdominal then transvaginal is safe with a well-defined technique and defines placenta praevia or accreta prior to any speculum or digital examination. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Perform an urgent Kleihauer-Betke test and administer anti-D within the next 4 hours before proceeding to imaging
options.rationale: The mother is Rh D positive, so anti-D is not indicated; Kleihauer is used in Rh D negative women or for suspected large feto-maternal haemorrhage volume estimation, not first-line here. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Discharge home once bleeding stops as the CTG is reassuring and she has stable observations at present time
options.rationale: Even a small antepartum haemorrhage from suspected praevia can herald a larger sentinel bleed; admission for further imaging, steroids if praevia confirmed, and observation is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Painless antepartum haemorrhage in the third trimester requires placenta praevia to be excluded before any digital vaginal examination. Transabdominal ultrasound with transvaginal follow-up is safe and defines placental edge relative to the internal os. If praevia is confirmed at 32 weeks, admit, give a course of antenatal corticosteroids, cross-match blood, and plan elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks unless bleeding forces earlier delivery. Screen for placenta accreta spectrum in women with prior caesarean.
key_points: Painless APH: exclude praevia before digital examination
TAUS then TVUS is safe and accurate
Steroids for lung maturity 24 to less than 34 weeks
Anti-D if Rh D negative; Kleihauer to quantify large FMH
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG lower placental edge threshold for praevia is any placental tissue within 2 cm of the internal os on TVUS in the third trimester; edges 2-5 cm from os are termed low-lying and may allow vaginal birth after individualised review.

subtopic_detail: OGTT cut-offs at 24-28 weeks and treatment escalation
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar reviewing a 34 year old G2P1 at 27 plus 2 weeks in a suburban tertiary hospital antenatal clinic. She had gestational diabetes controlled with diet alone in her first pregnancy and delivered a 4.1 kg baby at term. Her booking BMI is 31. She has completed a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 4 days ago. She is otherwise well and taking pregnancy multivitamins and iodine. She has no known thyroid disease and no family history of type 1 diabetes.

Her capillary fasting sugar this morning was 4.9 mmol/L.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.1 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Ultrasound (26 weeks): estimated fetal weight 70th centile, normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure her the OGTT is within normal limits and no gestational diabetes intervention is required at this time
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L and 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L both exceed ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds for GDM; the diagnosis is made and further management is required. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence dietary review and 4 times daily self monitoring of blood glucose
options.rationale: ADIPS thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5) diagnose GDM if any one is met or exceeded; first-line management is dietary modification with SMBG four times daily (fasting plus 1 or 2 hour postprandial), progressing to metformin or insulin if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line pharmacotherapy for gestational diabetes
options.rationale: First-line is diet and exercise with SMBG; pharmacotherapy is added when 1 to 2 weeks of dietary modification fails to achieve fasting <5.0 and 1 hour postprandial <7.4 (or 2 hour <6.7). (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Commence long acting insulin glargine 10 units nocte immediately given the previous large baby history and BMI
options.rationale: Insulin is added when dietary measures fail targets; jumping to insulin before a trial of diet plus SMBG is not the AU pathway even with risk factors for macrosomia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Repeat the 75 g OGTT at 32 weeks with random blood glucose in between to confirm diagnosis is accurate
options.rationale: A single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds diagnoses GDM; repeating the OGTT delays management and is not indicated. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

explanation.summary: Australian gestational diabetes diagnosis follows ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher (any one). Management starts with dietitian-led carbohydrate distribution and glucose monitoring four times daily. Targets are fasting under 5.0, 1 hour postprandial under 7.4, or 2 hour under 6.7. Pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks or if fetal macrosomia develops. Metformin and insulin are both first-line pharmacotherapy in Australian practice.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds diagnose GDM on any one abnormal value
Diet plus SMBG four times daily is first-line
Metformin or insulin added if fasting >=5.0 or 1 hour >=7.4
Universal 75 g OGTT screening at 24 to 28 weeks in AU
explanation.pearls: ADIPS uses a lower fasting cut-off than the WHO 1999 criteria (5.1 vs 7.0 mmol/L), yielding higher diagnostic rates; treatment reduces macrosomia and shoulder dystocia but effect on caesarean rate is modest.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic escalation after atony with a bleeding volume over 1.5 L
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 29 year old G1P1 who delivered a 4.0 kg male vaginally 25 minutes ago after a 90 minute second stage requiring vacuum assistance for maternal exhaustion. Estimated blood loss is 1.5 L and continues briskly. Bimanual compression is being maintained by the senior midwife. The placenta was delivered complete on the placenta tray. The uterus feels soft and boggy above the umbilicus. She has a history of essential hypertension on lifestyle measures only, controlled at booking.

IV oxytocin 10 units has been given and a further infusion is running.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Access: two large bore IVs, warm crystalloid running, cross-match sent
data_table.Uterine tone: soft, boggy above umbilicus despite bimanual compression
data_table.Prior medication: IV oxytocin 10 units bolus given, oxytocin infusion running at 40 mU/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and repeat the dose in 15 minutes if the uterus remains atonic
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disease because of severe hypertensive crisis risk; the RANZCOG PPH pathway skips ergometrine and moves to carboprost in hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately as the second line uterotonic escalation therapy step
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is an important step once uterotonics have failed but comes after the second uterotonic escalation; it is not the first response to persistent atony while carboprost remains an option. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: IM carboprost 250 micrograms and IV tranexamic acid 1 g with a second dose in 30 minutes if bleeding continues
options.rationale: With ergometrine relatively contraindicated in hypertension, next-line is IM carboprost 250 mcg (repeatable every 15 min to 2 mg total) plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g given within 3 hours; TXA reduces mortality per WOMAN trial. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Give sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms as the next line agent while awaiting theatre transfer arrangements
options.rationale: Misoprostol is used where injectable agents unavailable or as adjunct; carboprost is more potent and preferred where available with an IV in place, particularly with hypertension precluding ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Transfer to theatre immediately for hysterectomy given the ongoing bleeding despite the uterotonic given so far
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the last resort after failed uterotonics, tamponade, brace suture, and interventional radiology; a second uterotonic and TXA are earlier steps in the escalation pathway. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony is managed with a stepwise combination of resuscitation and uterotonics. First-line is oxytocin (10 units IM or IV bolus plus infusion). Second-line depends on comorbidity: ergometrine 250 mcg IM/IV is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; carboprost 250 mcg IM is the alternative and repeatable to 2 mg total; misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual is an adjunct where injectables are limited. IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours reduces bleeding-related mortality (WOMAN trial). Failure to control bleeding prompts intrauterine balloon tamponade, then brace sutures, uterine artery ligation or embolisation, and hysterectomy as last resort.
key_points: Oxytocin first, then carboprost if ergometrine contraindicated
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours in all cases
Escalate to tamponade, brace suture, embolisation, hysterectomy
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
explanation.pearls: Carboprost is a synthetic 15-methyl PGF2 alpha; contraindicated in active asthma because of bronchospasm risk; requires refrigeration; peak effect within 20 minutes.

subtopic_detail: Emerging chorioamnionitis at 30 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27 year old G1P0 at 30 plus 4 weeks who was admitted 4 days ago after confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. She has completed a course of betamethasone and is on oral erythromycin. Today she reports mild lower abdominal discomfort intermittently and offensive smelling liquor since this morning. Fetal movements are reduced compared to yesterday. She has no vaginal bleeding.

Her temperature has risen this shift; the midwife has just recorded a further rise now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4, fetal heart rate 172
data_table.Abdomen: uterus soft, palpable irregular contractions 1 in 10 minutes with mild tenderness
data_table.CTG: baseline 172, minimal variability, no decelerations, no accelerations for 30 minutes
data_table.Bloods: white cell count 18.6 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0 pregnancy), CRP 84 mg/L (<5), lactate 2.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Continue oral erythromycin, hydrate with IV fluid, and add IV paracetamol with reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia (maternal and fetal), raised inflammatory markers, uterine tenderness, and offensive liquor meet clinical chorioamnionitis criteria; oral macrolide alone is inadequate and delaying delivery risks maternal sepsis and fetal death. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Commence IV broad spectrum antibiotics and expedite delivery with neonatal team standby for the delivery event
options.rationale: Clinical chorioamnionitis mandates IV broad spectrum antibiotics (typical AU regimen ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and expedited delivery irrespective of gestation because ongoing infection worsens neonatal and maternal outcomes; neonatal team standby is essential at 30 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Give a second course of betamethasone and plan tocolysis with nifedipine to reach 32 weeks before delivery is planned
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in chorioamnionitis; a second course of steroids is not appropriate when the priority is delivery to reduce maternal and fetal harm from ongoing sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Perform an urgent amniocentesis to obtain amniotic fluid culture before deciding on delivery timing today
options.rationale: Amniocentesis in overt clinical chorioamnionitis delays definitive management; clinical criteria are sufficient to start antibiotics and expedite delivery without waiting for culture. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Discharge home with oral amoxicillin and clindamycin and daily antenatal review until 34 weeks completed for delivery
options.rationale: Discharge with oral antibiotics is unsafe in overt chorioamnionitis; the patient requires IV antibiotics and delivery in a facility with neonatal intensive care support. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever plus at least two of maternal tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, and maternal leukocytosis. Management is IV broad spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin plus gentamicin, adding metronidazole or clindamycin for anaerobic cover post-caesarean) and expedited delivery regardless of gestation because expectant management increases neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy, and maternal septic shock. Tocolysis is contraindicated. Vaginal birth is preferred unless obstetric indications require caesarean.
key_points: Fever plus two of: mat/fetal tachycardia, tender uterus, offensive liquor, leukocytosis
IV amp + gentamicin + metronidazole is typical AU regimen
Expedite delivery; do not tocolyse
Neonatal team standby for early onset sepsis
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE II arm found erythromycin (not amoxicillin with clavulanic acid) reduces neonatal composite morbidity in PPROM without chorioamnionitis; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in PPROM increased necrotising enterocolitis so amoxicillin plus clavulanate is avoided in this setting.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

subtopic: Pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic kidney disease
subtopic_detail: Diagnosis when baseline proteinuria confounds standard cut-offs
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 35 year old G2P1 at 33 plus 2 weeks with known IgA nephropathy and baseline proteinuria of around 500 mg per 24 hours pre-pregnancy on losartan (ceased pre-pregnancy). Her booking BP was 128/82. Today her BP is repeatedly 156/104 and she reports 2 days of frontal headache and blurring on the peripheries of vision. She has right upper quadrant discomfort and mild ankle swelling. Her creatinine baseline was 92 micromol/L pre-pregnancy.

Her partner has cared for their first child at home and asks whether she must stay in hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 158/104 (repeated 156/102), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 92), ALT 68 U/L (<40), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36)
data_table.Urine: protein-to-creatinine ratio 92 mg/mmol (baseline 55, threshold for pre-eclampsia >30)
data_table.Fetal: estimated fetal weight 15th centile, growth crossing centiles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Give a course of steroids for fetal lung maturity and defer delivery until 37 weeks to reach term status
options.rationale: Steroids are appropriate but deferring delivery to 37 weeks with severe features (visual symptoms, thrombocytopenia, LFT derangement, growth restriction) risks eclampsia, HELLP progression, and placental abruption; delivery is timely after stabilisation, typically within 24-48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Restart losartan for baseline renal protection alongside oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily and outpatient BP diary
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios); outpatient management is unsafe with severe features. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Give oral prazosin 500 micrograms three times daily as blood pressure control while continuing routine antenatal visits
options.rationale: Prazosin is a second or third-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral symptoms needs immediate parenteral or oral rapid-acting therapy (labetalol IV or nifedipine IR) and admission, not outpatient escalation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Discharge home with 4 hourly self BP monitoring and daily fetal movements diary and specialist review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharging severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms and fetal growth restriction is unsafe; the risk of eclampsia, stroke, and placental abruption mandates admission. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Admit for oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release, IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, and delivery planning
options.rationale: Severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms, thrombocytopenia trend, rising creatinine above baseline, raised ALT, fetal growth restriction, and proteinuria more than doubled from baseline meets superimposed pre-eclampsia with severe features; treatment is BP control (labetalol or nifedipine IR), magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/h, and delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Superimposed pre-eclampsia on chronic hypertension or chronic kidney disease is diagnosed when new severe hypertension emerges after 20 weeks with new organ dysfunction (thrombocytopenia under 150, creatinine above baseline, ALT/AST above 2x normal, cerebral or visual symptoms, pulmonary oedema) or a doubling of the baseline proteinuria plus new organ dysfunction. Severe features mandate admission, BP control with oral nifedipine IR, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g loading dose over 20 min then 1 g per hour), and timely delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity are appropriate 24 to less than 34 weeks.
key_points: Superimposed pre-eclampsia: new organ dysfunction on chronic HTN/CKD
Treat severe HTN: nifedipine IR, labetalol IV, hydralazine IV
MgSO4 4 g load then 1 g/h for seizure prophylaxis
ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: MgSO4 toxicity signs: loss of patellar reflex (first), respiratory depression, then cardiac; calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution IV is the antidote; monitor reflexes, respirations, and urine output rather than levels in most units.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines Hypertension in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Suspicion during spontaneous rupture with fetal distress
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a busy labour ward. A 32 year old G2P1 at 38 plus 3 weeks with a known velamentous cord insertion on 20 week ultrasound is in early labour at 3 cm dilated. The midwife has just performed an artificial rupture of membranes given inadequate contractions on syntocinon; there is a moderate amount of dark red blood immediately noted with the fluid. The CTG which was previously reassuring now shows sinusoidal pattern with baseline 100. Her observations are stable.

The attending consultant is scrubbed in theatre with another patient.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 120/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9, fetal HR 100 sinusoidal
data_table.Blood loss: moderate bright red with fluid at ARM, ongoing
data_table.Access: IV in situ with crystalloid running
data_table.Prior imaging: velamentous cord insertion documented at 20 weeks, no repeat targeted vasa praevia scan performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give an IV tranexamic acid 1 g bolus and IV fluid resuscitation to control maternal bleeding source volume
options.rationale: The bleeding is fetal, not maternal; tranexamic acid does not treat fetal blood loss and delays definitive delivery which is the only intervention that saves the fetus. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Stop syntocinon and reposition mother left lateral with oxygen by facemask and reassess CTG in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is appropriate for hypertonic decelerations but sinusoidal pattern with maternal bleeding at ARM signals fetal exsanguination; delay of 15 minutes risks fetal death, not category 1 caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Take an Apt test on the vaginal blood specimen to determine whether the blood is maternal or fetal in origin
options.rationale: Apt or Kleihauer testing is diagnostically supportive but takes time; sinusoidal CTG with bleeding at ARM in a known velamentous insertion is treated as vasa praevia and delivered immediately. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Perform an urgent transvaginal ultrasound to demonstrate vessel over the internal os before mobilising theatre
options.rationale: Ultrasound confirms vasa praevia prospectively but is not the correct step during acute rupture with fetal compromise; the diagnostic pathway is clinical and delivery is immediate. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Prepare for immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia while continuously monitoring fetal heart
options.rationale: Vaginal bleeding at rupture of membranes with sinusoidal CTG in a woman with velamentous cord insertion is vasa praevia rupture with fetal exsanguination; category 1 caesarean under general anaesthesia (fastest to delivery) with paediatric team standby is life-saving. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes unprotected fetal vessels traversing the membranes near the internal os, unsupported by cord or placental tissue. Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, low-lying or bilobed placenta, and multiple pregnancy from IVF. Antenatal diagnosis by TVUS with colour Doppler allows planned elective caesarean at 35-36 weeks. Undiagnosed vasa praevia presents with bleeding at rupture of membranes and rapid fetal decompensation (sinusoidal CTG or bradycardia) because fetal blood volume is around 250-300 mL; delivery must occur within minutes. Category 1 caesarean is life-saving; general anaesthesia is often quickest.
key_points: Velamentous cord and low placenta are the main risks
Antenatally diagnosed: planned CS at 35-36 weeks
Bleeding at ARM plus sinusoidal CTG: immediate CS
Fetal survival depends on delivery within minutes
explanation.pearls: Sinusoidal CTG has a smooth undulating baseline of 5-15 bpm amplitude with 3-5 cycles/min for at least 20 minutes and no accelerations; it reflects severe fetal anaemia (haemorrhage, alloimmunisation, feto-maternal haemorrhage).

subtopic: Postpartum haemorrhage with placenta accreta spectrum
subtopic_detail: Unexpected accreta at caesarean in a Jehovah's Witness declining blood products
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional tertiary hospital assisting a category 2 caesarean at 38 weeks in a 38 year old G4P3 with 2 previous caesareans and a documented low-lying anterior placenta. During delivery of the placenta there is dense adherence, unresponsive to gentle traction; there is now torrential haemorrhage with an estimated 1.8 L blood loss over 4 minutes and uterus not contracting despite oxytocin and carboprost. She is a Jehovah's Witness who declined all blood products in a written advance directive countersigned during antenatal clinic, though has accepted cell salvage.

The consultant obstetrician and haematologist have been called in and are 10 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 15 L Hudson, temperature 36.3
data_table.Bloods (pre-op): haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 210 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 3.8 g/L, INR 1.1
data_table.Advance directive: declines packed cells, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate; accepts cell salvage, recombinant factor concentrates, tranexamic acid
data_table.Uterine tone: atonic despite oxytocin and 500 mcg carboprost given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue oxytocin and carboprost with warmed crystalloid resuscitation and await consultant arrival before further step
options.rationale: Waiting 10 minutes with ongoing 1.8 L loss in a patient who refuses transfusion is unsafe; cell salvage should be activated immediately along with IV TXA 1 g and mechanical control (uterine compression, aortic compression, balloon) plus preparation for hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and observe for 30 minutes while awaiting the consultant obstetrician arrival
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is an option but relying on it alone with ongoing torrential bleeding from placenta accreta in a patient refusing blood is inadequate; cell salvage, TXA, aortic compression, and prompt hysterectomy planning are required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Give O negative packed cells 2 units and fresh frozen plasma while continuing uterotonics as haemodynamic support
options.rationale: The patient has an explicit written advance directive refusing donor blood products; overriding a competent adult's directive is unlawful and unethical, even in emergency. (Source: NHMRC Advance Care Planning)

options.text: Activate cell salvage, give IV tranexamic acid 1 g, apply aortic compression, and prepare for hysterectomy urgently
options.rationale: Refractory PPH with atony and adherent placenta with 1.8 L loss in a patient refusing donor blood requires simultaneous cell salvage activation, IV TXA 1 g, mechanical control (bimanual and aortic compression, balloon), and immediate progression to hysterectomy given placenta accreta spectrum and patient's advance directive limiting bridging measures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Give recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms per kg IV as first-line pharmacological adjunct to achieve haemostasis now
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is a salvage adjunct when fibrinogen and platelets are adequate and bleeding persists; it is not first-line before mechanical control, TXA, and cell salvage. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum in the presence of prior caesareans plus placenta praevia is a high-risk situation for massive haemorrhage; hysterectomy is often the definitive treatment when conservative approaches fail. In a Jehovah's Witness with a valid advance directive refusing donor blood products, the patient's autonomy must be respected and management planned around blood conservation. Accepted strategies include intraoperative cell salvage, IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours, meticulous surgical haemostasis, recombinant factor concentrates, and early hysterectomy rather than protracted conservative attempts. Uterine artery embolisation and internal iliac ligation are alternatives where accessible. Discussion of the advance directive should occur antenatally and be re-documented.
key_points: PAS spectrum needs multidisciplinary planning antenatally
Respect valid advance directive: no donor blood
Cell salvage plus TXA plus early hysterectomy is the pathway
Recombinant factor VIIa is salvage adjunct, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Cell salvage in obstetrics is safe when a leukocyte depletion filter is used to remove amniotic fluid contaminants; anti-D is required for Rh D negative women receiving Rh D positive salvaged blood, and the volume returned can be dose-guided by Kleihauer testing.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic timing after prelabour rupture of membranes at term in a colonised woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a healthy 32 year old primigravida at 40 weeks and 1 day. Her waters broke clear four hours ago at home and she has just presented to the birth suite with mild irregular tightenings. Her routine 36 week vaginal-rectal swab returned Group B streptococcus positive. She has no reported drug allergies and has had a normal pregnancy.

Examination confirms speculum-visible clear liquor and a cephalic presentation at station -2 with a closed and posterior cervix.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Fetal: cardiotocograph normal, baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Membrane status: ruptured at home 4 hours ago, clear liquor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until active labour is established and expectant management for up to 96 hours after rupture is complete
options.rationale: GBS-positive women receive intrapartum antibiotics from the time of PROM at term, not only in established labour. Expectant management beyond 24 hours in a GBS-positive woman substantially increases neonatal early-onset GBS sepsis risk. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g stat then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth and plan for induction of labour if not established within 24 hours of rupture
options.rationale: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS guidance recommends IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly for all women with GBS colonisation at any point of labour (or ruptured membranes) at term. Induction of labour is offered from the outset for term PROM to reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin 500 mg eight-hourly and reassess in the morning if labour has not established with membrane-rupture rounding to 12 hours
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin achieves inadequate intra-amniotic concentrations; intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is IV, not oral. Delaying by hours in a GBS-positive PROM woman is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

options.text: Perform an emergency category-2 caesarean section to avoid vaginal GBS exposure to the neonate in this colonised woman in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean. Antibiotic prophylaxis during vaginal birth is standard care and reduces early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis to below 0.5 per 1000 births. Caesarean carries substantially higher maternal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

options.text: Give a single stat dose of IV cefazolin 2 g and manage as expectant until spontaneous labour without further antibiotic doses
options.rationale: Adequate GBS prophylaxis requires a loading dose followed by regular dosing until birth (penicillin four-hourly, cefazolin eight-hourly). A single dose is inadequate. Cefazolin is reserved for low-anaphylaxis-risk penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

explanation.summary: Australia uses risk-based and universal-screening GBS prophylaxis policies depending on jurisdiction; where universal screening is done, the swab is collected at 35-37 weeks. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth. Adequate prophylaxis is at least 4 hours before birth, though any exposure confers some benefit. For non-anaphylaxis penicillin allergy, IV cefazolin 2 g then 1 g eight-hourly. For anaphylaxis-risk penicillin allergy with unknown susceptibility, IV vancomycin or clindamycin (if susceptible). Term PROM with GBS colonisation is an indication for immediate antibiotic commencement and induction rather than prolonged expectancy.
key_points: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g Q4H until birth
GBS-positive term PROM = antibiotics + induction
Adequate prophylaxis is ≥4 hours pre-birth
Non-anaphylaxis allergy: cefazolin; anaphylaxis: vancomycin/clindamycin
GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean
explanation.pearls: Late preterm PROM (34-36+6 weeks) with GBS-positive status also warrants immediate benzylpenicillin plus induction unless steroids are indicated; delaying birth in preterm PROM is a distinct decision balanced against pulmonary maturity.

subtopic_detail: Applying RANZCOG criteria for medical management with methotrexate
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment clinic reviewing a 28 year old para 1 with a positive urine pregnancy test and mild left iliac fossa discomfort for two days. Her last menstrual period was seven weeks ago. She has never had abdominal surgery. Her preferences discussed include a strong wish to avoid surgery if a safe alternative is available.

She is haemodynamically stable and reliable for daily blood tests and outpatient monitoring within a metropolitan area.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Abdomen: mild tenderness left iliac fossa, soft, no peritonism
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus with thickened endometrium; 2.2 cm mass in left adnexa without fetal cardiac activity; free fluid nil to trace in pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG monitoring only, no intervention unless symptoms worsen or bhCG rises
options.rationale: Expectant management is appropriate for very low bhCG (usually under 1000 IU/L) with a falling trend, minimal symptoms, no visible mass or trophoblast on scan. bhCG of 3400 with a visible 2.2 cm adnexal mass exceeds this threshold. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy on the next available emergency list given the presence of an adnexal mass on ultrasound
options.rationale: Salpingectomy is indicated for haemodynamic instability, mass over 3.5 cm, bhCG over 5000 IU/L, fetal cardiac activity or failed methotrexate. This patient meets criteria for medical management which is safer and preserves the tube. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and day 7 bhCG monitoring and clear return-if-worse advice
options.rationale: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: stable patient, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, no significant pain, no significant free fluid, no contraindications (normal renal, hepatic, haematological function, not breastfeeding, no folate replacement), reliable follow-up. This patient meets every criterion. Single-dose regimen is standard AU practice, with bhCG measured pre-treatment, day 4 (peak) and day 7 (expected 15 percent fall), then weekly to undetectable. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m2 on day 0 and day 4) as the standard Australian protocol in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Australian standard practice is a single-dose regimen with success rate around 88 percent for bhCG under 5000. A second dose is given if bhCG has not fallen by 15 percent between days 4 and 7. Routine day-0-and-day-4 dosing is a different (multi-dose) protocol used less commonly. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Direct methotrexate injection into the adnexal mass under transvaginal ultrasound guidance in theatre today
options.rationale: Direct intralesional methotrexate is not standard AU practice and offers no advantage over systemic IM administration in eligible patients with tubal ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy are: haemodynamically stable, no fetal cardiac activity, unruptured, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, no significant pain, minimal free fluid, no contraindications (normal renal, hepatic, haematological function; not breastfeeding; no folate supplements or immunosuppression; no active peptic ulcer), and reliable follow-up. The single-dose regimen is 50 mg/m2 IM, with bhCG day 0, day 4 and day 7. If bhCG has fallen ≥15 percent between day 4 and 7, weekly bhCG to undetectable. If not, second dose. Persistent trophoblast rates require weekly bhCG to zero over ~4 to 8 weeks. Give anti-D 250 IU IM if rhesus negative.
key_points: MTX criteria: stable, no FCA, <3.5 cm, bhCG <5000, no pain/fluid/contraindications, reliable follow-up
Single-dose 50 mg/m2 IM, day 4 and day 7 bhCG
≥15% fall day 4-7 = weekly bhCG to zero; <15% = second dose
Surgical management for bhCG ≥5000 IU/L or fetal cardiac activity
Give anti-D if rhesus negative and bleeding or MTX given
explanation.pearls: A woman treated with methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy should avoid conception for at least 3 months due to teratogenic risk and take a folate-free multivitamin during that interval; folate rescues methotrexate and reduces efficacy in the acute treatment window.

subtopic_detail: Simultaneous BP control and eclampsia prophylaxis at term
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old primigravida at 37 weeks and 3 days referred from her GP with a severe frontal headache and blurring of vision. She has no known chronic hypertension. On triage her BP is elevated and repeat readings 10 minutes apart confirm the finding.

She describes epigastric discomfort and reports reduced fetal movements today.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 178/116 (repeat 172/114), respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Reflexes: brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus bilaterally
data_table.CTG: baseline 145, reduced variability 3-5 beats, no decelerations, no accelerations over 20 min
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 88 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and admit for 24 hour observation with delivery deferred pending response to oral therapy in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Oral methyldopa is a maintenance agent for mild to moderate hypertension with slow onset (2-4 hours). Severe pre-eclampsia with BP ≥160/110 requires IV control within minutes to reduce stroke risk; oral first-line here is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg with a 4 g IV magnesium sulfate loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion, and prepare for expedited birth after obstetric consultant review
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at term with signs of severe features (BP ≥160/110, symptoms, hyperreflexia with clonus, biochemical abnormality, fetal compromise) demands immediate parallel control of BP and eclampsia prophylaxis. IV labetalol 20 mg (then 40 mg, then 80 mg every 10 min to max 220 mg) or hydralazine 5 mg is the first-line antihypertensive; magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hr is the eclampsia prophylaxis. At 37 weeks with severe features, expedited birth is indicated. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg and reassess in 15 minutes before starting magnesium sulfate given the risk of neuromuscular blockade combination
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled BP drop and is not standard; oral immediate-release nifedipine (not sublingual) is a valid option. Magnesium is given in parallel, not delayed - drug interaction is manageable clinically. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Administer IV furosemide 40 mg to offload volume and reduce blood pressure via preload reduction before more targeted antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Pre-eclamptic women are intravascularly depleted despite oedema. Furosemide worsens uteroplacental perfusion and is only indicated for confirmed pulmonary oedema, never for BP control in pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Empirical diazepam 10 mg IV over 5 minutes as eclampsia prophylaxis followed by BP monitoring every 15 minutes without antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclampsia prophylaxis and treatment (MAGPIE and Eclampsia Trial). Diazepam is not standard AU therapy. BP still needs treating. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by BP ≥160/110 or by any milder BP with severe features (persistent neurological symptoms, epigastric pain with hepatic tenderness, low platelets, hepatic transaminase elevation, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, or fetal compromise). Management is parallel BP control (IV labetalol 20-80 mg or hydralazine 5-10 mg, or oral nifedipine 10-20 mg immediate release), eclampsia prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate (4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/hr, 24 hours post-birth or last seizure), and expedited birth at ≥37 weeks. Fluid balance is meticulous - total fluids restricted to 80 mL/hr and total input under 2500 mL/24 hr - because pulmonary oedema kills.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP ≥160/110 OR severe features
IV labetalol/hydralazine + magnesium sulfate + expedited birth ≥37/40
Magnesium: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/hr, continue 24 hr post-birth
Fluids restricted (~80 mL/hr max, <2500 mL/24 hr) to prevent pulmonary oedema
Do not use furosemide for BP control - only for pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity monitoring: loss of patellar reflex (~4 mmol/L), respiratory depression (~5 mmol/L), cardiac arrest (~7 mmol/L); antidote is 1 g IV calcium gluconate slow injection.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and delivery decision at late-preterm gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29 year old para 2 at 34 weeks and 5 days referred by her midwife with two days of malaise and right upper quadrant pain. Her BP has crept up over the last week from 130/80 to 148/98 today. She had no problems in prior pregnancies. She has had no bleeding.

She describes a heavy sensation in the epigastrium and one episode of vomiting overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 100, blood pressure 148/98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Abdomen: tender right upper quadrant, no guarding, uterus 34 cm SFH, cephalic, longitudinal, fetal heart 148
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 285 U/L (<40), AST 340 U/L (<40), LDH 720 U/L (<250), bilirubin 32 micromol/L, film shows schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart with plan for birth after the second dose in an unhurried elective caesarean or induction
options.rationale: In HELLP with worsening features, delivery should not routinely be delayed 48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids because maternal deterioration risk (hepatic haematoma rupture, DIC, eclampsia) is high. If a short window is safe (12-24 hours) and clinical picture is stable, a single dose may be given while planning birth, but full 48 hour delay is not appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Transfuse two units of platelets prophylactically to bring the count above 100 and defer delivery decisions for 48 hours
options.rationale: Prophylactic platelet transfusion in HELLP is not indicated except for active bleeding or preparation for surgery/regional anaesthesia in a patient at <50 x10^9/L. Delaying delivery based on the platelet count worsens outcomes because HELLP typically continues to progress until birth. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly outpatient bloods and BP monitoring until 37 weeks aiming for spontaneous labour
options.rationale: HELLP is a life-threatening variant of severe pre-eclampsia with maternal mortality up to 4 percent; expectant outpatient management is contraindicated. Delivery is definitive; delay increases hepatic rupture, DIC and eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Perform an emergency category-1 caesarean section within 30 minutes irrespective of fetal status or cervical favourability
options.rationale: Category-1 caesarean is reserved for immediate threat to maternal or fetal life. Here, the mother is stable and the fetus is reassuring; delivery within 24-48 hours after stabilisation is safer than crash surgery in a coagulopathic patient. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

options.text: Admit, commence IV magnesium sulfate, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM (first of two doses), plan birth within 24 to 48 hours by the safest route
options.rationale: This is HELLP syndrome (haemolysis with schistocytes, LDH >600, elevated liver enzymes >70, platelets <100). At 34+5 with stable maternal status but worsening laboratory features, admit, start magnesium for eclampsia prophylaxis, give one antenatal corticosteroid dose, and plan birth within 24-48 hours. Route of delivery is guided by cervical favourability and fetal status. Multidisciplinary involvement (obstetrics, anaesthetics, haematology, neonatology) is essential. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe form of pre-eclampsia occurring in around 10 to 20 percent of severe pre-eclampsia cases. Diagnostic thresholds (Mississippi/Tennessee) include LDH >600 U/L or bilirubin >20 micromol/L with schistocytes, AST/ALT >70 U/L, and platelets <100 x10^9/L. Delivery is definitive. Beyond 34 weeks, deliver within 24-48 hours after stabilisation. Between 24 and 34 weeks, if maternal and fetal condition permit, give 48 hours of corticosteroids before delivery; if unstable, deliver sooner. Magnesium sulfate is used for eclampsia prophylaxis and continued for 24 hours postpartum. Complications include hepatic haematoma or rupture, DIC, acute kidney injury and abruption.
key_points: HELLP: LDH >600, AST/ALT >70, platelets <100 with schistocytes
Beyond 34/40 - deliver within 24-48 hours after stabilisation
Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis (24 hr postpartum)
Route by cervical favourability and fetal status - not automatic caesarean
Watch for hepatic rupture, DIC, AKI, abruption
explanation.pearls: Persistent HELLP over 72 hours postpartum should prompt consideration of thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes (aHUS, TTP, pregnancy-associated TMA), which require ADAMTS13 testing and complement studies plus a haematology consult.

subtopic_detail: Sequence of first-line manoeuvres when the anterior shoulder is impacted
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar attending a vaginal birth for a 35 year old para 2 who is being managed by the midwife. The last pregnancy had a birth weight of 4.1 kg with a difficult delivery. Second stage has lasted 90 minutes and the head is now born but retracts against the perineum. Restitution has not occurred. The midwife has already made a call for help and started the buzzer.

The next contraction is expected in about 40 seconds and you have declared shoulder dystocia to the team.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips onto the abdomen combined with a request to apply routine fundal pressure to expel the shoulder
options.rationale: McRoberts is correct but fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated - it worsens shoulder impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture and neonatal injury. Suprapubic pressure is the correct adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement followed by emergency caesarean section as the first response to declared shoulder dystocia in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort rescue after failed internal manoeuvres, associated with high fetal and maternal morbidity. It is never the first response. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Deliberate downwards traction on the fetal head with strong maternal pushing to attempt to disimpact the anterior shoulder immediately in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Increased downward traction on the head is the direct cause of brachial plexus (Erb's palsy) and clavicular injury in shoulder dystocia. Routine axial traction only is applied; force is never the answer. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Immediate deliberate fracture of the anterior clavicle to reduce shoulder diameter and permit delivery within the next contraction cycle in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Cleidotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre used only when all first- and second-line approaches have failed and there is no other route. Attempting fracture as first-line is inappropriate and unnecessarily traumatic. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips and suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally by an assistant while you attempt gentle axial traction with the next contraction
options.rationale: The Australian HELPERR/RANZCOG sequence starts with McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips to flatten the sacrum and rotate the pubic symphysis cephalad) plus suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally to dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubis. Only routine axial traction is applied; excessive downward traction risks brachial plexus injury. If unsuccessful within 30 seconds, proceed to internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is declared when routine axial traction fails to deliver the shoulders after birth of the head. The RANZCOG HELPERR sequence is: Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic - downward and lateral), Enter (internal rotational manoeuvres - Rubin II or Woods screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin all-fours). Each step is given 30 seconds before escalating. Force is not the answer - do not apply excessive traction, do not apply fundal pressure. Cleidotomy, symphysiotomy or Zavanelli manoeuvre are last resort. Team communication and clear time-stamped documentation are essential.
key_points: HELPERR: Help, Evaluate episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin)
Never apply fundal pressure - worsens impaction
Only routine axial traction - excessive traction causes brachial plexus injury
30 seconds per manoeuvre before escalating
Time-stamped documentation and post-event debrief mandatory
explanation.pearls: The posterior arm delivery (Menticoglou manoeuvre) has the highest success rate of the internal manoeuvres and should be the primary internal step when first-line external manoeuvres fail in most contemporary AU teaching.

subtopic_detail: Combining latency antibiotics, corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection at extreme preterm gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 26 year old primigravida at 24 weeks and 3 days who presents with a gush of clear fluid and continued leaking. Speculum examination confirms pooling of amniotic fluid. She is afebrile and not contracting. She is very keen for everything possible to be done to give her baby a chance.

Her BMI is 22 and there is no history of urinary or genital infection during this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Speculum: pooling of clear amniotic fluid; cervix closed, long, no bleeding
data_table.CTG (variocam): baseline 145, variability appropriate for gestation, no contractions palpable
data_table.Ultrasound: single fetus 24+3, EFW 610 g, cephalic, AFI 4.2 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management bundle to commence in the next hour?

options.text: Immediate expedited birth by classical caesarean section at 24+3 given the extreme preterm gestation and risk of chorioamnionitis with expectant management in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Expectant management is offered at 24+3 without evidence of infection or fetal compromise, with continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis and fetal wellbeing. Immediate delivery of a 610 g fetus has extremely poor outcomes without the benefit of corticosteroids or magnesium. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Latency amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 500/125 mg orally three times daily plus dexamethasone 12 mg IM stat and admission for observation only, without magnesium sulfate in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated in PPROM because of the necrotising enterocolitis signal from the ORACLE I trial - erythromycin is the correct AU choice. Magnesium neuroprotection is offered under 30 weeks per AU guidance and is a critical omission here. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally loading dose then 20 mg six-hourly for tocolysis and betamethasone alone; no antibiotics until symptomatic or biochemistry abnormal in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Tocolysis has no proven benefit in PPROM (it may prolong latency briefly but does not improve neonatal outcome) and can mask chorioamnionitis. Latency antibiotics improve neonatal outcomes and are not withheld until infection is manifest. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Latency erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM stat (first dose), and IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for neuroprotection while awaiting neonatology counselling
options.rationale: PPROM at 24+3 without infection warrants latency antibiotics (erythromycin - not amoxicillin with clavulanic acid which increases necrotising enterocolitis risk per ORACLE trial), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection where delivery is anticipated within 24 hours before 30 weeks (Australian NNS/AAGBI recommendation extends to 30 weeks with MAGENTA data). Neonatology counsels the mother about survival and morbidity at extreme preterm gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Reassure and discharge home with weekly outpatient bloods and ultrasound; no admission or intervention required in the absence of infection or contractions in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: PPROM at extreme preterm gestation warrants inpatient admission for daily observation of temperature, uterine tenderness, CTG and inflammatory markers, and readiness to expedite birth for chorioamnionitis. Outpatient management is not standard AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: PPROM before 24 weeks carries very poor prognosis - counsel about the futility threshold with neonatology involvement. Between 24 and 34 weeks, expectant inpatient management is standard, with latency antibiotics (erythromycin, 10 days), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone), and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection where delivery is likely within 24 hours (under 30 weeks in Australian guidance). Continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis (temperature, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, rising inflammatory markers, purulent discharge) mandates expedited birth. Tocolysis is not standard. Beyond 34 weeks, expectant management for GBS-negative women is reasonable to 37 weeks; GBS-positive women deliver at 34-36 weeks.
key_points: Erythromycin (NOT amoxicillin with clavulanic acid - NEC risk) for 10 days latency
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 (24 hr apart) or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x 4 (12 hr apart)
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection <30 weeks when delivery imminent
Inpatient surveillance for chorioamnionitis; deliver if infection develops
Tocolysis is not standard in PPROM
explanation.pearls: For PPROM approaching 34 weeks, the PPROMT trial supports expectant management to 37 weeks in GBS-negative women without infection, but jurisdictional practice varies; GBS-positive PPROM at 34 weeks typically triggers delivery with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

subtopic_detail: Surgical management decision when the contralateral tube is already absent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old para 1 presenting with acute right iliac fossa pain and lightheadedness. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is positive. She had a right ruptured tubal ectopic three years ago managed by right salpingectomy. This morning she completed her family planning with her partner, who was hoping for a second child but is prepared to accept whatever is safest for her.

On ultrasound the current pregnancy is in her only remaining tube.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Abdomen: peritonism localised to left iliac fossa, mild rebound
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with fetal cardiac activity present, moderate haemoperitoneum in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Prior surgical history: right salpingectomy 3 years ago for ruptured ectopic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingotomy to preserve the only remaining fallopian tube, accepting the associated 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast risk
options.rationale: In a woman with a prior contralateral salpingectomy, the remaining tube is her only conduit for spontaneous conception, but the risk of recurrent ectopic in the SAME tube after salpingotomy is 15-20 percent, plus persistent trophoblast requiring further treatment. Contemporary RANZCOG and international consensus favour salpingectomy in this specific scenario because ART (IVF) bypasses the tube entirely and salpingotomy leaves a damaged residual tube that dominates recurrence risk. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Systemic methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM as the definitive treatment given the wish to preserve tubal function for future spontaneous pregnancy
options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated - fetal cardiac activity is present, bhCG exceeds 5000 IU/L, there is significant haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic instability. Immediate operative management is mandatory. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with counselling that IVF is the recommended route to future pregnancy, given that the residual tube carries a high recurrence risk
options.rationale: In a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy, salpingectomy of the affected tube is preferred over salpingotomy because the recurrent-ectopic risk in the same (damaged) tube outweighs the loss of tubal fertility, and IVF bypasses the tubal factor entirely. This trickiness pattern (T14 historical bilaterality flip) inverts the standard 'preserve the tube' teaching. Counsel about IVF pathways preoperatively. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Emergency laparotomy with left oophorectomy in addition to salpingectomy to remove any ovarian source of the pregnancy in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Oophorectomy is not indicated in tubal ectopic pregnancy. Laparotomy versus laparoscopy is a decision based on stability and surgeon skill; laparoscopy is preferred if stable and appropriately equipped. Preserving the ovary is important for future ART cycles. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Ultrasound-guided direct methotrexate injection into the ectopic sac followed by monitoring, avoiding surgical trauma to the last remaining tube
options.rationale: Direct intralesional methotrexate is not standard practice and is contraindicated in unstable patients with active bleeding. Surgery is mandatory given haemoperitoneum, fetal cardiac activity, and haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The decision between salpingotomy and salpingectomy in tubal ectopic pregnancy hinges on the state of the contralateral tube. If the contralateral tube is healthy, salpingotomy preserves natural fertility potential and is preferred if surgeon-appropriate. If the contralateral tube is absent or diseased, contemporary evidence favours salpingectomy of the affected tube: the recurrent-ectopic risk in a damaged residual tube is high, persistent trophoblast complicates salpingotomy in 5-15 percent, and IVF bypasses tubal factors entirely with acceptable success. This inverts the intuitive 'preserve the tube' response. Preoperative counselling should explicitly discuss the IVF pathway.
key_points: Salpingotomy = preserved contralateral tube; salpingectomy = absent/damaged contralateral tube
Salpingotomy carries 5-15% persistent trophoblast + 15-20% recurrent ectopic in same tube
IVF bypasses tubal factor entirely - acceptable path to conception
Fetal cardiac activity, bhCG >5000, haemoperitoneum = surgery, not methotrexate
Counsel about IVF preoperatively when salpingectomy is planned
explanation.pearls: In tubal ectopic managed by salpingotomy, weekly bhCG monitoring to undetectable is mandatory - persistent trophoblast requires additional single-dose methotrexate or repeat surgery if bhCG plateaus above 5 IU/L.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between uterine artery embolisation and peripartum hysterectomy after failed conservative surgery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in theatre with the consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist and haematologist for a 36 year old primipara who has bled 3.4 L after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, carboprost 250 micrograms IM x3, and rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms) have failed. Bimanual compression and an intrauterine balloon achieved partial slowing. A uterine artery ligation with a B-Lynch brace suture has just been placed and bleeding continues at ~200 mL/5 min.

The interventional radiology suite is 15 minutes away and staffed within the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 82/48 on noradrenaline 8 microgram/min, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98% on 15 L NRB, temperature 35.8
data_table.Coagulation: fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (1.5-4.0), INR 1.6, platelets 78 x10^9/L, thromboelastography reduced maximum amplitude
data_table.Transfusion: 4 red cells, 4 FFP, 1 cryoprecipitate given; MHP activated 20 minutes ago
data_table.Airway: intubated after fifth unit red cells for ongoing haemorrhage
data_table.Family: primigravida, expressed wish for future pregnancy antenatally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses in total while awaiting the interventional radiology team
options.rationale: Carboprost has already been given at appropriate intervals with failure; escalating to further doses in a decompensating patient causes bronchospasm and hypertension without meaningful additional haemostatic effect. Definitive intervention is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Immediate intra-hospital transfer to interventional radiology for bilateral uterine artery embolisation as a fertility-preserving definitive intervention
options.rationale: Uterine artery embolisation is fertility-preserving and effective (85-95 percent success) but requires a haemodynamically stable patient who can tolerate the transfer and procedure. This patient is coagulopathic, hypothermic, requiring rising vasopressors, and bleeding ~200 mL every 5 minutes; transferring to the radiology suite risks decompensation in transit and delays definitive haemostasis. UAE is indicated for controlled ongoing bleeding in a stabilised patient, not for exsanguinating haemorrhage in theatre. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII (NovoSeven) 90 micrograms/kg as the next haemostatic intervention prior to surgical escalation
options.rationale: rFVIIa is an off-label rescue therapy considered only after correction of pH, temperature, calcium and fibrinogen and after all surgical options have been exhausted. It is expensive, prothrombotic (thromboembolic events 5-10 percent), and does not substitute for definitive surgical control. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Insert a second intrauterine balloon at higher inflation volume alongside the existing balloon to increase tamponade pressure
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is a single-device therapy; over-inflation risks uterine rupture and cervical injury. Sequential attempts at conservative measures that have already failed waste time in a decompensating patient. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

options.text: Proceed immediately to peripartum hysterectomy given failure of all conservative measures and ongoing life-threatening haemorrhage
options.rationale: In refractory PPH with ongoing haemorrhage, escalating vasopressor need, coagulopathy and hypothermia, the priority is definitive haemostasis over fertility preservation. Peripartum hysterectomy is the appropriate life-saving step when the patient is already in theatre, intubated, coagulopathic and continuing to bleed. Transfer to interventional radiology in an unstable coagulopathic patient with continuing 200 mL every 5 minutes bleeding introduces unacceptable risk. The RANZCOG PPH stepwise pathway explicitly places hysterectomy as the final surgical option and time-to-decision is a mortality determinant. Fertility conversations occurred antenatally but survival dominates in decompensated shock. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG PPH management follows a stepwise algorithm: uterotonics, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, examination for genital tract trauma or retained products, bimanual compression and intrauterine balloon, uterine artery ligation and B-Lynch or similar compression suture, then uterine artery embolisation (if stable and transfer feasible) or peripartum hysterectomy. Each step is time-critical - PPH deaths cluster in the second hour of bleeding, and delay in progressing to definitive surgery is a modifiable mortality determinant. UAE is fertility-preserving but requires haemodynamic stability. Hysterectomy is the definitive intervention when the patient is exsanguinating, coagulopathic, and already in theatre - fertility conversations, however important, do not override the immediate need for survival.
key_points: PPH pathway: uterotonics → TXA → tamponade → suture → UAE/hysterectomy
UAE requires stability; hysterectomy for exsanguinating decompensation
Coagulopathy + hypothermia + rising vasopressor need = surgical control now
rFVIIa is last-resort adjunct AFTER surgical control
Time-to-definitive-haemostasis is a mortality determinant
explanation.pearls: Massive transfusion protocol activation aims for 1:1:1 red cells:FFP:platelets with fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate 3-4 g when fibrinogen <2 g/L), calcium replacement, and active warming; permissive hypotension is a trauma concept and does not apply to peripartum haemorrhage where uteroplacental perfusion needs pressure.
